eliot-george-mill-on-floss-1860:
George Eliot published The Mill on the Floss in 1860, her most autobiographical novel of a brother and sister. Maggie Tulliver's passionate, doomed devotion to her brother Tom drives the tale of a miller's family. Eliot drew Maggie from herself, the clever girl of a provincial world too narrow for her mind and heart.

Maggie, bookish and intense, is judged by a town that prizes her brother's plodding respectability over her gifts. The Tullivers lose the mill in a lawsuit, and Tom's vow of repayment rules the family's pinched, bitter years at home. Maggie's loves, Philip Wakem and Stephen Guest, end in scandal, renunciation, and a flood that joins brother and sister in death. In their deaths they were not divided, says the tombstone, in Eliot's most quoted epitaph. The novel's psychology of provincial life remains unmatched in English fiction.
emerson-conduct-of-life-1860:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published The Conduct of Life in 1860, his late essays on practical philosophy. The set treats fate, power, wealth, and culture in Emerson's most aphoristic and worldly manner of writing. It was his best-selling book in his lifetime, read as a guide to action and character.

Fate grants that heredity and circumstance bind us, then bids thought build altars to them in freedom. Power and Wealth praise energy and economy while warning what each costs the soul that serves them. Culture and Behavior polish the rough individualism of the early essays for society and city life in America. Worship closes the book with a call to moral sentiment over creed, rite, and church form in religion. Mature readers often rank this autumnal volume as Emerson's wisest and most usable work.
europmc-pmc10182360:
Liu and a large team review immunosenescence, the aging of the immune system, in a 2023 paper. As people grow old, their immune defenses weaken in known ways. Infections hit harder, vaccines work less well, and the risk of cancer and chronic disease climbs, while a low level of inflammation runs in the background.

The review explains the molecular changes behind this decline, in both the fast innate defenses and the slower learned ones. It links those changes to the diseases of old age. It also surveys treatments that aim to restore youthful immune function.
europmc-pmc10287560:
Nassiri and a large trial team report a phase one and two trial of a virus therapy plus an immune drug in recurrent glioblastoma, in a 2023 study. Glioblastoma is a fast-growing brain tumor that nearly always returns after standard care. The treatment paired DNX-2401, a virus engineered to attack tumor cells, with pembrolizumab, a drug that frees the immune system.

The virus was injected into the tumor, followed by the immune drug. The paper reports safety and survival results for the combination. The approach tests whether a virus can turn a cold tumor hot for immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc10420560: Victorian doctors tested a barely-there anaesthetic dose as a cure, and this paper shows their practical results. The faint treatment, tried on patients. The article preserves that old clinical experiment. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc1043860:
Brennecke and co-authors set out the rules in 2005 for how a microRNA finds its target gene. A microRNA is a short RNA piece that does not build a protein. It binds a gene message and dials that gene down. How exact that match must be was still unclear at the time.

The team split target sites into two broad classes. In one class, a strong match at the microRNA's head end suffices, with weak pairing at the tail. In the other class, a weak head match needs a strong tail match to work. Genome-wide data backed both classes in real genes. Each microRNA holds about 100 target sites on average, Brennecke found.
europmc-pmc10477960:
The GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis Collaborators counted the world burden of osteoarthritis from 1990 to 2020. Osteoarthritis is the most common joint disease in adults. It wears down joint tissue, causing chronic pain and loss of movement. It strikes most often after age 40 and climbs steeply with age.

In 2020, 595 million people had the disease, 7.6% of the world population. Case counts had risen 132.2% since 1990. The study covers hand, hip, knee, and other joint sites in 204 nations. Forecasts run to 2050, with knee cases set to rise 74.9%. For people aged 70 and over, the disease ranked seventh as a cause of years lived with disability.
europmc-pmc11164360:
Open2C presents a toolkit that turns raw DNA reads into chromosome contact maps in this 2024 paper. Hi-C and related methods reveal how chromosomes fold by recording which DNA regions touch. These methods pour out massive, varied sequencing data. Turning reads into contact pairs needs fast and flexible processing.

Their suite, pairtools, splits the job into modular command-line steps that can be chained into pipelines. Core steps parse alignments into pairs, sort them, and remove duplicate copies made during copying of DNA. Extra tools handle filtering, quality control, and pair editing. Benchmarks against popular pipelines showed gains in speed and flexibility, the authors report. Special tools cover cut-based protocols, single-cell Hi-C, and maps split by parent of origin. The suite plugs into Python analysis libraries.
europmc-pmc11631760:
Guzman and a large team present an ultra-fast method for measuring proteins by mass spectrometry in this 2024 paper. Mass spectrometry weighs molecules to identify and quantify the full protein set of a sample, its proteome. Speed and coverage usually trade off against each other. Their strategy, called narrow-window data-independent acquisition, pairs high-resolution survey scans with very fast fragment scans.

A new analyser scans fragments at about 200 per second with high accuracy, they report. The setup profiles over 100 full yeast proteomes per day. For human samples it reaches about 10,000 protein groups in half an hour, or about 7,000 proteins in five minutes. That is three times the coverage of the current state of the art. Pre-separated samples give comprehensive human proteome coverage in about three hours. Quantitative precision was shown on a three-species mixture.
europmc-pmc1185560:
Hausdorff wrote a 2005 overview of gait variability, the small changes from stride to stride. Walking looks steady, yet each step differs a bit. Those small shifts can reveal aging and disease effects. They may also track how well therapy or rehab works.

Past work ties stride shifts more closely to falls than average speed does. The overview gathers nine reports on fresh findings. Topics span wearable sensors, math models, and animal studies. One study shows dim light slows some walkers and unsettles others. Hausdorff frames stride shifts as a rich health signal.
europmc-pmc1713260:
Detecting family structure in gene data lacked a formal test of significance. Patterson, Price, and Reich supplied one in 2006, placing principal components analysis on solid statistical ground. The method compresses genetic variation into axes that reveal population splits.

Their theory uncovered a phase change in detectability. Below a threshold of divergence, structure in a fixed data set is essentially invisible. A little above the threshold, detection becomes easy. The flip lets researchers predict how much data a study needs to find structure. Patterson turns a descriptive plot into a testable claim about populations.
europmc-pmc1769360:
Children as young as five can report their own quality of life soundly. Varni, Limbers, and Burwinkle tested that claim in 2007 in 8,591 children aged 5 to 16, using the same PedsQL survey given to parents in a companion study.

Even the youngest children left few items blank. Most self-report scales in each age group, including age five, passed the 0.70 reliability standard. Total scores approached or passed 0.90, the bar for judging single patients. Validity checks held as well. Varni argues the results support hearing the child's own voice in trials, not only the parent's.
europmc-pmc1821060:
Rusch, Venter and co-authors reported in 2007 the main haul of the Global Ocean Sampling expedition aboard Sorcerer II. The ship collected surface water microbes along a transect of several thousand kilometers. The route crossed the North Atlantic, passed through the Panama Canal, and ended in the South Pacific.

Shotgun sequencing of those samples produced 7.7 million reads totaling 6.3 billion DNA letters. A few major microbe groups dominated the surface ocean niche. Still, the data held great diversity: 85 percent of assembled sequence was unique at a strict 98 percent identity cutoff, as was 57 percent of the unassembled data. The team also built new methods for assembly and for comparing genomes across samples. Sample metadata, such as location and conditions, anchored those comparisons.
europmc-pmc1868760:
Montanini, Chalot and co-authors sorted in 2007 a family of proteins that ferry heavy metals across cell membranes. The CDF family, short for cation diffusion facilitator, occurs in bacteria, archaea, fungi, plants, and animals. Its members matter for human health and for cleaning polluted land with microbes or plants.

The team gathered family members from all three domains of life and aligned their sequences. The alignment sharpened the family's signature pattern, the fingerprint used to spot new members in genomes. Tree building split most members into three groups matching the metal each carries: zinc alone, iron with zinc, or manganese. A new member's metal can thus be guessed from its branch. Mutating conserved building blocks in one member tested which spots set that selectivity.
europmc-pmc2124860: A medical paper on malarial pigment, its nature and mode of production. The fever's dark stain. This article preserves that parasitology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2125960: A medical paper on the factors concerned in the appearance of nucleated red blood corpuscles. The nucleated reds again. This article preserves that hematology. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2128360: A medical paper with studies on changes produced by roentgen rays in inflamed connective tissue. The irradiated tissue. This article preserves that radiology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131060: A medical paper on the soluble specific substance of Friedlander's bacillus, paper two, chemical. The Klebsiella chemistry. This article preserves that biochemistry. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131260: A medical paper on the mechanism of the serum sensitization of acid-fast bacteria. The sensitized TB. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131560: A medical paper on the functional and pathological response of the kidney in dogs subjected to a procedure. The dog kidneys. This article preserves that nephrology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
europmc-pmc2131660: A medical paper on the fate of tubercle bacilli in the organs of reinfected rabbits. The TB's return. This article preserves that bacteriology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2140660: A biology paper on the combination of salts and proteins. The salty proteins. This article preserves that biochemistry. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2140760: A biology paper on time relations of growth, genetic growth constants of animals, the growth math. This article preserves that biology. It awaits future readers. History keeps its place secure. It is kept for readers to consult. It is kept for study by scholars.
europmc-pmc2169260:
Tugwell and co-authors described OMERACT in 2007, an international network improving outcome measurement in rheumatology. OMERACT began informally in 1992, after European and North American rheumatoid arthritis trials used different endpoints, making results hard to compare. The network holds consensus conferences every two years around the globe. Expert working groups prepare data-driven recommendations, including core measure sets for major rheumatic conditions.

An executive committee chairs the network, and patients have joined the process actively since 2002. Conferences use evidence reviews, small-group debate and electronic voting to reach majority agreement. The first 1992 meeting in Maastricht aimed to agree a minimum outcome set for all rheumatoid arthritis trials. It also weighed what size of difference clinicians judge important. The authors stress that a trial's credibility stands or falls with its endpoints.
europmc-pmc2180260: A medical paper on the skin response of rabbits to non-hemolytic streptococci, attempts to desensitize. The rabbit skin again. This article preserves that immunology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2211560:
Cloughesy and a large team tested the drug rapamycin in 2008 in patients with recurrent glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour. Preclinical work suggested tumours lacking the suppressor PTEN are sensitive to blocking mTOR, a growth-control protein that rapamycin targets. This proof-of-concept Phase I trial gave daily rapamycin before surgery. It aimed to check safety, tumour drug levels, and whether cell growth slowed in PTEN-deficient tumours.

Drug levels inside every tumour were enough to inhibit mTOR in lab tests, but actual inhibition varied widely between patients. Cell proliferation fell dramatically in seven of fourteen patients after one week. That drop tracked the degree of mTOR inhibition, not drug concentration. Tumour cells from non-responders stayed drug-sensitive outside the body, so resistance was not cell-intrinsic. Rapamycin also activated Akt in seven patients, and that activation linked to faster progression later.
europmc-pmc2242660:
Kreike and co-workers profiled 97 triple-negative breast cancers in 2007, tumours lacking estrogen, progesterone and HER2 markers. This subtype is aggressive and lacks targeted treatments. The team generated gene-expression profiles using 35,000-probe microarrays. They also characterised the tumours by tissue examination and staining, and linked features to clinical outcomes, especially spread to distant sites.

Every triple-negative tumour classified as basal-like by its expression profile, making the two terms effectively synonymous here. Clustering still split them into five distinct subgroups, showing internal diversity. Two tissue features predicted freedom from distant metastasis. A large amount of infiltrating lymphocytes gave a hazard ratio of 0.30, and absence of central fibrosis gave 0.14 on the same scale. Both confidence intervals excluded no effect. The analysis was multivariable and covered a tumour series from the Netherlands.
europmc-pmc2376960:
Forrest and colleagues built a simple blood-based score for lung cancer outlook in 2003. The patients had inoperable non-small-cell lung cancer, the common form, which usually cannot be cured. Standard outlook measures lean on cancer stage and how active a patient is, both partly matters of judgement.

Their score combined albumin, a blood protein that falls when patients are run down, with C-reactive protein, a marker of body-wide inflammation. Together they predicted survival about as well as stage plus fitness combined. The score's hazard ratio was 1.70 in their analysis, against 1.48 for the standard pairing, and both links were statistically firm. The authors stressed the practical edge: both blood tests are cheap, routine, and measured the same way everywhere, unlike fitness ratings that vary between doctors.
europmc-pmc2377260:
Zhang and Rothenbacher reviewed how common chronic kidney disease is worldwide in 2008. Chronic kidney disease means lasting kidney damage or weak filtering, and it raises the risk of kidney failure and heart disease. Counts depend heavily on which formula doctors use to estimate filtering from a blood test.

They gathered 26 population studies using one standard definition, with samples from 237 to 65,181 people. The median rate was 7.2% among adults aged 30 and over. Among people aged 64 and older, rates ran far higher, from 23.4% to 35.8% across studies. The newer MDRD formula had become the favourite tool over the older Cockcroft-Gault method. The authors warned that detection stays weak in older people, women, and some ethnic groups.
europmc-pmc2475660:
Fazekas and co-authors tested candidate DNA barcodes for land plants in 2008. Animal barcoding works well with one standard gene, but plants lacked an agreed region. The team compared eight regions from the plastid genome, the small DNA set inside plant chloroplasts, plus one from the mitochondria, across 251 samples.

The samples covered 92 species in 32 diverse plant genera, including several taxonomically tricky groups. Single regions resolved between 7% and 59% of species as clean separate groups, with a spacer region called trnH-psbA the best single marker. Getting the sequences at all varied: one gene, matK, needed ten primer pairs to reach 88% recovery. Combining four to seven regions lifted resolution only to 69% to 71%, barely above good two-region mixes. The authors said practical ease of recovery deserves as much weight as raw variability.
europmc-pmc2478660:
Andersson and colleagues mapped three related RNA-binding proteins across human tissues in 2008. The proteins, FUS, EWS, and TAF15, form the FET family. They were first found through the broken fusion genes they create in sarcomas and leukaemias, and they help run gene expression and message processing.

All three appeared in cell nuclei in nearly every tissue, each with its own pattern. FUS and TAF15 also sat in the cell body fluid of most cell types, while EWS showed there mainly in secretory cells. Levels fell as embryonic stem cells matured, and two fully mature cell types, pigment cells and heart muscle, had none at all. Under heat or oxidative stress the proteins moved into stress granules, packets where the cell parks its messages. FUS needed its RNA-binding region for that move. The authors said these are specialised players, not housekeeping constants.
europmc-pmc2547860:
Bionaz and Loor charted in 2008 which genes switch on and off as a cow's udder makes milk fat across a lactation cycle. The molecular control of milk fat was largely unknown, so the team measured 45 genes tied to fat building and release in mammary tissue. Samples ran from late pregnancy through the end of the following lactation, alongside milk fat composition.

Genes for pulling fat from blood, building new fat, and packaging it into droplets all rose sharply during lactation. One gene, INSIG1, climbed more than twelvefold, while SREBF1, long cast as the master switch, barely doubled, challenging its central role. The most abundant gene measured was SCD, which softens fats. The authors propose a network model in which PPARG, PPARGC1A, and INSIG1 jointly steer milk fat synthesis.
europmc-pmc2568860:
Kiebel, Daunizeau, and Friston proposed in 2008 that the cortex is organised as a hierarchy of time scales mirroring the world it tracks. Fast levels handle fleeting sensory detail, while higher levels follow slow changes in context under which the fast details unfold. The paper first presents a mathematical model of this sensory encoding.

In the model, slowly shifting neuronal states track the trajectories of faster sensory states, proving the scheme can work in principle. The authors then review brain evidence fitting the idea. A cortical area's time scale, they argue, can be read from its position along a front-to-back gradient of distance from the primary sensory areas. The framework explains prefrontal cortex functions as operations on slowly changing representations, and it yields testable predictions.
europmc-pmc2642860:
Shanks, Greek, and Greek argued in 2009 that animal tests used to predict drug effects in people rest on weak ground. Their essay works as science philosophy. It asks what the word predict should mean. It then checks whether animal models meet that standard in drug safety testing and disease research.

Judged against clear standards, the authors say, the models fall far short. They point to deep differences between species in how genes are switched on and off, and in body chemistry shaped by evolution. Such gaps, they argue, mean a drug that is safe or harmful in an animal may behave quite differently in a person. They accept that animals serve science in many other ways, but deny that prediction of human response is one of them.
europmc-pmc2714960:
Marcusson, Frimodt-Møller, and Hughes tested in 2009 how resistance to fluoroquinolone drugs affects the fitness of E. coli bacteria. These drugs block two enzymes that manage DNA coiling during copying. High resistance needs several mutations, and some of those changes were known to slow growth, which should favor fitter mutants over time.

They built strains with up to five resistance mutations and raced them in lab and in animals. Some mutations did cut fitness sharply. Yet adding a fourth mutation in the parC gene to a weak triple mutant raised fitness greatly and cut drug sensitivity at the same time. Without any drug present, selection still favored those less sensitive mutants.
europmc-pmc2739160:
Almén, Nordström, Fredriksson, and Schiöth mapped in 2009 the human membrane proteome. That is all proteins that sit in cell membranes, where most drug targets live. They mined the full human protein set with three helix-prediction tools, removed duplicates against the genome, and clustered the rest into families that they curated by hand against many databases.

They identified six thousand seven hundred eighteen membrane proteins and classified most into two hundred thirty-four families. Receptors, transporters, and enzymes formed the largest functional groups, while about forty-one percent were singletons with no family match. Membrane proteins made up an estimated twenty-seven percent of all human proteins. Shapes differed by job: most transporters span the membrane many times, while most enzymes cross it once.
europmc-pmc2784760:
Frank-Cannon, Alto, McAlpine, and Tansey reviewed in 2009 whether neuroinflammation fans the flame in neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and multiple sclerosis. The brain was once thought immune-privileged, yet it mounts its own inflammatory responses. A short-lived response after infection, trauma, or stroke activates microglia, the resident immune cells, then settles. Trouble starts when activation never switches off.

Chronic neuroinflammation keeps microglia switched on for years. They steadily release cytokines and chemokines, signal molecules that recruit still more microglia. Harmful oxygen-based stress builds in the same loop. The review lays out the hallmarks of acute and chronic responses, and explains why microglia sit at a crossroads where diverse insults meet. It then weighs population, drug, and genetic evidence tying this smoldering inflammation to the diseases. That slow burn is what sets these diseases apart from a brief infection of the brain.
europmc-pmc2795760:
Wallace, Schmid, Lau, and Trikalinos introduced Meta-Analyst in 2009, a free program for meta-analysis, the method that pools results from many studies into one answer. Most researchers then ran such work in general statistics packages or in costly dedicated tools.

The program runs models for yes-or-no outcomes, measured outcomes, and tests that judge how well a diagnosis works, in both standard and Bayesian styles. It also runs cumulative and leave-one-out analyses, which show how the pooled answer shifts as studies arrive or drop out. Users can edit the forest plots it draws and export results as images or documents. The team checked its math against a standard package across thousands of published reviews from the Cochrane Library, and the numbers matched.
europmc-pmc2814860:
Prasanna, Gopalakrishnan, Shankar, and Vasandan compared stem cells from two sources in 2010 under inflammatory attack. Mesenchymal stem cells can dampen immune responses, a talent that makes them candidates for cell therapy. Cells from Wharton jelly, the cord tissue around umbilical blood vessels, are easier to get than bone marrow cells and grow faster.

Two inflammatory signals, interferon gamma and TNF alpha, did not strip either cell type of its calming effect. Cord cells suppressed immune cell growth more strongly in most tests. The two sources also leaned on different calming tools, with distinct levels of an enzyme called IDO and two secreted factors. Inflammation reshaped each source in its own way, the team concludes.
europmc-pmc2829060:
Grönke, Clarke, Broughton, Andrews, and Partridge mapped the evolution and jobs of fruit fly insulin-like peptides in 2010. These seven signals, called DILPs, drive growth, metabolism, reproduction, and lifespan through one shared pathway. The team compared the genes across twelve fly species and knocked out each gene in the standard lab fly.

The seven genes split apart before the species did, and membership stayed stable, hinting their jobs are guarded by selection. Knockouts showed the peptides backing each other up and covering for losses. Removing DILP2 lengthened life, removing DILP6 shrank growth, and removing brain peptides lengthened life only when a partner bacterium called Wolbachia was present. Losing brain peptides also blocked responses to diet restriction.
europmc-pmc2848560:
Sionov, Lee, Chang, and Kwon-Chung uncovered in 2010 how the yeast Cryptococcus neoformans survives fluconazole, the drug used long-term against its deadly brain infections in AIDS patients. Some strains grow despite drug levels that should stop them, a puzzle called heteroresistance. Using genome scans and gene counting, the team compared resistant and normal strains of both major types.

Resistant cells carried extra copies of whole chromosomes. Chromosome one doubled first; higher drug doses doubled more chromosomes, and tolerance rose with each extra copy. Removing the drug let cells shed the copies and regain sensitivity. Chromosome one holds both the drug's target gene and a drug pump gene, explaining the trick as a reversible copy-number dodge.
europmc-pmc2874360:
Dutil and a national surveillance team warned in 2010 that an antibiotic used in Canadian chickens was breeding drug resistance in a salmonella strain that also infects people. The strain, Salmonella Heidelberg, ranks among the top causes of salmonella illness in Canada and turns invasive more often than most. About nine in a hundred lab isolates came from blood, a sign of severe disease.

Resistance to ceftiofur, a farm drug related to front-line human antibiotics, turned up in bacteria from both chicken meat and sick people with matching patterns. The overlap points to poultry as a route to human cases that are harder to treat. Using the drug in chickens may blunt the whole antibiotic family for human medicine, the authors caution, which argues for tighter farm use.
europmc-pmc2898760:
Wang and colleagues assembled in 2010 the first broad gene catalogue of the whitefly Bemisia tabaci, a sap-sucking pest that devastates crops worldwide and spreads hundreds of plant viruses. Almost nothing was known of its genes for development, insecticide resistance, or virus carriage. With no genome to read against, they stitched its transcriptome, the full set of active messages, together from scratch using short sequencing reads.

One run produced tens of millions of reads that assembled into well over one hundred thousand unique sequences, ten times everything previously deposited for this insect. Tens of thousands matched known proteins and were annotated by function. Comparing life stages with digital expression counting flagged genes tied to development and to insecticide resistance, ready-made targets for pest science.
europmc-pmc2965160:
Saederup and colleagues built glow-tagged mice in 2010 to track immune cells entering the inflamed brain and spinal cord. Monocyte groups marked by two different docking proteins are hard to tell apart inside tissue, and reagents for one marker were missing.

Their mice glow red where one marker appears and green where the other does. In a model of multiple sclerosis, the red-marked inflammatory monocytes needed their marker to gather inside the cord coverings. Surprisingly, neutrophils largely replaced a quieter monocyte group when the marker failed. The tags finally separate invading cells from resident brain defenders.
europmc-pmc3010660:
Rastogi and co-authors reviewed how ultraviolet light damages DNA and how living things repair it, in a 2010 article. Sunlight's UV-B band creates fused bases, altered photoproducts, and strand breaks that can mutate or kill cells, a threat growing as the ozone layer thins.

Organisms answer with a conserved toolkit. It includes light-driven reversal and cutting out damaged patches from one strand or both. It also fixes mismatches. Across breaks it rebuilds by copying a sister strand or joining ends. Checkpoints pause growth and, failing repair, ordered cell death removes the danger. The review organises each lesion with its matching repair routes.
europmc-pmc3016360:
Sinka and a large team mapped the dominant malaria-carrying mosquitoes of Africa, Europe, and the Middle East in a 2010 article, the second of a three-part world series. Africa bears most malaria partly because its Anopheles gambiae complex is so effective at passing the parasite to people.

Gathering records from literature and other sources, they built a database of thousands of geo-referenced sites for seven African species and six more across Europe and the Middle East. Combined with expert judgement, the records became distribution maps plus summaries of each species' habits. The resource targets control planning and alerts about malaria returning to Europe.
europmc-pmc3026760:
Félix and a large team announced in 2011 the first natural viruses found infecting tiny roundworms in the wild. Worms gathered from rotting fruit in France showed damaged gut cells, yet no bacteria or fungi explained the harm. Two new viruses were identified, one in each of two closely related worm species. Both resemble a known family of small RNA viruses.

Infection spread from worm to worm through contact, and some worm strains resisted better than others. Infected worms mounted a defense using small RNA molecules, showing that this system fights viruses in nature. One source strain turned out to be poor at that defense. The discovery gives biologists a complete, natural host and virus pair. They can now study every step of infection and immunity in a simple animal.
europmc-pmc3035360:
Mogi and Kuwano reviewed in 2011 the role of one damaged guardian gene in the most common form of lung cancer. The gene, called TP53 in short, normally stops faulty cells from growing, and it is altered in many human cancers. The review focuses on non small cell lung cancer, which makes up about four fifths of lung cancers and is becoming more common.

Studies link changes in this gene to worse outlook for patients and to weaker responses to chemotherapy and radiation. The authors work through how the gene fails, how often it fails in this cancer, and what that means for care. Understanding the failure could guide treatments aimed at the exact defect. Such targeted care, they argue, offers the best hope of raising survival in this disease.
europmc-pmc3050760:
Bosl, Tierney, Tager-Flusberg, and Nelson explored in 2011 whether the complexity of a baby's brain waves can flag early risk for autism. They recorded resting brain activity from infants who had an older sibling with autism, and from typically developing infants, between six months and two years of age. A complexity measure that tracks signal richness across time scales was used to train a computer classifier.

The complexity path over age differed between the two groups, with the clearest gap around nine to twelve months. At nine months the classifier sorted infants into the right group with high accuracy, and for boys the accuracy was near perfect at that age. Results for girls peaked earlier and faded sooner. The authors present this as a proof of principle. An early, brain based marker could one day trigger support long before behavior raises concern.
europmc-pmc3052360:
Zhu and coauthors took in 2011 a brute force approach to finding every protein that one pneumonia bacterium injects into host cells. Legionella pneumophila lives inside cells and uses a molecular syringe to send in effector proteins that remodel the host. Earlier hunts had relied on shared features of known effectors, which may have biased what was found. This team instead tested nearly every uncharacterized gene in the genome, one by one.

They attached a reporter tag to each candidate and measured whether it crossed into mammal cells through the syringe system. The sweep confirmed many known effectors and added seventy new ones, lifting the confirmed total to well over two hundred fifty. Studying the tails of the new proteins showed the syringe accepts a wider range of signals than expected. The catalog gives researchers a fuller parts list for studying how this pathogen takes over cells.
europmc-pmc3101260:
Marchesi and colleagues produced in 2011 the first detailed map of how gut bacteria differ between colon tumors and the healthy tissue beside them. Bacteria are increasingly implicated in starting and feeding bowel cancer. The team deep sequenced bacterial genes from tumor tissue and matched normal lining taken from the same patients. That gave a side by side comparison free of most person to person noise.

Tumors formed a distinct niche. They consistently hosted more of one bacterial group known for living on mucus, plus several species usually classed as friendly probiotics. Meanwhile, bacteria suspected of helping trigger the disease were scarcer on tumors than expected. The authors suggest the tumor's changed chemistry recruits bacteria that forage well there, displacing the possible early culprits. The map points toward microbe based diagnostic tests, and perhaps toward treatments that reshape the tumor niche.
europmc-pmc3136460:
Livia Vastag and colleagues watched two related herpesviruses rewire cell chemistry in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. Viruses must borrow the host cell's energy and building blocks to copy themselves. Using mass measurement tools, the team tracked hundreds of small molecules in infected skin and lining cells over time.

Both viruses changed cell chemistry strongly, and each kept its own style across cell types. One virus sped up sugar burning and flooded its central energy cycle to feed fat building. The other fed the same cycle by a side route that supports making DNA building blocks. Current drugs attack DNA building for both viruses; the split suggests the first virus may be better fought at other chemistry points.
europmc-pmc3145960:
Konstantina Skourti-Stathaki, Nicholas Proudfoot, and Natalia Gromak dissected how human genes switch off cleanly in a 2011 paper in Molecular Cell. After copying a gene into RNA, the copying machine must stop and let go. Behind the machine, the fresh RNA can stick back onto the DNA, forming tangles that are common at pause points rich in one DNA letter.

A protein called senataxin, tied to two nerve-degeneration diseases, unwinds those tangles. Clearing them lets a chewing enzyme reach the RNA tail and destroy it, which knocks the copying machine off the gene. Without the unwinding, termination falters. The study names the tangle and its removal as core steps in ending gene copying, linking a basic process to human disease.
europmc-pmc3176260:
John Cole and colleagues scanned the genomes of American Holstein cows for links to thirty-one dairy traits in a 2011 paper in BMC Genomics. Knowing which regions govern milk output, health, fertility, and body shape sharpens breeding choices. The analysis used predicted transmitting abilities, the standard merit scores, across the national herd.

Strong signals clustered in sensible places. A known fat gene region governed milk fat share, a growth region yields, and one chromosome stretch affected calving ease, stillbirth, and many other traits at once. Body shape, udder, and leg traits each mapped to their own chromosome sets. The catalogue helps annotate the dairy genome and builds consensus on trait regions for genome-based selection programmes.
europmc-pmc3189760:
Giuseppe Vasapollo and colleagues reviewed plastics moulded to recognise single target molecules in a 2011 paper in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The method builds plastic around a template molecule, then removes the template, leaving pockets shaped and lined for that target alone. The resulting polymers act as fake receptors.

Unlike natural antibodies, these materials are cheap, rugged, and reusable, suiting them to sensors, separation columns, drug delivery, and cleaning polluted sites. The review surveys how imprinting methods have spread, from bulk polymers to surface and nano formats, and where results still lag behind natural receptors, notably in water-based use. The authors map the field's prospects for displacing fragile biological recognition parts in routine analysis.
europmc-pmc3202860:
Susan McCormick and colleagues reviewed trichothecene mycotoxins in this 2011 article in Toxins. Trichothecenes are poisons made by molds that infect grain crops, and contamination appears to be rising as climate and farming changes favor fungal growth. These toxins can cause serious illness in people and livestock that eat contaminated grain.

The review works through the family from its simplest members to its most complex forms, including the macrocyclic types. It lays out the proposed step-by-step pathways by which fungi build these molecules. By mapping the types and how they are made, the authors give food-safety researchers a reference for a toxin group that threatens the safety of the world grain supply.
europmc-pmc3291360:
Maunder and a large team of colleagues studied the lasting effects of the SARS outbreak on hospital staff, reporting in 2006. During the 2003 outbreak, spread happened mainly inside hospitals, and many workers fell ill or faced quarantine. The group surveyed staff in Toronto, where patients were treated, and in Hamilton, a nearby city whose hospitals took precautions but had no SARS patients.

One to two years later, staff who had worked through the outbreak still reported higher strain and worse effects on their jobs and daily lives. The study points to both personal traits and workplace conditions that raised or lowered the risk. Its lessons were meant to guide hospitals facing later outbreaks, including a possible flu pandemic.
europmc-pmc3335060:
Tseng and colleagues reported a warning sign from SARS vaccine testing in mice, in a 2012 study. SARS killed hundreds of people in 2002 and 2003, and fears of its return or deliberate release pushed vaccine work forward. Earlier animal tests of some vaccines protected against infection yet left vaccinated animals with inflamed lungs after exposure.

The team tested four candidate vaccines in two mouse strains, including whole killed virus and a lab made surface protein. All raised neutralizing antibodies and sharply cut virus in the lungs after challenge. Yet every vaccinated group developed a distinctive lung inflammation rich in a white blood cell type linked to allergy style responses, a pattern absent from control groups. The authors say the vaccines triggered a harmful sensitivity to virus parts, and urge great caution before human use.
europmc-pmc3391360:
Scheeren, Schober, and Schwarte reviewed in 2012 a bedside method for watching oxygen levels inside tissue, called near infrared spectroscopy. Standard heart and blood pressure monitoring can miss tissue starving for oxygen. The technique shines harmless light through skin and reads how much oxygen the tissue below holds.

It is used most often to watch brain oxygen during heart surgery, where low tissue oxygen is common. In emergencies, even before hospital arrival, its readings carry information about a patient's outlook and response to treatment. The review covers the physics behind the method and its growing clinical uses. Which treatments best restore tissue oxygen, the authors note, remains unsettled.
europmc-pmc3396660:
Dicks and colleagues derived a new vaccine delivery virus in 2012 from a chimpanzee adenovirus called Y25. Adenoviruses make promising vaccine shuttles, but prior exposure to common human types can blunt them. Rare animal types dodge that problem. The team also fixed how virus doses are measured, since sloppy counts can distort comparisons.

Built in an artificial chromosome for easy editing, the new vector raised cell-level immune responses in mice on par with a leading chimp virus already in human trials. Blood surveys in Britain and Gambia found especially few people carrying antibodies against it. Those two results support taking the Y25 vector toward clinical use.
europmc-pmc3403960:
Yang and colleagues ran a pilot trial in 2012 on picking a single embryo for transfer in IVF using chromosome screening. Transferring one embryo avoids twin risks but lowers pregnancy odds, so picking the best one matters. First-time patients under thirty-five with good outlooks were randomized to selection by appearance alone, or appearance plus a full chromosome scan.

The scanned group achieved far higher clinical pregnancy rates than the appearance-only group, and more pregnancies continued. Nearly half the scanned embryos carried chromosome errors despite looking fine, which exposes how imprecise looks alone are. No twins occurred in either group. The authors call for larger studies to confirm the benefit.
europmc-pmc3406960:
Gong and colleagues showed in 2012 that signaling through TGF-beta is essential for macrophages to take their calming, repair-minded form. Macrophages can gear up for attack or settle into the alternative state, which clears dead cells and heals tissue. The hormone IL-4 was known to drive the switch, but TGF-beta's part was untested.

Mice lacking the TGF-beta receptor in blood cells developed runaway lung inflammation and a lethal autoimmune syndrome while young. Their macrophages, grown in dishes, failed to switch on hallmark repair genes even when given IL-4, and made little of the enzyme arginase. The failure tracked with lowered activity in other internal pathways. Repair macrophages, it seems, need this signal to exist.
europmc-pmc3482660:
Marguerat and colleagues counted the actual molecules of RNA and protein inside fission yeast cells, in a 2012 paper in Cell. Most gene studies report only relative changes, which limits math models of how cells work. The team measured both growing cells and resting cells that had stopped dividing for lack of nitrogen, a state many body cells also enter.

Proteins proved far more numerous and wide-ranging in amount than RNA messages. Most messages sat just above one copy per cell, while long non-coding RNAs were held below one copy. When cells rested, proteins did not simply fade; their amounts scaled with the shrunken cell volume. Marguerat's dataset gives modelers a rare absolute reference for a whole cell.
europmc-pmc3484760:
Buckle, Walker, and Black estimated the worldwide burden of typhoid and paratyphoid fever for 2010, in the Journal of Global Health in 2012. These fevers, spread through dirty water and food, still sicken millions in poorer countries, and sound counts guide prevention spending. The team gathered population studies from three decades and reports from countries with strong tracking systems.

Rates varied hugely by region, from near zero in parts of Europe and Asia to the highest levels in sub-Saharan Africa. Their count put typhoid episodes for 2010 in the tens of millions once missed cases were allowed for. Buckle's group stresses that thin data from Africa and Latin America still limit the count. Cleaner water and better tracking remain pressing needs.

frus-1861-d160:
On 7 November 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton on the last day of the old calm. The letter is document 160 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote the day before a Union warship stopped the Trent off Cuba. His November note to Paris keeps the normal course of the autumn. In the file it reads as the last calm page before news that shook two continents. The Trent lay off Havana that week, on her run toward the English Channel. Calm pages before a storm gain a poignancy that no writer could have planned.
frus-1861-d260:
12 October 1861 is stamped on a letter Seward got from James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. The printed record keeps it as Document 260 in the President's message volume for 1861. The date falls in the autumn of the war's first year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d60:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 July 1861. The dispatch is document 60 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two days later the Union army broke and ran at Bull Run. Adams's letter left London before that news could cross the sea. It stands in the file as a last report from the brief age when the war was still expected to be short. The next mails would bring the Bull Run news and test every word of this calm. The dread fact, when it came, found Adams ready with a steady hand.
frus-1862-d160:
On 10 October 1862 Charles Francis Adams wrote from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward, and the report appears as Document 160 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams was the American minister to Britain, posted there since 1861.

That week a Newcastle speech by Gladstone had stirred talk that Britain might soon treat the South as a separate nation. What Adams heard from British leaders in such days carried real weight in Washington. His report is one piece of the record historians use to judge how near Britain came to changing the war in October 1862. Union consuls in British ports fed the legation word of ships fitting out for the South.
frus-1862-d260:
A Dayton report of 25 March 1862 stands as Document 260 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, wrote it to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.

Late March 1862 brought a Union win at Kernstown in the Shenandoah Valley and steady fighting talk in the French press. Dayton's task included countering French claims that the South could not be beaten. His reports home armed Seward with facts about French opinion, which the Secretary then used in his own dealings with the French minister in Washington. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d360:
Document 360, dated 3 March 1862, is Marshal Pelissier's answer to a circular sent out by a Mr. De Long. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume alongside his letter to the French foreign minister of the same date.

An answer to a circular is a formal reply to a question put to many officials at once. And such replies were gathered to guide policy in Paris. Filed in the American volume, this one shows the French government collecting views from its senior men on questions stirred by the war. The record gives no more of De Long than his name.
frus-1862-d460:
On 9 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to John Lothrop Motley in Vienna. The instruction is Document 460 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

October brought Seward better material to work with: Antietam had checked Lee, and the emancipation order had been announced. His instructions that month spread the news and its meaning to every post, Vienna included. Motley could now tell the Austrian court that the war had become openly a war against slavery, a fact that changed European debate. The dispatch is part of the autumn effort to lock in the gains of September. It went out before winter councils in Europe took up the American question again.
frus-1862-d560:
A second instruction dated 6 October 1862 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. It is Document 560 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, beside its same-day companion.

Two letters in one pouch meant two subjects, handled apart as the Department required. For Brussels in the autumn of 1862 the subjects ranged from Confederate agents in Europe to the court's reading of emancipation. Sanford's energy made his post a clearinghouse, and Washington fed it steadily. Paired with Document 559, this order shows the working granularity of the system. Nothing was bundled. Every question got its own sheet, its own date, and its own answer.
frus-1862-d60:
Dated 9 May 1862, a report from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London went to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 60 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d660:
On 5 February 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote once more to Robert H. Pruyn, the American minister bound for Japan. The letter is document 660 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Pruyn was taking over a legation that Townsend Harris had built from nothing.

Seward's early-1862 letters kept adding detail to Pruyn's charge as the new man neared his post. They show a State Department that, war or no war, meant to hold its place in Japan. For a reader, this letter fills in the gap between the naming of an envoy and the start of his real work abroad.
frus-1863p1-d160:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 17 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 160 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last sheet of the set wound up a day spent on the Union's British brief at its most taut. Adams's April letters are the record of a fight won by facts, law, and patience in London. This one ends the 17 April three. It is a working piece of that record, valued now as part of the whole great run.
frus-1863p1-d260: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 7 August 1863. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d360:
On 12 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It appears as document 360 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Cases in these notes can look small, one ship or one arrested man, yet each tested the rules of neutrality. Both governments treated the precedents as serious business. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d460:
A dispatch dated 15 April 1863 went from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d560:
Secretary William H. Seward took up his pen on 9 June 1863 and wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d60:
On 22 January 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams held the American legation in London. The letter is document 60 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Split mail was the legation's habit: short sheets, each on one head of business. Adams had talks, press, and Southern agents to cover, and he kept them apart for clean filing. This letter is the mate to document 59, sent the same day. In line with the run, it shows a post working at full pace in the heart of winter.
frus-1863p1-d660:
The 13 November 1863 mail between Washington and London included a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d160: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on October 23, 1943, in a letter the editors placed in the Moscow Conference section as Document 160 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Its date falls in the middle of the Moscow meeting, when the foreign ministers were testing how far three-power agreement could go. The record gives the date and the two names. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series with the Moscow papers.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d260: For an informal Cairo meeting of 23 November 1943, no official record has been found, and the volume prints an editorial note in its place. The gathering, held in the villa occupied by the British Chiefs of Staff, is mentioned in the memoirs of Generals Arnold and Leahy and in Alanbrooke's diary. None of those accounts gives any sign that business was discussed. The editors print the note simply to account for the meeting's place in the conference record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d360:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record the first plenary session of the Tehran Conference, on 28 November 1943 at four in the afternoon. The three leaders and their staffs sat down together for the first time, and Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin each spoke words of welcome before the war survey began.

Roosevelt, joking that as the youngest present he would welcome his elders, promises complete frankness and nothing made public. Churchill calls the gathering the greatest concentration of power the world has ever seen. Roosevelt then surveys the Pacific war. Over a million American men and most of the navy are there. Supply ships make only three round trips a year. The strategy is attrition: sinking Japanese tonnage faster than Japan can replace it. Keeping China in the war, through the north Burma road, is the western aim.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d460:
British officials kept their own minutes of a meeting on December 7, 1943, the day after the Second Cairo Conference closed, and the State Department printed the record in its Cairo-Tehran volume. Where the combined minutes speak for both allies, a United Kingdom minute shows the meeting as London's side saw and filed it.

That single-side view is exactly what makes the record useful. A reader can compare British wording, emphasis, and memory of the discussion with the joint accounts from the same days. Summit history depends on such comparisons, because each capital wrote the alliance's story slightly differently. This minute is one side's version, preserved in the American record.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d560:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on March 7, 1944, keeping the March correspondence at full pace. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, among the follow-up papers the editors printed after the conference records proper.

That spring the Western allies were balancing the coming invasion against the demands of Italy, the Pacific, and their Soviet partner. Churchill's letters were the main vehicle for Britain's view on all of them. For readers, this message is part of the long paper bridge between London and Washington over which the coalition's strategy traveled, week by week, until the landings in France.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d60: Roosevelt wrote to President İsmet İnönü of Turkey on October 26, 1943, a rare entry in a volume mostly passed among four capitals. The letter is Document 60 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Turkey stayed neutral through most of the war, and the allies courted Ankara steadily that autumn. The record names the two presidents and the date. What Roosevelt asked or offered is in the printed text.
frus-1944-quebec-d160:
Ambassador Winant wrote privately to Harry Hopkins on September 1, 1944, in one of the most personal letters in the volume. Churchill had arrived ill, though recovering, and regretted Hopkins's absence. Winant then turned to his real subject: Britain's exhaustion after five years of war, and the looming fight against Japan.

Britain was at the bottom of the manpower barrel, he wrote, with men conscripted from 16 to 65 and services visibly aging. Worse, a belief had seeped in that the British Navy was not wanted in the Pacific. If Britain were shut out of smashing Japan, Winant warned, the result would be postwar hatred and schism. A repetition of the tragedy of 1918 would be unforgivable.
frus-1944-quebec-d260:
The draft report of September 14, 1944, encloses the agreed summary of conclusions the Combined Chiefs reached at Octagon. It restates the coalition's war plan in formal language. The over-all objective is the unconditional surrender of the Axis. Europe would be defeated first, while pressure on Japan never slackened. Full resources would then turn against Japan, with Russia if possible.

The basic undertakings follow, including aid to Russia with coordination of forces, aid to China, and help for French, Italian, and other co-belligerent forces. One phrase betrays the week's hardest drafting fight. Moving forces to the Pacific was to have regard to other "agreed and/or inescapable commitments," a compromise welding the British and American wordings together.
frus-1944-quebec-d60:
The United States Chiefs of Staff set down this memorandum on September 7, 1944, five days before the Quebec Conference opened. The American chiefs would travel to Canada with the President. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Position papers written just before a conference state what a delegation must win and what it may trade. The American chiefs carried to Quebec the questions of the final German campaign and the balance of effort against Japan. For readers, this memorandum shows the United States military arriving at the summit with its case prepared, in the last days of staff work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d160:
The title "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 5" heads a text dated 8 July 1946. The State Department prints it as document 160 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Once a directive went out, staff worked to its terms, and later papers cite its number as their warrant. They name the office in charge, the work to be done, and the limits that apply, line by line. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d260:
"Office of Special Operations Directive No. 18/5 (Interim)" bears the date 24 February 1948. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 260 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

The form is stiff because it has to be: each line is a rule that a named office can be held to. The shelf of such orders, read in order, is the true org chart of the system as it grew. The mark 18/5 ties the order to the Council paper behind the covert tasking. The word interim in the title shows the rules were still being set.
frus-1945-50-intel-d360:
Allen W. Dulles addressed a memorandum to Mathias F. Correa and William H. Jackson on 21 January 1949. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 360, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d60:
General Craig wrote to Secretary of War Patterson on 24 December 1945. A paper dated Christmas Eve shows the War Department's intelligence business running to the year's last days. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Craig had written to the Lovett Committee six days earlier; now he wrote to his own secretary. The two papers together show a staff chief working the question at both levels, study group and department head. Readers closing the volume's 1945 run here should feel the pause that follows. Within a month, the president's directive would settle the contest these papers had waged since August. The Christmas Eve date gives the long autumn a human full stop.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d160:
“Disturbed and deeply disappointed” is how Roosevelt opened his protest to Stalin on 30 December 1944. His top secret message, number 153, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It answers Stalin's refusal to delay recognizing the Lublin Committee.

No serious trouble, Roosevelt argues, would have followed from holding the purely formal act of recognition for the one month left before the three leaders meet. He had not asked Moscow to cut its practical dealings with the Lublin body. Nor had he asked it to accept the London government as it stands. What he dreads is the effect on world opinion, and on enemy morale, if Moscow crowns one Polish government while most allies still recognize the other.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d260:
Stalin named his price for entering the Pacific war on 14 December 1944, and Harriman reported the talk the next day. His top secret message to the President is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The two men had a map open between them.

The Kurile Islands and the lower half of Sakhalin should be returned to Russia, Stalin said. Japan now holds the approaches to Vladivostok, and every outlet to the Pacific is held or blocked by the enemy. He then drew a line around the southern Liaotung Peninsula, taking in Port Arthur and Dairen. Russia wished to lease those ports and the land around them once more. Harriman recalled the Tehran talk, and answered that the President had seemed to have in mind an international free port instead.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d360:
Freed prisoners and civilians drive this letter from Foreign Secretary Eden to Secretary Stettinius, written at Yalta on February 5, 1945. Eden recalled that the conference was to take up a reciprocal agreement with Moscow. It would cover Soviet citizens freed by Allied armies in the west and south, and British and American nationals freed by Soviet forces in the east.

The British chiefs had approved a draft, Eden wrote, and the Combined Chiefs would take it up that day. Speed mattered. Soviet forces were already overrunning the sites of British and American prisoner camps. The letter shows a humane problem becoming urgent diplomacy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d460:
Too many "joints" — Churchill's complaint opens Hiss's notes of the last plenary, at noon on February 11, 1945. The leaders were editing the draft communiqué word by word. Molotov offered an amendment making a separate paragraph on reparations. On naming the men who took part, Churchill wanted the names at the end; Stalin preferred the beginning.

The President and Prime Minister settled it: names at the beginning, as at Tehran. Churchill asked whether generals should be put in as well; Stalin agreed. On Germany, Molotov withdrew an amendment adding "Hitlerite," since it narrowed the term. Hiss catches the famous document being copy-edited by its authors.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d60:
Ambassador Averell Harriman answered the President on 17 January 1945 about the food arrangements at Yalta. His telegram from Moscow is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It follows up Roosevelt's request for his own cooks and stewards.

Harriman reports that Foreign Minister Molotov agreed at once. Molotov treated the request as natural, just as it had been handled at Tehran. The President's mess would be set up in the twenty-one room palace at Livadia. Harriman adds that, weather permitting, he will inspect the site on 21 January, taking his daughter Kathleen along since such household matters were her department.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d160:
Acting Secretary Grew sent the President a briefing memo on economic questions on June 18, 1945. The memorandum is document 160 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It lists the economic issues that might properly come up at the three-power meeting, and the papers being prepared on each.

For Germany, the memo urges treating the country as one economic unit, with uniform ration scales, trade, and currency across all zones, and no barriers to goods moving between them. It also covers German exports before a reparations settlement, land cessions, and joint transport and coal agencies under the Control Council. Grew suggests that at least three economic officials join the American delegation. The paper shows economic unity in Germany was an American aim from the start.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d260:
A briefing paper urged bringing Russia into Europe's economic bodies, in extracts dated July 3, 1945. The paper is document 260 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It concerns the new organizations being built to run Europe's transport, coal, and food in the wake of the war.

The recommendation is to win Soviet agreement to take full part in the European Central Inland Transport Organization, including naming representatives for its day-to-day work. A row over Polish representation had kept the Soviets out of recent talks, the paper notes. Their London delegation, however, has quietly indicated that the present draft agreement has substantially met their objections to earlier versions. The full text of the paper is printed later in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d360:
Pauley wrote directly to General Eisenhower from Moscow on June 27, 1945, to put the new restitution rule in force. The President, he reports, had approved his recommendation. Matters of restitution, and transfers of property as restitution, now required the approval of the Allied Commission on Reparations.

Eisenhower was to present to Pauley, for approval, any planned removals of property for restitution from American-held regions in Germany and Austria. Pauley adds the President's caution: coordination must not needlessly slow the return of goods, works of art among them. He also names his own men in Frankfurt, Captain Faigle and Frank Adams, to act promptly on the spot.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d460:
Yugoslav anger at Greece fills extracts from Shantz's Belgrade telegram of July 9, 1945. Borba and Politika of July 8 featured speeches by government officials at meetings across Serbia marking the anniversary of the Partisan uprising of 1941. Borba also printed a three-column editorial against the expansionist threat of leading political circles in Greece.

The editorial printed a Greek map showing a greater Greece. It took in Yugoslav Macedonia, half of Albania and Bulgaria, and all of European Turkey. Its writer concluded that the peoples of Yugoslavia, Albania, and Bulgaria cannot be indifferent to events in Greece. A Fascist reign of terror over Greece's minorities, he charged, put relations between the countries in question.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d560:
Two lines from Ambassador Alexander Kirk in Caserta carry big news on June 20, 1945. The urgent secret wire is document 560 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It concerns the Allied talks with Yugoslav officers over Venezia Giulia.

Kirk reports that General Morgan had just phoned from Monfalcone. An agreement with the Yugoslavs was signed at nine o'clock that morning. The deal put into effect the Belgrade agreement of June 9 on the disputed zone. Its full text, with appendices, was printed in a Yugoslav treaty volume. A linked note on civil rule in the zone follows as the next document in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d60:
Ambassador W. Averell Harriman wrote to President Truman from Moscow on June 14, 1945, asking if there was anything he should raise with Stalin. The top secret telegram is document 60 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Practical planning for the Berlin meeting was split between Eisenhower in Germany and the embassy in Moscow.

Harriman assumes Eisenhower will work out Berlin arrangements with Marshal Zhukov, but expects some points will need settling in Moscow first, so that Zhukov gets proper orders. From his time at Tehran and Yalta, he warns the Russians will soon ask about Truman's plans and who he means to bring, so they can pick their own party. He wants guidance before they ask.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d660:
Washington told Ambassador Winant the U.S. would join the Tangier administration in a wire of June 29, 1945. Signed by Grew and Henderson, it is document 660 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The wire answers Winant's query of June 26.

Winant may state that the U.S. government is willing to take part in the administration. Subject to conditions he judges fit, he may recommend joining under the proposed pact's terms. Early inquiries suggest the U.S. money share could come from emergency funds in principle. A firm estimate of that share is still needed before a final decision. Grew asks that Villard produce the estimate quickly, after consulting British and French colleagues in Paris.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1060:
George Allen, a deputy director for Near Eastern affairs, wrote to Assistant Secretary James Dunn at Potsdam on July 18, 1945. His subject is the proposed joint supervision of Greek elections. A Washington telegram of the day before, he notes, makes a separate delegation draft needless.

Allen backs the Department's objection to calling the approach an invitation. Better, he says, that the four powers simply propose to share supervision among themselves. He offers to work out a text with the right British delegate if Dunn wishes. He also agrees with Washington's apparent wish to cover only the parliamentary elections. The later plebiscite on the king, he writes, is another bridge to cross in its turn.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1160:
Taft, who directed the office for transport and communications policy, wrote to Assistant Secretary Clayton on 19 July 1945. His office dealt with the systems that moved people, goods, and word across borders: shipping lanes, air routes, cables, and the rules that governed them.

Writing to the department's money chief linked that technical world to the summit's talks. Transport terms would shape how fast Europe could trade and recover. A note of this kind is policy on the plain systems under daily life. It shows the State Department's expert staff feeding their piece into the whole, one office at a time.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1260:
Sato reported to Togo on 30 July 1945. The Moscow exchange was nearing its end. Japan had given no answer the Allies would accept, the Soviet door stayed shut, and the war's machinery moved toward its final acts.

An envoy's late reports in a failing mission carry a special weight. Sato wrote as a man who had tested the door often enough to know it would not open. His cables urged Tokyo, in careful shades, to end the war before worse befell it. This dispatch belongs to those last urgings. It closes the July run of the Moscow thread in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1360:
Ambassador John Winant cabled the acting secretary of state from London on 26 July 1945, his third message in this part of the volume. That date fell in the last week of the Potsdam Conference. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

By late July, London itself was changing: Churchill's government fell on 26 July after the election count. Winant's cable came from a capital in political upheaval, reporting to a Washington whose leaders were abroad. Readers who follow the Winant run get the substance of his reports. They also feel how much the alliance depended on steady men in post when events shook the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-160:
Delegation staff prepared this working paper on August 1, 1945, the last day of the Potsdam Conference. Working papers served to the very end. Even as leaders adopted final texts, officers still drafted, checked, and compared lines. The paper stayed in the American files and joined the second Potsdam volume.

A last-day draft shows that agreement was handmade to the finish. Staff kept shaping words while the clock ran down. Readers see the settlement's final texture being worked. The paper also marks a truth of big talks: nothing is done until the last line is checked. It closes the run of working papers in this set.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-60:
Thompson's minutes record the fifth meeting of the foreign ministers, on Sunday, July 22, 1945. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Eden sat in the chair, and the meeting opened at 11:10 a.m.

Eden proposed clearing the air first on the state of every outstanding subject. Only then could the meeting decide which items were ready to discuss. He began with the admission of neutral states, Spain excepted, into world organizations. Molotov asked about Italy at once, and Eden replied that Italy was linked to that subject. The Council of Foreign Ministers and German economic questions were named next. Byrnes asked after a further item of his own suggestion, the supply of oil for Western Europe. Molotov answered with subjects of his own, among them reparations from Germany and Austria.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d760:
Riddleberger wrote to the Secretary of State on July 31, 1945, in document 760. The chief of Central European affairs sent his counsel as Potsdam closed. His division owned the files on the lands the conference had spent two weeks dividing. The letter was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

An expert's closing letter has a summing force. Riddleberger could judge the outcome against years of preparation. Readers see Washington's deep bench speaking at the decisive hour. The document also shows the flow reversing. All week the field fed the summit. Now its results flowed back to the desks that would run them.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d860:
Document 860 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 18, 1945. Staff prepared it during the conference's opening days. It belongs to the first layer of American drafting at Potsdam. The paper was preserved in the delegation files and printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Opening-days papers show the team's starting picture of its tasks. Writers worked from briefs prepared over months. Readers can compare that picture with the conference that actually unfolded. The document also shows the sheer start-up speed of a summit. Within two days of arrival, the delegation was producing the texts on which its case would rest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d960:
Britain's delegation proposed this Soviet share of reparations at Potsdam on July 30, 1945. Russia would take removals and deliveries from its own zone as its base share. On top of that, it would receive 10 percent of equipment removed from the western zones. The gear would come mainly from the Ruhr's heavy metal plants.

The agreed plan must cut German war potential hard. At the same time, it must leave enough industry for approved living standards in Germany. In return, other claimant powers should draw yearly timber and potash from the Russian zone. The Reparations Commission would work out the details.
frus-1950v07-d360: A 1950 FRUS document from the U.S. Representative at the UN on Korea. America's diplomat made its case. This entry holds that record. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
frus-1961-63v10-d60: National Security Action Memorandum No. 60 on Cuba, in the 1961-1963 FRUS volume. The presidential order. This entry preserves that memorandum. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
gao-gaoreports-b-297060: Symplicity Corporation took its November 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
