gao-gaoreports-b-297660: Novex Enterprises doubled its March 2006 protest — two case numbers, one enterprise fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297960: Del-Jen International took its May 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-306860: The housing regulator's Freddie Mac settlement got a fiscal ruling in this February 2006 GAO call, which tests the agreement. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the settlement stood. The law had the final word. The settlement had to stand legal scrutiny.
gao-gaoreports-b-310460: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Connectec Company, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-b-311060: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Potomac Electric Corporation. Decided April 2, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. It is kept here as part of the lasting public record.
gao-gaoreports-b-400060: This 2008 GAO ruling is about designated Employee Agent at Bill Henson. These rulings interpret appropriations law for federal agencies. It becomes part of the body of federal fiscal law. The library keeps it as part of the public record.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-160: VA ward planning made strides in 2005, and GAO's report says the big moves matched beds to future needs. The review credits the foresight. The veterans' beds deserved the planning. The planning was sound. The strides were real. The beds were matched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-660: Thin Army Reserve ranks needed one fix-it plan in 2005, and GAO's report says the people-and-gear gaps called for a single strategy. The findings demand the plan. The report warns that the reservists deserved full ranks. The reservists deserved full ranks.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-160: Army truck armor production lagged in wartime 2006, and GAO's report says several factors limited the output and installation. The findings document the shortfall. The report warns that the troops' trucks needed their steel. The production had to speed up. The troops' trucks needed their steel.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-360: The IRS's 2006 spending plan got a GAO review, and the report examines the business systems modernization expenditure plan. The findings grade the budget. The report warns that the tax machine's upgrade dollars needed watching. The plan had to be sound.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-460: Katrina's billions needed firm rules in 2006, and GAO's report says full policies were due to keep the spending honest. The findings demand the rulebook. The report warns that the storm's money deserved strict counts. The rules had to be complete.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-560: The IRS's audit homework got a GAO check in 2006, and the report tracks the status of financial audit recommendations. The findings grade the follow-through. The report warns that the tax agency's books deserved fixing. The recommendations had to be addressed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-60: Servicemember employment rights needed better management in 2005, and GAO's report says federal oversight could be further improved. The findings demand the upgrades. The report warns that the deployed workers deserved their jobs back. The management had to improve. The deployed workers deserved their jobs back.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-860: Disaster aid for small businesses was too slow in 2006, and GAO's report says the SBA needed to provide more timely assistance. The findings demand the speed. The report warns that the ruined shops could not wait on paperwork. The aid had to arrive faster.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1160: A 2007 Government Accountability Office report finding the IRS could improve how it manages paper case files — the physical folders behind tax disputes and collections. In an agency handling hundreds of millions of accounts, lost or mishandled files meant delays and errors. GAO's recommendations target the unglamorous plumbing of tax administration, where better filing cabinets translate into better service.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-360: The Joint Strike Fighter was inching forward in 2007, and GAO's report says progress had been made while serious challenges remained. The findings balance the gains against the risks. The report reads as the cautiously optimistic chapter of the costliest weapons story ever told.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-60: The Guard's gear gaps needed measuring in 2007, and GAO's report says the domestic equipment needs and readiness had to be identified. The findings demand the inventory. The report warns that the hometown troops should not deploy with empty racks. The weekend warriors needed weekday gear.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-660: Air cargo bound for America was barely screened in 2007 — GAO's report says the federal effort was young and needed muscle. The findings flag the flying freight gap. The report warns that the bomb in the belly was the hole in the fence.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-860: The Army could not find its own stuff in 2007 — GAO's report says the asset-tracking investment lacked a joined-up strategy. The findings warn that billions for visibility software would blur without a master plan. An army that cannot see its gear, the report argues, cannot move it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-160: The Government Accountability Office dug into federal Acquisition: Oversight Plan Needed to Help Implement Acquisition Advisory Panel Recommendations in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-360: GAO published its findings on defense Contracting: Army Case Study Delineates Concerns with Use of Contractors as Contract Specialists in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-60: This 2007 GAO report takes on the VA's care of seized homes — houses the agency takes back when vets fall behind on backed loans. GAO found the VA barely watched the firms hired to guard and sell these homes. The report calls for a firm grip on the hired help, so the homes keep their worth and the public purse takes no needless hit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-660: In 2008, the Government Accountability Office published this report on coast Guard: Strategies for Mitigating the Loss of Patrol Boats Are Achieving Results in the Near Term, but They Come at a Cost and Longer Term Sustainability I. GAO is Congress's watchdog, and its work lays out what the team found and what should change. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-860: The Government Accountability Office dug into combating Terrorism: Actions Needed to Enhance Implementation of Trans-Sahara Counterterrorism Partnership in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
geneva-bible-1560:
English Protestants who had fled to Geneva under William Whittingham and his fellow exiles produced the Geneva Bible, first printed in full in 1560. It was the first English Bible to divide the text into numbered verses. For decades it was the Bible most English homes actually owned and read.

The translation covers the full Old and New Testaments, with the Apocrypha included. Its clear prose and helpful verse numbers made study far easier than in earlier editions. Shakespeare quoted from it, and the Pilgrims carried it to America. Few English books shaped private faith and plain English reading as much as this one.
gosse-romance-of-natural-history-1860:
Philip Henry Gosse loved the sea shore and all its wonders, and wrote of them in 1860. The Romance of Natural History treats sea serpents and ocean marvels as romance, in his own word. Gosse was a famed Victorian naturalist who made the aquarium a craze.

He sifts tales of the deep with a believer's heart and a scholar's hand. Oudemans and the serpent men cite his pages to this day. The book shows Victorian science and wonder walking side by side. Gosse's charm is that he will not laugh a good tale out of court.
hawthorne-marble-faun-1860:
Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Marble Faun in 1860, his last completed romance of Italy. The tale gives Rome, art, and the Fall in a story of four young friends. Henry James called it the bridge to the international theme in the American novel tradition later.

Donatello, an Italian count with faun-like ears, loves the American artist Miriam in Rome's studios. A model who haunts Miriam is thrown from a cliff, and guilt transforms the glad faun. Hilda, a pure copyist, is crushed by a secret she witnesses and seeks a confessional in Rome. Kenyon, a sculptor, watches love and sin work on his friends across Roman ruins and galleries. Hawthorne asks if a fall can deepen the soul, his old fortunate fall theme.
herrn-georgii-von-welling-opus-mago-cabb: Herrn Georgii von Welling Opus mago-cabbalisticum, 1760. The Welling opus. This book preserves that work. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. The archive guards it with care.
heydon-rosie-crucian-axiomata-1660:
John Heydon's Rosie Crucian Infallible Axiomata appeared in London in 1660, as the monarchy returned to England. The slim book is a rule-book of general axioms, Rosicrucian doctrine in its most concentrated form. Where Heydon's Holy Guide sprawls, the Axiomata compresses the teaching into short, sharp sayings for the adept.

Each axiom states a principle of the Rosicrucian art or life. The Restoration-era statement aims at certainty: infallible is its own chosen word. Heydon marketed himself as the fraternity's English spokesman, and such handbooks were his wares. The Axiomata lets readers hold his whole doctrine in a few pages. It is the Rose Cross boiled down, doctrine as a pocket creed.
holmes-professor-1860:
Oliver Wendell Holmes followed his Autocrat with The Professor at the Breakfast-Table in 1860. The scene returns to the same Boston boarding house, with a new presiding talker. Holmes was then at the height of his powers as doctor, professor, and man of letters.

The Professor's talk runs deeper into theology and human nature than the Autocrat's, with the famous Little Bostonian among the listeners. The volume contains The Chambered Nautilus, Holmes's beloved poem of the soul outgrowing its shells: build thee more stately mansions, O my soul. Serious argument and table wit alternate in Holmes's easy manner. The book confirmed the breakfast-table series as a fixture of American letters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowy-adolf-1016:
Adolf Löwy, a German physiologist born in Berlin on June 29, 1862, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer. Physiology is the study of how the living body works. He studied at the gymnasium and university of his native city, earned his medical degree in 1885, and rose to assistant professor in 1900.

Löwy’s prize-winning study examined breathing and circulation when the pressure and the oxygen content of the air change. The Smithsonian Institution gave it a prize in 1895. The article adds that many more of his papers appeared in leading German journals of physiology and anatomy. The entry is short, with no list of individual titles, but it fixes the main facts of his training, his Berlin posts, and the research that brought him notice outside Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maggid-steinsch:
Hillel Noah Maggid, a Russian genealogist and historian of Wilna, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Wilna in 1829, he descended from the family of Saul Wahl. His grandfather Phinehas had been rabbi at Polotsk and Wilna. Losing his father at eighteen, Maggid learned the trade of a lapidary. He died at Wilna in 1903.

The article links his craft to his scholarship. Cutting tombstone inscriptions led him to compose them, and then to genealogy. He published articles in the Hebrew periodicals and helped Fuenn write Wilna's community history. His chief work, Ir Wilna, appeared in 1900. It holds biographies of more than three hundred rabbis, preachers, and communal workers of the city. Its notes show command of responsa and historical literature alike. Two further volumes stayed in manuscript at his death. The entry honors a stonecutter who became his city's historian.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manessier-de-ve:
Manessier de Vesoul, a French communal leader, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He came from Vesoul, probably of the Heliot family of that town. His known work belongs to Paris. It was Manessier who negotiated the return of the Jews to France around 1358.

The article explains the office the king then gave him. As procureur general of the Jews, he granted or withheld permission for any Jew to enter France. In return he answered for their payments to the treasury. He still held the post in 1376. Around 1370 Jacob de Pont St. Maxence worked beside him, then quarreled with him. Jacob accused Manessier of mishandling funds and building a synagogue without royal leave. Manessier was jailed in the Chatelet and faced a heavy fine. The penalty was probably remitted, since he later regained the court's credit. The entry shows one man holding a kingdom's gate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mashiah-hasun-b:
Hasun ben Mashiah, a Karaite scholar of the tenth century, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé. He worked in Egypt, or possibly Babylonia, in the first half of the century. Steinschneider held that "Hasun" is a corrupted form of the Arabic name Husain, its letters easily confused in manuscripts.

Hasun was a younger contemporary of Saadia Gaon, the great rabbinic leader, and reportedly once challenged Saadia to a public religious debate. His known work was a polemic, probably written in Arabic, answering an unpublished anti-Karaite writing of Saadia's that reached him after Saadia's death. The entry carefully sorts out other works that later writers credited to him by mistake, a useful caution about how Karaite authorship was recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-me-ilah-trespas:
Me'ilah, “trespass in regard to a holy thing,” is a tractate of the Mishnah. Solomon Schechter and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach describe it chapter by chapter in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The treatise stands eighth in the order Kodashim. It has six chapters and thirty-eight paragraphs across the Mishnah, Tosefta, and Babylonian Talmud. Its subject is the law of Leviticus on the trespass-offering: what repair a person owes who has used something consecrated to the Temple.

The summary shows how fine the distinctions run. Which parts of which sacrifices can be trespassed against, and at what moment? What changes once the blood is sprinkled? Can there be trespass in the grass of a consecrated field or the fruit of a consecrated tree? It notes the rule of R. Joshua: once the priests gain the right to eat of a sacrifice, no trespass in it can occur.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendelsohn-jose:
Joseph Mendelsohn, a German author who came to literature from the print shop, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling. Born at Jever in 1817, he was schooled at the Jewish free school in Hamburg and apprenticed in 1831 to a Brunswick printing house, where he remained as journeyman until 1839. His first book announced the fact in its title: "Blüthen," Blossoms, poems and tales by a typesetter.

Back in Hamburg he wrote full-time, studied in Paris with Solomon Heine's help, and produced steadily: "Pariser Briefe," "Wilde Blumen," the anti-Jesuit "Ueberall Jesuiten" of 1846, and comedies adapted from the French. He died at Hamburg on April 4, 1856, not yet forty. The entry is brief, but it preserves the outline of a workingman's literary career in the age of Heine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-m-wilhelm:
M. Wilhelm Meyer, a German astronomer born at Brunswick on February 15, 1853, is sketched in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Isidore Singer, published in 1906. He began in the book trade, then left it to study astronomy at Göttingen, Leipsic, and Zurich. By 1876 he was teaching at Zurich, and a year later he joined the Geneva observatory staff.

Meyer lectured at Geneva University, then moved through Vienna to Berlin, where in 1888 he became director of Urania, a society for spreading natural science to the public. He edited its journal Himmel und Erde from 1889 and helped revise Diesterweg's popular astronomy. His own books brought the sun, the earth, and nature study to general readers in plain German.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montefiore-1096:
Montefiore is the great Anglo-Jewish family. It takes its name from an Italian town. Three towns bore the name in the Papal States, and which one is the family's is not definitely known. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind write this in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Montefiores were merchants at Ancona by 1630. A branch moved to Leghorn around 1700.

The pedigree then fans out across the world. Moses Vita Montefiore married at Leghorn in 1752 and had seventeen children. One line produced Haim Guedalla. Another produced Sir Moses Montefiore himself. A third line, through Eliezer's emigration to the West Indies, produced the brothers who became early pioneers of Australia. The entry's family tree is a map of the Sephardic diaspora in business dress.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-adolph-11:
Adolph Moses was an American rabbi whose early life ran through two European struggles for freedom. Cyrus Adler and I. George Dobsevage wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born at Kletchevo in Prussian Poland on May 3, 1840, he trained in Talmud and studied at the Breslau seminary. In 1859 he left to fight in Garibaldi's army in Italy.

In 1863 Moses served as an officer in the Polish insurrection and was imprisoned by the Russians when it failed. Formed in the Reform line of Abraham Geiger, he came to America and held pulpits in Montgomery, Mobile, and Louisville. He worked for the education of the blind and late in life took a medical degree. He died at Louisville in 1902, leaving books such as The Religion of Moses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-uri-b-jos:
Moses Uri ben Joseph ha-Levi was a rabbi at Emden and a founder of the Portuguese community at Amsterdam. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1544, probably at Wittmund, he was living at Emden in 1593. That year a ship of Marranos under Jacob Tirado was driven into the port.

Tirado found Moses Uri's house by a Hebrew inscription and asked to be received into Judaism. Moses sent the party on to Amsterdam and followed with his family. There he circumcised the Marranos, set up a house of prayer, and became their rabbi, with his son Aaron as hazzan. Father and son are said to have circumcised twenty-five hundred Marranos in all.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-ben-joel:
Nathan ben Joel Falaquera was a Spanish Jewish doctor. Isidore Singer and J. S. Raisin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked in the later half of the thirteenth century. His father was a doctor, and he studied medicine early. He may be the Nathan of Montpellier named elsewhere.

Falaquera wrote a medical book called Zori ha-Guf. It gathers views on treatment and health from five masters. They are Hippocrates, Galen, Averroes, Avicenna, and Maimonides. He used medical and plant terms found in the Talmud. For other terms he used Arabic words, then translated them. A work on the spheres of heaven is also credited to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neuda-abraham-1:
Abraham Neuda was an Austrian rabbi caught in a legal fight. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Loschitz, Moravia, in 1812. His father Aaron was rabbi of that town. Abraham studied at Nikolsburg under Trebitsch, the district rabbi.

His father died in 1834, while Abraham studied away. Loschitz chose the son to succeed his father. Trebitsch vetoed the choice under a legal privilege. Six years of bitter court proceedings followed that veto. Neuda won at last, after passing an examination. He married Fanny Schmiedl, herself an authoress. His sermons were printed at Vienna in 1845. Studies of Talmud names and colors stayed in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nissim-ben-jaco:
Nissim ben Jacob ibn Shahin taught Talmud at Kairwan. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first half of the eleventh century. His father headed Kairwan's yeshivah before him. Hushiel's teaching formed him next, and he succeeded Hushiel.

Letters linked him to Hai Gaon of Sura. He passed Hai's rulings to Samuel ha-Nagid of Granada. So Babylonian learning crossed through him into Spain. Poor himself, he took support from Samuel's purse. His great work is a Key to the Talmud's locks. It spells out every passage the old teachers cite briefly. A second book gathers his private notes on rulings. He also made a book of some sixty comforting tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-odessa-11660:
Odessa is a city on the north shore of the Black Sea. Herman Rosenthal and S. Penn wrote its long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews were there when Russia took the place in 1789. It had been a Turkish fort named Khadzhi-Bei. In 1794 it took the name Odessa.

In 1795 the Jewish count in Odessa stood at 240 souls. Most came from Volhynia, Podolia, and Lithuania. Later Jews came from Galicia and from Germany. These new folk set up aid groups at once. A book of rules from 1795 is still kept. It set out care for the sick and the dead. A school and a town board soon followed. A Jewish hospital with six beds opened in 1800.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palagyi-ludwig-:
Ludwig Palágyi was a Hungarian poet born at Becse. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there on April 15, 1866. His first name at birth was Silberstein, the entry notes. His father taught him at home in his youth.

His elder brother Melchior taught the boy as well at home. Ludwig began to write at the age of thirteen years. His first poem came out in print in 1879. He soon wrote for the best known sheets of Hungary. In 1890 he won a prize of one hundred gold ducats. That prize was for a poem at a shrine of martyrs. For his work for the Hungarian tongue, he won a post. He taught at a state school for women at Budapest.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peshat-12060:
Peshaṭ is the plain, literal sense of a Bible passage. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word comes from a verb meaning to spread out. A full explanation spreads the text open.

At first peshaṭ and derash meant much the same thing. The early sages saw their midrash as the true sense. Later scholars felt some readings were forced. They split the plain sense from the derived one. A rule guarded the split from going too far. Interpretation must never wipe out the literal meaning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinczow-joseph-:
Joseph Pinczow was a Polish rabbi and Talmud author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He descended from the famed Jacob Pollak. He first headed a yeshivah at Wilna. His son Moses became rabbi of Copenhagen.

In 1688 Pinczow became rabbi of Kosovi. He later kept a yeshivah at Seltzy. Persecution drove him to Hamburg for four years. Plague and threats drove him out again in 1706. At Berlin he printed his Rosh Yosef in 1717. The book ranges over law and lore by tractate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pledges-11960:
Pledges for debt stand under strict biblical limits. Solomon Schechter, Lewis N. Dembitz, and Gotthard Deutsch wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. No creditor may take a debtor's millstone. To seize it is to seize his life itself.

A widow's clothing may never be taken at all. A poor man's pledge goes back by nightfall. The Mishnah widens the shield to all food tools. The pillow returns for the night, the plow for the day. A debtor keeps food, clothes, bed, and tools. Even a costly robe stays on his back.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polygamy-12260:
Polygamy means having more than one wife at the same time. The Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They say the custom is very old among the Jews. The Law set limits on it rather than ending it. Prophets and scribes looked on it with disfavor.

Still, the custom lasted into fairly late times, the writers note. It was never as common in Israel as among other nations. Jewish life leaned toward one wife all along. The first man, Adam, had one wife only. The first case of two wives comes in the line of Cain. Noah and his sons each had one wife. Abraham, too, is shown with a single wife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-priluk-przyluk-: Aryeh Löb Priluk was a Polish author of the seventeenth century. The Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He wrote notes on the Zohar, the chief book of Cabala. His notes run from the part Shemot to the part Hukkat. They were printed at Berlin in 1724 with another book. That second book, the Sefer Yirah, is also credited to him. Little else of his life is known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-querido-jacob-c:
Jacob Querido was the heir of the false messiah Shabbethai Zebi. Gotthard Deutsch and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Salonica and died at Alexandria in 1690. His father was Joseph, called the Philosopher. His sister had been the wife of Zebi himself.

That sister made a bold claim for her brother's sake. She said Jacob was her son by Zebi, not her brother. On that claim Jacob was to lead the sect in turn. A learned Talmudist, Solomon Florentin, joined the cause. With his help Jacob won a large following of believers. The entry tells how the sect held on after its master's death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-12860:
Rosenthal, in this entry, names one of several Russian Jewish families bearing that surname. Herman Rosenthal and Peter Wiernik wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It traces the line from Solomon of Wirballen, a financier at Frederick the Great's court.

Solomon's son David married into the Rosenthal family and took its name. The entry then follows his children and grandchildren town by town. Branches reached Pinsk, Grodno, Krementchug, and other Russian centers. One granddaughter married a director of the Siberian Bank in St. Petersburg. Readers get a careful family tree rather than a single life story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ibn-adiy:
Joseph Jacobs and Mary W. Montgomery wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel ibn 'Adiya. He was a poet and warrior in Arabia in the first half of the sixth century. Samuel owned a strong castle near Taima, built by his grandfather. Travelers between Syria and Medina stopped there. Arabs still call a loyal man more faithful than Samuel.

That fame came from the prince Amru al-Ḳais. Fleeing his enemies, Amru left his daughter, his cousin, and five suits of mail in Samuel's care. An enemy prince later seized Samuel's young son. He offered the boy's life for the stored goods. Samuel refused, and his son was killed before his eyes. The entry also weighs Samuel's poems, including one in the famous Ḥamasa collection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-san-daniele-del:
Isidore Singer and Giuseppe Jare wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on San Daniele del Friuli. The small Italian town stands near Udine. About 1600 two brothers named Luzzatto settled there. One line led to Hezekiah Luzzatto. Hezekiah was the father of Samuel David Luzzatto, the famous scholar.

A law of 1777 let Jews live again in Venice. It came with many harsh limits. A Hebrew paper of the time says Jews could not live in the state's villages. Quarrels between native and foreign Jews at Venice caused that ban. The San Daniele community was later dissolved, like many others. Young Hezekiah, then sixteen, left with his family for Triest. The entry shows how one decree scattered a small town community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scherschewski-z:
Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Ẓebi Hirsch ha-Kohen Scherschewski. He was a Russian Hebrew writer. Scherschewski was born at Pinsk in 1840. As a boy he taught himself Hebrew grammar and archaeology. He served as secretary of the Pinsk community. Later he assisted Zederbaum in editing Ha-Meliẓ.

During the Russo-Turkish war, Scherschewski followed the army as a sutler. In 1883 he settled at Rostov-on-the-Don and opened a bookstore. His Boser Abot, from 1877, is a satirical poem. It mocks the neglect of Jewish children's schooling in Russia. His 'Iyyun Sifrut, from 1881, traces Jewish literature's growth. It argues that letters can lift the Jews morally. His notes appear in a Warsaw edition of the Midrash Shoḥer Ṭob. His rhymed parodies were also printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shechem-shoulde:
Shechem, meaning shoulder or ridge, became a key religious center after Israel entered Canaan. Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the city. It sat between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Levites were to recite blessings from those twin peaks.

Under Joshua that rite was carried out at Shechem. Joshua set up his laws and a witness stone there. Near death, he gathered Israel's elders there for last counsel. Later the city crowned Abimelech king under its oak. Three years on, its people revolted and were slain. The city was destroyed and sown with salt. The entry follows a holy place repeatedly undone by strife.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silberstein-sol:
Solomon Silberstein was an American philosophical writer born at Kovno, Russia, in 1845. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. Privately educated, he received a rabbinical diploma in 1864. He served as rabbi at Dershunisok from 1867 to 1868.

Later Silberstein emigrated to the United States and settled in New York. There he turned from the pulpit to philosophy books. His works appeared in both Hebrew and English over decades. They treat religion and Torah, and the universe's evolution. Others cover God's existence and the general laws of nature. A 1904 book tackles the Jewish problem and theology together. The entry lists a rabbi remade as a popular thinker on science and faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simuna-semona-1: Simuna, also called Semona, was a Sabora of the second generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He headed the Academy of Pumbedita from 520 to 540. At the same time, Rabbi Ena held a like post at Sura. Little else is known about his life or work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-the-exi:
Solomon the Exilarch was the eldest son of the exilarch Hasdai. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He ruled as exilarch from 730 to 761. A lack of teachers forced a bold step from him. He set a Pumbedita scholar over the Academy of Sura.

That step broke with traditional usage of the academies. Solomon left no children of his own at his death. That fact let Anan rise to influence in Babylonian Jewry. Anan later founded the Karaite sect in the eighth century. A second Solomon, also son of a Hasdai, ruled later. He flourished in the middle of the twelfth century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spina-espina-al:
Alfonso de Spina was one of the most bitter enemies of the Jews. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He never belonged to Judaism, despite claims by some writers. He was general of the Franciscans and rector at Salamanca. He was also confessor to King Henry IV of Castile.

In sermons he made the Jews a constant target of attack. His Fortalitium Fidei gathered every charge against the Jews. It repeated tales of well poisoning, host desecration, and ritual murder. Its whole third book was devoted to attacking the Jews. He demanded that secret Jews be burned without mercy. The idea of the Spanish Inquisition began with Spina, the article says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-synagogue-14160:
The synagogue is the house where Jews gather to worship and learn. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its origin is wrapped in obscurity, the entry says. Tradition traced it back to the time of Moses. By later ages it stood at Judaism's center.

The synagogue likely arose during the Babylonian captivity. Exiles needed a shared place for prayer and teaching. Isaiah's phrase house of prayer may echo that need. A Jeremiah phrase, house of the people, was read as synagogue. Aramaic speakers called it bet amma in popular speech. Hellenistic Jews kept the term in their own usage. The long entry traces names, roots, and spread. It shows an exile-born institution becoming Judaism's backbone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-totemism-14460:
Totemism, the clan system built around an animal or plant ancestor, is tested against Israel. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Maclennan first claimed the system existed among early Hebrews. Robertson Smith took up the idea from Frazer's research. Smith tied it to his theory of sacrifice as blood covenant.

Animal names crowd the Bible's clan lists. Oreb the raven and Zeeb the wolf led Midian. Caleb means dog, and Jonah means dove. Tribes include fox, serpent, camel, and lion clans. The Horites show many animal names in one genealogy. That pattern hints at totem clans among nomads. Exogamy, marriage outside the clan, forms the next argument.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tunis-13460:
Tunis, a former Barbary state under French rule since 1881, had Jews from antiquity. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A monument found in 1883 attests Jews there by Christianity's dawn. Local tradition claims far earlier settlement. Titus sent many Jewish captives to Mauritania after 70.

Those settlers farmed, raised cattle, and practiced trades. They lived in clans under their own heads. Rome taxed them two shekels a head yearly. Under Romans and Vandals they grew and prospered. Church councils then passed restrictive laws against them. Justinian's edict of 534 classed Jews with heretics. Spanish Jews fleeing Visigothic persecution swelled the towns in the 600s. Many Berber tribes adopted Judaism through them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-veit-johannes-1:
Johannes Veit was a German painter of religious scenes. He was born in Berlin in 1790 and died at Rome in 1854. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Veit studied at Vienna and at Rome. At Rome he took the painter Vanucci as his model.

Veit joined the neo German school with his brother Philipp. He stood out for his rich use of color. He painted an altar piece for the cathedral at Liège. He also painted an Adoration of the Shepherds for a Berlin church. Several portraits of the Madonna brought him further fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-waldenburg-loui:
Louis Waldenburg was a German doctor of chest and throat diseases. He was born at Filehne, Posen, on July 31, 1837. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He died at Berlin on April 14, 1881. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1860.

Waldenburg settled in Berlin as a specialist. He edited medical journals for many years. From 1868 he ran the Berliner Klinische Wochenschrift. In 1871 he became assistant professor at Berlin. He later served as department doctor at the Charité. His books treat breathing therapy and lung disease. One studies tuberculosis and scrofula in depth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-welt-die-14860:
Die Welt was a Zionist weekly paper published at Vienna. Joseph Jacobs and A. M. Friedenberg wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its first number appeared on June 4, 1897. It has been issued regularly ever since. For some years Theodor Herzl funded it himself. He sank much of his own money into it.

The paper speaks for Zionism across the world. It covers Hebrew literature's revival and Jewish life. It also prints Jewish national tales. Supporting Jewish art is another of its aims. At the fifth Basel Congress it became official. It now serves as the Zionist movement's organ. A Yiddish edition appeared for a time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-witchcraft-1496:
Witchcraft, in the Bible, names the banned arts of telling the future by signs and spirits. Emil G. Hirsch and George A. Barton wrote the study for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article sorts the Hebrew words for these acts. It shows that views on them shifted over time.

One old practice was asking the dead for news of things to come. A spirit of the dead was called an ob. King Saul used such a rite at En-dor on the night before he died. The article says the rite was banned even then. Other acts counted as sorcery in some ages passed as harmless in others. The piece is a guide to how the Bible and later Jews drew that line.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yannai-known-al:
Yannai the Great was a scholar of Palestine of the first rank. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn wrote his long entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A chart found at Jerusalem traced his line to Eli. He was a rich man with four hundred vineyards, men said.

He gave an orchard of his own to the public. His first home was at Sepphoris in the north. There he seems to have held a post of trust. At the death of Rabbi Judah he spoke a kind word. He let priests join the march to the grave that day. Some hold that he lived all his life at Akbarah. There he set up a school of his own name. He was a top hand at both law and tales.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zamosz-zebi-hir:
Zebi Hirsch ben Benjamin Zamosz (1740-1807) was a German rabbi of wide reach. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as rabbi in more than one town. Brody and Glogau both held his post in their turns.

From 1803 to his death he led three towns as one. Those towns were Altona, Hamburg, and Wandsbeck in the north. He wrote more than one work in his long life. Most of them are court replies and text notes. They treat the Bible, the Talmud, and the law chiefs. Just one work of his reached print in his life. It is a set of his replies on two parts of the code. Its name is Tiferet Zebi in the Hebrew tongue. More of his replies stand in the books of two peers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zimmern-helen-1:
Helen Zimmern was a German-born author who wrote lives of famous figures and translated classic tales. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born at Hamburg on March 25, 1846. She moved to England while young and lived there until 1887, when she settled in Florence.

Her biographies cover the philosopher Schopenhauer, the novelist Maria Edgeworth, and the painter Sir Laurence Alma-Tadema. She translated Tales from the Eddas and the Epic of Kings into English. Her translations also include comedies by Goldoni and the Pentamerone. For the Story of the Nations series, she wrote a volume on the Hansa towns, the old German trading league.
l-alchimie-et-les-alchimistes-essai-hist:
Louis Figuier wrote this French history and critique of alchemy and the alchemists. Victor Lecou published it in Paris in 1860. Figuier held doctorates in science and medicine and taught chemistry.

Figuier opens by noting that alchemy still stirs curiosity and imagination. Its mystery, marvels, and famous adepts keep a strange prestige. Poets from early times to Goethe's Faust drew on its legends. His essay offers a critical history of hermetic philosophy for general readers. Figuier writes for curious general readers, not for adepts. He treats marvels with caution while honoring their hold on the mind.
leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-v-pg9:
This second Gutenberg copy of Leila's Book Five opens with the great battle. Moors watch from Granada's battlements at dawn. Ferdinand's army marches on the city below them.

Blackened, smoking wrecks litter the field at a distance. The siege that began in 1491 reaches its end here. Leila's divided loyalties come to their final test. Lytton gives the fall of Granada a romantic, mournful glow. Readers can compare this file with the library's other Book Five copy. The Alhambra's fate hangs over every battlefield scene. Lytton ends with loss on the winning side too.
les-dovze-clefs-de-philosophie-de-frere-:
A French translation of Basilius Valentinus's Twelve Keys appeared at Paris in 1660. Pierre Moët, bookseller near the Pont Saint-Michel, published it. The work treats true metallic medicine, its title says.

An added piece, the Azoth, explains how to make the philosophers' hidden gold. A poem on that Azoth joins the volume as well. Basilius was famed as a Benedictine monk and alchemist. His keys use pictures and riddles to hide doctrine. This edition shows French readers still studying him in 1660. Gobille, a Paris engraver, is named in its record. The keys' emblem pictures were central to Valentinus's fame.
levi-histoire-de-la-magie-1860:
French mage Eliphas Levi told the long tale of magic in Histoire de la magie, first out in 1860. Levi had been a priest in training, then a sage of the occult. He traces spells, rites, and lore from old Egypt and the East down to his own day in France.

Levi treats magic as a lost branch of deep truth, not mere tricks. His grand sweep gave the new occult wave a past to claim. The book, in French here, is the ground stone of that wave's view of its own roots. Levi wrote in French, and this text keeps that tongue in full. Waite's English take came later and spread the work far past France.
motley-united-netherlands-vol-1-1860:
John Lothrop Motley published History of the United Netherlands, Volume 1, in 1860. The work continues his Dutch epic after the rise of the republic. This volume covers the years after William the Silent's murder in 1584. The young republic fights Spain while seeking aid from England and France.

The Earl of Leicester's troubled command in the Netherlands fills much of the story. Motley follows diplomacy and war together, in courts and camps. His research and narrative sweep match his earlier volume. The series in time reached four volumes. Readers who finish the Rise will want this sequel. It shows the republic in its golden, perilous age.
mr-standfast-pg560:
John Buchan's 1919 novel is the third tale of Richard Hannay. A note points back to The Thirty-Nine Steps and Greenmantle. The book honors South African troops on the Western Front. Chapter names borrow from Pilgrim's Progress, from Wicket-Gate to Valley of Humiliation.

Hannay works under cover in wartime Britain to hunt a German spy. He must pose as a man who shuns the fight. The plot runs through air raids, chateaus, and secret lines. Friends like Blenkiron join the hunt. V1 called it the most personal Hannay book, with a strong close.
nightingale-notes-on-nursing-1860:
Florence Nightingale wrote Notes on Nursing in 1860 as a guide for anyone caring for the sick. She states her rule at once: nursing means putting the patient in the best state for nature to act. Fresh air, clean water, light, quiet, and clean rooms form her core teaching. The book founded modern nursing as a skilled practice.

Nightingale writes for homes as much as for hospitals, in plain direct sentences. She teaches close observation of the patient's face, food, and rest. Her stress on sanitation also spread statistical thinking into daily care. The Gutenberg text keeps her sharp voice intact. Few manuals have saved more lives.
notanda-chymica-manuscript-1660: Notanda Chymica is a manuscript dated 1660, held as Burndy manuscript number fourteen. The record ties it to Isaac Newton and to Michael Maier, and names Bern Dibner as donor. It describes the piece as handwritten notes and extracts, in Latin, from Maier's Arcana Arcanissima. The hosted sample is garbled character text from the manuscript pages, and it preserves no readable content. Page numbers of an edition are cited in the notes, per the record. Readers should treat this note as a record level guide only.
openalex-w2025526060:
Julie Perez, Fabrice Brescia, Jerome Becam and colleagues tracked rats and leptospirosis in New Caledonia. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2011. Rodents are the main reservoir of Leptospira bacteria. Outbreaks there peak in hot, rainy periods. Some local areas have extremely high case rates.

The team surveyed rodents twice a year for two years. The sites were two tribal areas with very high rates. They counted rodents and tested them for Leptospira. In a hot, rainy season, rodents were more numerous. More of them also carried the bacteria. Flood waters raise human contact with contaminated ground. The authors advise rodent control in cool, dry seasons. Then both rodents and disease are at their lowest.
openalex-w2048100860:
Mariafe Calingacion, Alice Laborte, Andrew Nelson and colleagues surveyed what rice quality means in world markets. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Demand for high quality rice is rising worldwide. Different markets prize different grain traits. Breeders need a full picture of those preferences.

The team drew on an international network for quality rice. They compared markets across many producing and consuming countries. Traits like texture, aroma and appearance vary in importance. Western buyers weigh quality factors differently from local ones. Breeding for one market may miss another's needs. The authors outline the science needed for targeted breeding. Consumer taste must guide rice research from the start.
openalex-w2060586060:
Adrien Wulff, Peter Hollingsworth, Antje Ahrends and colleagues set conservation priorities for rare plants in New Caledonia. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. The islands are a world biodiversity hotspot. They also face severe environmental damage. Many plant species grow in very few places.

The team assessed all flowering plants and conifers there. Species in three or fewer places counted as narrow endemics. Over six hundred species met that test. Only a minority had formal conservation assessments. Rare species clustered in clear hotspot areas. Mining threatens many of those sites. The authors mapped where protection is most urgent. Their data can guide new conservation assessments.
openalex-w2094514360:
Alison Burgess, Carlos Ayala-Grosso, Milan Ganguly and colleagues delivered stem cells to rat brains without surgery. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2011. Stem cells may treat brain diseases and injuries. Reaching the brain usually needs risky surgery. The blood-brain barrier blocks entry from the blood.

The team used focused ultrasound guided by brain scans. Sound briefly opened the barrier at chosen spots. Stem cells injected into the blood then entered. They targeted two brain regions, the striatum and hippocampus. Scans tracked the labelled cells arriving. Tissue checks a day later confirmed living stem cells. Some had begun turning into neurons. The method offers a gentler delivery route.
openalex-w2096162460:
Karine Brudey, Jeffrey Driscoll, Leen Rigouts and colleagues mined a world database of tuberculosis fingerprints. Their paper appeared in BMC Microbiology in 2006. Spoligotyping reads a marker pattern in TB bacteria. Labs worldwide shared results into one database. The fourth edition held records from many countries.

The team used the data to classify TB strains. They studied population patterns across regions. Some strain families clustered in single geographic areas. Others spread widely around the world. The database supports tracking of TB transmission routes. It also helps compare outbreaks between countries. Shared standards make such global tracking possible. The paper remains a reference for TB typing.
openalex-w2098109360:
Mandi Gandelman, Hugo Peluffo, Joseph Beckman and colleagues studied how spinal cord support cells can kill motor neurons. Their paper appeared in Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2010. The disease focus was ALS, a fatal nerve disease. In ALS, astrocytes carrying a gene fault turn harmful. Extra ATP outside cells may drive that change.

The team grew motor neurons together with astrocytes. Repeated ATP pulses made normal astrocytes toxic to neurons. A drug-like ATP mimic had the same effect. Blocking the ATP receptor protected the neurons fully. Speeding ATP breakdown also removed the toxicity. Faulty astrocytes depended on that same receptor signal. Blocking it might calm nerve inflammation in ALS.
openalex-w2151177060:
Stephen Goodwin, Sarrah Ben M'Barek, Braham Dhillon, and colleagues published this genome study in PLoS Genetics in 2011. They fully sequenced Mycosphaerella graminicola, the fungus behind septoria tritici blotch of wheat. The disease cuts wheat yield and quality worldwide, and the fungus hides inside leaves for a long latent spell before damage shows.

The finished genome holds twenty-one chromosomes. Remarkably, eight of them can be lost with no visible harm to the fungus. This spare set, called the dispensome, shifts between field strains and differs from the core genome in genes and repeats. The genome gives researchers a base for decoding the fungus's stealthy infection style.
openalex-w2750298560:
Gualberto González-Sapienza, Martín A. Rossotti, and Sofía Tabares-da Rosa reviewed single-domain antibodies in Frontiers in Immunology in 2017. Most antibodies pair heavy and light chains, but some animals make heavy-chain-only versions. Their single binding domain can be produced alone as a tiny, sturdy reagent. The review covers their use in analysis and diagnosis.

Antibodies detect trace targets inside complex samples with unmatched specificity. Recombinant fragments can be tagged and brewed cheaply by microbes, suiting them for sensors and test kits. Single-domain versions add stability and simple engineering to that toolkit. The authors first explain heavy-chain-only antibodies, then survey their applications. These small binders can reach targets that full antibodies fit poorly. Their rise expands the design space for immunoassays, biosensors, and point-of-care diagnostics.
openalex-w4387966260:
Mathew Maurer, Parag Kale, Marianna Fontana, and colleagues tested the drug patisiran in heart disease caused by transthyretin amyloidosis. Their report appeared in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2023. In this disease, a blood protein folds wrongly and builds up in the heart, stiffening it over time. Patisiran uses RNA interference to cut production of that protein in the liver. The phase three trial was double-blind and placebo-controlled.

Three hundred sixty patients with the inherited or wild-type form of the disease took part. Half received patisiran every three weeks for twelve months, half a placebo. The main measure was change in six-minute walking distance, with quality of life scores close behind. Later measures combined deaths, heart events, and hospital visits.
openalex-w7204531360: Parents who post their children's photos online rarely think about consent. This law article studies sharenting through the lens of children's vulnerability in the digital age, now sharpened by AI that can copy faces and voices. The authors weigh parents' free expression against children's rights to privacy and identity. A sharp legal analysis of a everyday habit with lasting consequences.
openalex-w7204707960: Ancient rock paintings in Tocantins face sun, rain, vandals, and time. This article studies the main forces damaging rock-art sites in the Serra do Lajeado protected area and sets out guidelines for watching, protecting, and managing them. The authors treat the sites as fragile cultural treasures needing active care. A heritage-conservation study where archaeology meets park management.
owen-footfalls-boundary-another-world-18:
Robert Dale Owen made the case for ghosts to his land in Footfalls on the Boundary of Another World, out in 1860. Owen was a man of state and print in the United States. He gathers tales of shades seen at death's hour, sounds with no source, and dreams that came true in grim detail from folk he trusts.

His tone is grave, fair, and free of cult zeal. Crowds took the book to heart at once. It gave the new faith a stamp of rank in that land. Few books did more to launch it.
plos-pbio-0020160:
Holger Prokisch, Curt Scharfe, David G. Camp, and a large team built a parts list for yeast mitochondria in PLOS Biology in 2004. Mitochondria are the cell's power plants. The team combined several methods to name the proteins that work inside yeast mitochondria, then sorted them by job.

A merged list beats any single method, since each one misses some proteins. The catalog gives the field a shared base for testing what each part does. Yeast mitochondria are a stand-in for our own, so the list also guides human work. Many human diseases trace to broken mitochondrial proteins, and a good map is the first step to finding them.
plos-pbio-0020260:
Stewart A. Weber, Jennifer L. Gerton, and Joan E. Polinsky studied chromosome centers in yeast for PLOS Biology in 2004. The kinetochore is the handle that pulling fibers grab to move chromosomes during division. Cohesin, the glue between sister chromosomes, binds most thickly around that handle's region.

The team found the kinetochore itself boosts that nearby glue binding. So the handle helps load the very glue that resists its pull, a neat balance of forces. Getting this balance wrong leads to lost or extra chromosomes. The study sharpens the picture of how cells make division accurate, a process whose failure is a hallmark of cancer cells.
plos-pone-0000060:
Devon Brewer, John Potterat, Stephen Muth, and co-authors measured what happens after an arrest in a 2006 study of deterrence. Their subject was men arrested for patronizing a prostitute. Criminology calls it specific deterrence when punishment stops the punished person from repeating the act, as opposed to scaring off others in general.

Following arrested men, the team found a large specific deterrent effect: arrest sharply cut repeat offending. That result speaks to a live policy fight over whether these arrests do anything beyond their cost. Evidence either way matters, and this study brought follow-up data, not just opinion, to a debate usually run on instinct.
plos-pone-0000160:
Matthew D. Carling and Robb T. Brumfield published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Population geneticists estimate genetic diversity, written as theta, from samples of genes across many loci. The authors compare gene sampling strategies: how many loci, and how many individuals per locus, give the best estimate for the effort.

Sequencing budgets force trade-offs, and a poor sampling plan wastes money or yields weak estimates. The authors test which designs hold up across multiple loci. Their guidance helps field biologists plan DNA sampling for wild populations, where the estimates feed into conservation and evolution studies.
plos-pone-0000260:
Arja Kaipainen, Mark W. Kieran, Sui Huang, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. PPAR-alpha is a protein that helps control fat metabolism and inflammation. The authors report that when inflammatory cells lack PPAR-alpha, tumor growth is suppressed, showing the protein's role depends on which cells carry it.

A gene can help a tumor in one cell type and hinder it in another. Separating the inflammatory cells' role from the tumor's own cells clarifies that picture. The finding warns drug developers that targeting PPAR-alpha will cut both ways unless the cell type is taken into account.
plos-pone-0000360:
Jesús Gómez-Zurita, Toby Hunt, Fatos Kopliku, and colleagues published this insect evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Leaf beetles, the Chrysomelidae, are a huge family of plant-eating insects. The authors present a recalibrated family tree of the beetles, dated with molecular clocks. They conclude that angiosperms, flowering plants, and their insect herbivores diversified independently rather than in lockstep.

The classic story says beetles radiated because flowering plants did. A recalibrated tree that uncouples the two timelines challenges that story. The paper is a careful piece of evidence in the long debate over co-evolution between plants and the insects that eat them.
plos-pone-0000460:
Evan H. Hurowitz and colleagues sped up an old measurement with a computational shortcut, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. A northern blot is a classic lab test for gene activity, but it is slow and one-gene-at-a-time. Their virtual northern analysis infers the same information for the human genome from existing sequence and expression data.

A virtual method that matches the bench test would let researchers screen the whole genome before spending weeks in the lab. Tools like this mark the point where genome databases became rich enough to answer questions once left to wet experiments. The study checks the shortcut against the real thing.
plos-pone-0000560:
Gustavo T. Rosa and colleagues found a side door a herpesvirus uses to enter cells, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Murine gamma-herpesvirus-68 is a mouse virus used to model human herpesviruses. The team showed that IgG Fc receptors provide an alternative infection route. When antibodies coat the virus, cells that grab antibodies can pull the virus in.

Antibodies are supposed to neutralize viruses, so a route that turns coating into entry is a trap in the defense. This trick, related to antibody-dependent enhancement, matters for vaccine design, since a vaccine that produces the wrong antibodies could help the virus. The mouse model lets researchers study the route safely.
plos-pone-0000660:
Kamini Singh, Devraj Mogare, Ramprasad Obula Giridharagopalan and colleagues studied a tumor suppressor gone wrong in breast cancer, for PLOS ONE in 2007. SMAR1 is a protein that interacts with p53, the famous cancer guard, and stabilizes it by a phosphate tag at one site. The team shows SMAR1's own production is switched on by p53 through a response element in its promoter.

When DNA damage was triggered by the drug doxorubicin, modified p53 was recruited to that element. The title reports SMAR1 is dysregulated in breast cancer, and the study follows its role in how cancer cells migrate and invade. A broken p53 partner fits the spread story.
plos-pone-0000760:
Jared L. Strasburg, Michael Kearney, Craig Moritz and colleagues combined family trees with range maps for an Australian gecko. Many parthenogenetic organisms, which reproduce without males, seem to have evolved recently and spread rapidly. Those patterns bear on the merits of sexual versus asexual reproduction, yet their interpretation is contested. The team's gecko lives in Australia's arid zone.

Combining phylogeography, the geography of gene lineages, with distribution modeling, they report multiple Pleistocene range expansions. Ice-age climate swings pushed the gecko's range out repeatedly. Each expansion left genetic traces that the combined methods can read. Asexual lineages are often dismissed as short-lived; this one's history is long and dynamic.
plos-pone-0000860:
Mariana de Napoles, Tatyana Nesterova and Neil Brockdorff watched the silent X chromosome wake up early in mouse germ cells, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The inactive X chromosome, characteristic of female body cells, is reactivated during development of the female germ cell lineage. In mouse, analysis of products of X-linked genes and transgenes had indicated when reactivation occurs. Primordial germ cells are the precursors of eggs.

Their title reports an early loss of Xist RNA expression, plus the chromatin modifications of the inactive X, in developing primordial germ cells. Xist is the RNA that coats and silences one X. Losing it early starts reactivation sooner than gene products reveal.
plos-pone-0000960:
Michael Poulsen, Daniel Erhardt, Daniel Molinaro and colleagues studied conflict inside the fungus growing ant partnership, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Ants, a fungus they farm for food and other microbes live in a famous mutualism. Theory says conflict inside such partnerships should threaten their stability.

The team focus on antagonistic interactions between bacteria in the system. Rival microbes may, in fact, help shape how host and symbionts relate over time. That twist matters: a partnership can be held together partly by the quarrels of its smaller members. The study adds hard detail to a textbook example of cooperation in nature.
plos-pone-0001060:
Michael Crossland, Steven Dakin and Peter Bex used illusions to reveal blind spots in damaged retinas, in PLOS ONE in 2007. People with retinal disease are often unaware of large gaps in their visual field. The brain fills in the missing area, hiding the loss from its owner.

That filling in makes standard tests unreliable. The team attempt to use illusory stimuli, images that exploit the filling in process, to identify the true blind spots. Finding hidden loss matters because patients who cannot see a gap cannot report or adapt to it. A clever test that outwits the brain's patchwork could change eye screening.
plos-pone-0001160:
What a mother experiences during pregnancy can shape her offspring before birth, though most evidence concerns harm from stress. Alessandro Sale and colleagues tested the opposite idea in a 2007 PLOS ONE article: whether an enriched environment during pregnancy speeds development of the fetus. They studied the visual system of the offspring.

The team reports that maternal enrichment during pregnancy accelerates retinal development in the fetus. The retina is part of the eye that senses light, and its early growth is easy to measure. The result suggests that positive conditions for the mother reach the developing brain, not just harmful ones.
plos-pone-0001260:
HIV-infected children are vaccinated on the same schedule as other children under the Expanded Program on Immunization. Mathurin Tejiokem and colleagues asked whether the protection from those vaccines lasts. Their study, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article, covered children living with HIV in Central Africa. Antiretroviral therapy was expected to prolong these children's lives considerably.

The authors report low persistence of antibodies to the program's vaccines in these children. Antibodies that fade early leave children unprotected against diseases the schedule was meant to prevent. Their findings raise the question of booster doses or adjusted schedules for HIV-infected children.
plos-pone-0001360:
Emotional blunting, a diminished ability to respond to emotionally salient stimuli, is a common and disabling feature of schizophrenia. Charmaine Pietersen and colleagues present an animal model of it, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The disturbance may stem from dysfunction of the amygdala, a brain region central to fear responses.

Negative emotional states, such as fear, are where the blunting shows most. A valid animal model lets researchers test the circuit basis of the symptom and screen candidate treatments. The authors describe their model's behavior and its relevance to the human condition.
plos-pone-0001460:
Flavio Rizzolio and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on short stature tied to hormone lack. Lack of growth hormone, alone or with other hormone lacks, causes most such cases. Faults in known genes explain some cases, but many stay unsolved. The team looked at a key region of chromosome 18.

They note stretches of DNA that do not code for proteins but are kept near unchanged across species. Such kept stretches often hold gene switches. Faults there could cause the same ills as gene faults do. The work argues for a shared cause that spans both kinds of DNA change.
plos-pone-0001560:
Jan Alexander Hiss and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on how malaria parasites ship proteins out. The parasite lives inside red blood cells and sends proteins out to reshape its home. A short mark on each shipped protein was the known guide. The team ran a computer scan of the parasite's full protein set for that mark.

They found the zones beside the mark hold a kept pattern that varies by protein family. That pattern refines who gets shipped and who stays. A sharper export rule helps labs predict parasite tricks. It may also flag points to jam the shipping line with drugs.
plos-pone-0001660:
Sandra Blanco, Marta Sanz-García, Claudio R. Santos, and their co-authors studied how a human kinase tempers inflammation signals in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A cell's response to any trigger reflects a balance among many signaling pathways, and protein interactions tip that balance. The kinase VRK2 can modulate several pathways.

The team reports that VRK2 interacts with JIP1, a scaffold protein that holds signaling parts together. Through that contact, VRK2 changes the gene response driven by interleukin-1, a strong inflammation messenger. The full text gives the interaction tests, the gene activity changes, and the pathway maps. Work like this shows how single protein contacts can retune a cell's answer to inflammation, a process at the heart of many diseases.
plos-pone-0001760:
Junghee Lee, Bradley S. Folley, John Gore, and their co-authors scanned the brains of people with schizophrenia during memory tasks in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Faulty prefrontal function is central to the working memory deficits of schizophrenia, but how activation and memory performance relate was undetermined. Working memory is the mental scratchpad used to hold and use information over seconds.

The team used two imaging methods together, functional MRI and near-infrared spectroscopy, during spatial working memory tasks. The full text gives the activation maps and where patient patterns diverged. Dual imaging cross-checks results, and locating the origin of the deficit helps target cognitive training and drug trials for schizophrenia.
plos-pone-0001860:
Kazuo Okanoya, Naoko Tokimoto, Noriko Kumazawa, and their co-authors trained rodents to use tools in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Tool use is defined as manipulating an inanimate object to change the position or form of a separate object. The expansion of cognitive niches and tool-use capabilities probably stimulated each other in hominid evolution, which makes simpler animal cases valuable.

With training, the rodents developed tool use with an optimal motor strategy and functional understanding, per the paper's title. The full text gives the training regimen and the animals' technique changes. Showing that a rodent can learn genuine tool use narrows the gap between human and animal cognition and gives labs a trainable model of it.
plos-pone-0001960:
Anna Syme and Gary Poore wrote a taxonomy study in PLOS ONE in 2008 that sorts out a small sea crustacean and its genus. The animal is an ostracod, a tiny shrimp-like creature in a two-part shell, named Cypridina mariae. Its story was tangled: the first account, from 1850, described only the shell, and that shell was thought lost.

The genus built on it, Cylindroleberis, had a messy naming history as well. The pair give a fuller account of the species and a fresh diagnosis of the genus. Careful naming work of this sort keeps species records stable, so field and lab studies can be sure they mean the same animal.
plos-pone-0002060:
Benoit Doublet and co-authors charted new landing sites of a drug-resistance island in Salmonella, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The Salmonella genomic island 1 is a block of DNA that can move between bacteria. It was first found in an epidemic, multidrug-resistant strain of Salmonella Typhimurium called DT104, and it carries a complex set of resistance genes.

The team report a secondary attachment site where the island can dock in the genome, and tandem integration, where copies line up in a row. Each extra docking route helps the island spread and persist. Tracking them aids the fight against drug-resistant food poisoning.
plos-pone-0002160:
Isabel Porto and co-authors surveyed the tiny algae that live alongside reef macroalgae in the Caribbean, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Symbiodinium are dinoflagellates, single-celled algae best known for living inside corals and feeding them energy from sunlight. That coral partnership has drawn much study as reefs decline worldwide.

Far less was known about Symbiodinium cells that live free or cling to seaweeds rather than coral. The team sampled Caribbean reefs to map where these forms occur and how they spread. Knowing the full range of these algae matters, since free-living stocks may help reefs recover after bleaching.
plos-pone-0002260:
Laure Perrin-Cocon, Sophie Agaugué, Olivier Diaz, and co-authors studied immune cells from people with long-term hepatitis C, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Chronic hepatitis C leaves patients with weak antibody and killer cell responses. A defect in dendritic cells, the scouts that start immune attacks, has been suspected. The matter stayed controversial, though.

The team grew dendritic cells from patients' blood cells and stimulated them through a sensor called TLR4. They report that the cells' Th1-driving function, the branch of immunity that fights viruses, was disabled. A defined defect like this points to where immune therapy for chronic hepatitis C might push.
plos-pone-0002360:
Shao-Yin Chen, Yulei Wang, Marilyn Telen, and co-authors read the small RNAs inside mature red blood cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mature red cells have no nucleus or organelles, and it was commonly thought they hold no nucleic acids at all. That assumption had rarely been tested directly with modern tools.

The team analyzed the transcriptome of purified human mature red cells and found microRNAs present and varied. In sickle cell disease, where red cells are the whole story, the microRNA expression pattern differs. Leftover RNA in red cells may help regulate their lifespan and could offer new markers for blood diseases.
plos-pone-0002460:
Müller and colleagues set out their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The author list runs from Martina S. Müller, Julius F. Brennecke, Elaine T. Porter, and others. Its subject is perinatal Androgens and Adult Behavior Vary with Nestling Social System in Siblicidal Boobies. Exposure to androgens early in development, while activating adaptive aggressive behavior, may also exert long-lasting effects on non-target components of phenotype.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002560:
Led by Flierl, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Michael A. Flierl, Daniel Rittirsch, Anthony J. Chen, and others. Its subject is the Complement Anaphylatoxin C5a Induces Apoptosis in Adrenomedullary Cells during Experimental Sepsis. Sepsis remains a poorly understood, enigmatic disease.

One of the cascades crucially involved in its pathogenesis is the complement system. Especially the anaphylatoxin C5a has been shown to have many harmful effects during sepsis. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002660:
Work by Martina Buck and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was direct infection and replication of naturally occurring hepatitis c virus genotypes 1, 2, 3 and 4 in normal human hepatocyte cultures. Authorship is credited in the record to Martina Buck and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection afflicts about 170 million individuals worldwide. The authors add a further point. However, the HCV life cycle is only partially understood because it has not been possible to infect normal human hepatocytes in culture. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002760:
Work by David González and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was brucellosis vaccines: assessment of brucella melitensis lipopolysaccharide rough mutants defective in core and O-Polysaccharide synthesis and export. The full author list in the catalog record begins with David González, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. The brucellae are facultative intracellular bacteria that cause brucellosis, one of the major neglected zoonoses. The authors add a further point. In endemic areas, vaccination is the only effective way to control this disease. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002860:
Work by Eduardo Lugo and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was ubiquitous crossmodal stochastic resonance in humans: auditory noise facilitates tactile, visual and proprioceptive sensations. The catalog record names Eduardo Lugo first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Stochastic resonance is a nonlinear phenomenon whereby the addition of noise can improve the detection of weak stimuli. The authors add a further point. An optimal amount of added noise results in the maximum enhancement, whereas further increases in noise intensity only degrade detection or information content. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002960:
Patrick Mardulyn, Marie-Anne Vaesen and Michel Milinkovitch grew lab populations with known history in 2008 to test inference methods. Natural populations whose past is known in detail would be ideal for checking tools that reconstruct history from genes. Such populations are extremely rare in the wild.

As an alternative, the team cultured replicate populations in the lab and generated microsatellite data from them. Since the true history was controlled, methods could be scored against fact. Published in PLOS ONE, the setup gives evolutionary biologists a benchmark for tools used on wild populations. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003060:
Nicholas Lesica, Toshiyuki Ishii and Garrett Stanley improved estimates of receptive fields from natural stimuli in 2008. Natural stimuli show that neural responses differ in key ways from responses to artificial ones. Yet natural inputs contain strong correlations and uneven intensity distributions, which bias standard estimates.

A receptive field is the pattern a neuron responds to. The team tackles asymmetric intensity distributions head-on in how they estimate these fields. Published in PLOS ONE, better estimates from real-world stimuli help sensory research leave simple lab patterns behind and still stay exact. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003160:
Yao-Zhong Liu, Scott G. Wilson, Liang Wang and colleagues search for genes behind hip bone size in women in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Osteoporosis is the most common metabolic bone disease in older people and raises the risk of hip fractures from minor falls, which carry high illness and death rates. Hip bone size is one key measurable risk factor for those fractures.

In a genome-wide association study, the authors identify the PLCL1 gene for variation in hip bone size in females. Readers get a concrete gene lead from a broad scan. Such leads can improve risk prediction and point to the biology of bone growth.
plos-pone-0003260:
Heather B. Jaspan, Lyen C. Huang, Mark F. Cotton and colleagues review bacterial disease in HIV-infected children in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serious bacterial infections are a major source of morbidity and mortality in HIV-infected children. The spectrum of disease is wide, and the germs at fault vary according to setting. Use of antibiotic prophylaxis and emergence of multi-drug resistant bacteria made local data needed.

Their retrospective cohort study covers bacterial disease and antimicrobial susceptibility patterns in children in hospital with HIV. Readers get a record for one setting of which bacteria caused illness and which drugs still worked. Such patterns guide first-choice antibiotics where lab testing is scarce.
plos-pone-0003360:
Brigitte Mack and Olivier Gires examine CD44 forms in head and neck tissues in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. CD44 splice variants are long known as being associated with cell transformation. Recently, the standard form of CD44 was shown to be part of the signature of cancer stem cells in colon, breast, and head and neck squamous cell carcinomas. This was somewhat surprising given the variant history.

The authors compare CD44s and CD44v6 expression in head and neck epithelia. Readers see normal tissue expression set beside tumour-associated claims. Baseline expression matters, because a cancer stem cell marker is useful only if healthy tissue lacks it or uses it differently.
plos-pone-0003460:
Shelley R. Starck and co-authors found a hidden source of cell surface markers in this 2008 paper. Cells display protein fragments on MHC class I molecules for immune checks. Those fragments were thought to come only from normal protein production. Some fragments, though, start at unusual start signals in the message.

The team showed a distinct way of starting protein building makes these hidden fragments. They call the products cryptic peptides. Immune cells can then spot cells making odd proteins. The finding adds a secret supply line to immune surveillance. Hidden protein bits like these may explain some responses doctors could not trace before.
plos-pone-0003560:
Iuliia Vitko and co-authors studied how a helper subunit steers calcium channels in this 2008 paper. Voltage-gated calcium channels pass signals in nerves and muscles. A beta subunit controls the main pore unit's traffic and behavior. Crystal studies had mapped where the two parts touch.

The team showed the beta unit's orientation toward the pore is critical. Twist that angle, and channel regulation changes. How contact leads to control was the open question. Precise geometry thus helps set nerve and muscle signaling. Calcium channels sit at the heart of pain, mood, and heart rhythm drugs.
plos-pone-0003660:
