Alessandro Muzzi, Monica Moschioni, Antonello Covacci, and colleagues published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major disease-causing bacterium. It grips host cells with hair-like pili, whose genes sit together in one operon.

Such grip tools face two pressures: keep working, yet change enough to escape the immune system. The team traced the pilus operon's history and found positive selection and recombination driving it. Their work shows how a pathogen's surface gear can evolve fast while staying useful to the bacterium. That balance helps the germ stay a step ahead of its host.
plos-pone-0003760:
Tobias Mourier and Eske Willerslev published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Retroelements are DNA pieces that copy themselves around the genome. They make up about forty percent of the human genome. Yet large regions of mammal genomes contain none at all.

The authors test whether selection against transcriptional interference keeps those regions clean. A retroelement landing near genes could garble how they are read, and selection may remove such inserts. Their analysis asks whether that pressure, rather than chance, sweeps certain genomic yards clean. Their answer bears on how genomes guard their working genes.
plos-pone-0003860:
Shireesh Srivastava, Linxia Zhang, Rong Jin, and colleagues published this bioinformatics paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. A main goal of microarray analysis is picking the genes that separate one condition from another. Earlier work showed that using prior knowledge about gene function can surface more meaningful hits.

The authors present a method that folds Gene Ontology information into unsupervised clustering and feature selection. The ontology tells the algorithm what each gene is known to do. The approach finds gene groups that make biological sense, not just statistical clusters. The same trick can serve other chip studies beyond this one.
plos-pone-0003960:
Meta Roestenberg, Ed Remarque, Erik de Jonge, and co-authors trialed a malaria vaccine candidate in 2008. The vaccine uses AMA1, a protein of Plasmodium falciparum. The parasite needs AMA1 to enter red blood cells and liver cells. Antibodies that block AMA1 can stop that entry.

Their PLOS ONE article tested the vaccine with three different adjuvants. Adjuvants are added ingredients that boost immune response. The team compared safety and immune response across Alhydrogel, Montanide ISA 720, and AS02. Picking the best partner formula is a required step toward field trials. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004060:
Joan Reibman, Michael Marmor, Joshua Filner, and co-authors linked a stomach germ to lower asthma odds in 2008. Germ exposure early in life may guard against allergic disease. Asthma has risen as many gut microbes have become rarer. Helicobacter pylori, a common stomach bacterium, has declined in cities.

Their PLOS ONE article reports asthma was inversely tied to H. pylori status. People carrying the germ had asthma less often in this urban sample. The pattern supports the idea that lost microbes changed immune training. It does not by itself prove the germ prevents asthma. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004160:
Ai Ling Wang and colleagues published this eye study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Age-related macular degeneration is a leading cause of lost central vision in older people. Early in the disease, deposits called drusen form on a membrane behind the retina.

The study looks at the ageing retinal pigment epithelium, the cell layer that feeds the retina. It focuses on two of the layer's cleanup systems. One is autophagy, where cells digest their own worn parts. The other is exosomes, tiny parcels that cells release. The authors weigh how these systems may contribute to drusen formation. Their ideas connect everyday cell housekeeping to a common cause of blindness.
plos-pone-0004260:
Hyun Kwon and colleagues published this smell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Olfactory marker protein is the hallmark of mature olfactory sensory neurons, the nerve cells that detect odors. Since its discovery, what the protein actually does had stayed poorly understood, though knockout mice showed it shapes olfactory signal handling.

The team examined how calcium leaves these neurons after a smell response, a step handled by the NCX exchanger. They report that calcium extrusion by NCX is compromised in mice lacking the marker protein. The result assigns the mysterious protein a concrete job in resetting the sense of smell.
plos-pone-0004360:
Yoshinori Yamakawa and colleagues published this social neuroscience study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Across cultures, social relationships are often described in spatial terms: close friends, distant relatives, high lords. The authors ask whether this cognitive mapping of social concepts onto physical space arises from shared brain resources for processing social and physical relationships.

Using brain imaging, they studied the evaluation of social distance in the human parietal cortex. That region is famous for handling physical space and number. Finding it also handles social closeness would show the metaphor is built into the brain.
plos-pone-0004460:
Faces carry clues to a person's ancestry, and Yann Klimentidis and Mark Shriver tested how well those clues can be measured in PLOS ONE in 2009. People read ethnicity from faces every day, and those readings shape social life. They may also reflect a long history of human groups living apart and adapting.

In the United States, recent mixing between groups from different continents makes faces a mixed record. The authors estimated ancestry proportions from facial features and checked them against genetic measures. If faces track ancestry with fair accuracy, they become a cheap research tool. The study also raises care points, since reading ancestry from looks can mislead, and has a charged social history.
plos-pone-0004560:
Different steps in a growth signal chain respond with different sensitivity, model Jeongah Yoon and Thomas Deisboeck in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cell growth depends on signaling pathways, chains of proteins that pass messages from the cell surface inward. Their regulation is a major focus of cancer research.

The team applied computational methods to the MAPK signaling cascade as triggered by the growth factor EGF. They used a multi-parametric global sensitivity analysis, which varies many factors at once to see which ones control the outcome. They did so without assuming in advance which components matter most. Maps of sensitivity like this tell drug designers where a pathway is fragile and where it will shrug off a single blocked step.
plos-pone-0004660:
Whether two asthma-linked signals can cross the placenta from mother to fetus is tested by Robert Lim and Lester Kobzik in PLOS ONE in 2009. The mechanisms by which prenatal events affect the development of adult disease are incompletely characterized. In a mouse model of maternal transmission of asthma risk, mothers pass a tendency toward asthma to their pups.

The candidate couriers are interleukins 4 and 13, pro-asthmatic cytokines, immune signal proteins. The team sought to test their role by assessing whether they make the transplacental passage. If such signals cross, a mother's immune state could directly tutor the fetal immune system. That would help explain how asthma risk is set before birth, and where prevention might start.
plos-pone-0004760:
Robert Gaeta and colleagues measured gene activity in newly remade oilseed rape hybrids using Arabidopsis chips, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Remade hybrids let scientists watch what happens right after two genomes merge in one plant. Past work showed chromosome swaps in later generations change gene activity by losing or doubling matched genes.

Swaps may also affect genes far from the swap site in indirect ways. The team used chips from a model plant to profile activity in the hybrids. Their data help separate direct from indirect effects. That matters for breeding crops from wide crosses. Replication in other settings will show how robust the findings really are.
plos-pone-0004860:
Julie Pendergast and colleagues reported robust food anticipatory activity in BMAL1 deficient mice, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Food availability is a potent cue directing circadian locomotor activity in rodents. Even though nocturnal rodents prefer to forage at night, daytime food anticipatory activity is observed prior to short meals presented at a scheduled time. Persisting even when the central clock gene BMAL1 is absent.

Anticipation survives loss of the master clock gene. A separate food entrainable oscillator must exist. Finding its location remains a major goal. Meal timing affects metabolism broadly. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004960:
Birds sing hardest at dawn and dusk. Scientists have proposed many explanations for these choruses. Vincenzo Penteriani and Maria del Mar Delgado added an owl's-eye view in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied eagle owls, which call at dusk. Eagle owls carry a white throat badge that shows during calling.

The owls vocalized most when the badge contrasted most with the fading light. Timing matched the badge's visibility, not just the hour. That suggests the call and the badge form one combined display. The signal is tuned to twilight. The study links song output to a visual signal in a nocturnal bird.
plos-pone-0005060:
Synovial sarcoma is a soft-tissue cancer. A recurrent chromosome swap creates a fusion protein in it. The protein is called SYT-SSX2. Roy Barco and colleagues studied its effects in PLOS ONE in 2009. They found it antagonizes Bmi1. Bmi1 is a key member of the polycomb complex. That complex silences genes.

By jamming the silencer, the cancer protein deregulates polycomb activity. Normal gene control gets scrambled. The finding reveals how one fusion protein rewires the cell's rulebook. It connects a single genetic accident to broad gene chaos. That connection may suggest treatments. Restoring polycomb balance could counter the fusion's effects. The study maps a mechanism, not just a marker.
plos-pone-0005160:
Mitochondria split and fuse to stay healthy. A protein called GDAP1 drives the splitting, called fission. Konstanze Wagner and colleagues studied how GDAP1 reaches its post. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Many such proteins anchor into the mitochondrial outer membrane by a tail. That tail-anchor sits at the protein's end.

GDAP1's targeting and function both depend on its tail-anchor. The tail is not just glue. It modulates what the protein does once anchored. Whether tails tune function was unknown before this. The finding reveals how location and activity intertwine. GDAP1 defects cause a nerve disease in humans. Understanding its anchoring may explain how those defects harm nerves.
plos-pone-0005260:
Flu surveillance often relies on lab reports that arrive late. Phone triage lines, where nurses advise callers, log symptoms much earlier in an outbreak. Yih and colleagues tested those logs as a flu signal in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study asked whether telephone triage data can detect influenza-like illness in the community. Call patterns could act as an early-warning sensor for seasonal flu and for a pandemic. Cheap, fast signals like this help health officials time warnings and stock supplies. Phone lines log each call the day it is made, so a spike in cough and fever calls can warn a city days before lab reports come in.
plos-pone-0005360:
A variant near the TNF gene had already been tied to higher risk of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. TNF's protein product switches on NF-kB, a master regulator of inflammation. Wang and colleagues widened the search across those gene families in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The study tested common variants in the TNF and TNF receptor superfamilies and in NF-kB transcription factors. Each variant was checked for association with lymphoma risk. Since inflammation and lymphoma are linked, a full family scan can reveal which steps in the pathway matter most. Lymphoma care turns on how fast the disease moves, and gene marks tied to risk may one day help sort new cases. Pick the depth of care each one needs at the start.
plos-pone-0005460:
David Haskell and Anupam Adhikari tested an old idea of Darwin's in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. In his famous book on species, Darwin guessed that the making of new species runs at different speeds in different groups. He also guessed that groups rich in species at one level tend to be rich at other levels too.

Using bird data, the authors found that both guesses hold up. They also showed that the pattern can predict which living birds face the highest risk of dying out. An old hunch, tested with modern data, turns into a tool for protecting birds.
plos-pone-0005560:
Linda Heinemann, Andreas Kleinschmidt, and Notger Müller studied brain responses during visual attention in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. When people focus on one spot, the brain's vision areas react even in parts that map places with nothing on screen. The team measured those responses at set distances from the attended spot.

They varied the scene to see what drives the quiet responses in unstimulated areas. Such responses show that attention spreads through the visual field in a structured way. Knowing that spread helps explain how the brain picks out what matters in a busy scene.
plos-pone-0005660:
Fabienne Ripoll and co-authors published the genome of an emerging lung pathogen in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mycobacterium abscessus is a fast-growing relative of the tuberculosis germ. It causes a stubborn lung disease, above all in people with cystic fibrosis whose lungs are already damaged.

Reading its genome revealed virulence genes borrowed from unrelated germs, not just from its own family. Borrowed genes may explain how a soil and water germ became a lung pathogen. The genome gives drug hunters a full parts list to work from. Its lung disease is hard to cure with current drugs, so each borrowed virulence gene is a possible weak point.
plos-pone-0005760:
Dong Gao and co-authors named a new immune booster protein in 2009. Cells detect viral RNA through sensors such as RIG-I, which then switch on interferon defenses. The team found a ring-finger protein, which they named REUL, that binds this pathway.

REUL acts as an E3 ubiquitin ligase, a tag-placing enzyme, and it stimulates RIG-I's alarm. Placing the right tags strengthens the signal that produces type I interferons. Those interferons are the body's early antiviral blanket. A new booster in that chain is a fresh lead for antiviral design and for understanding immune faults.
plos-pone-0005860:
Robert Beckman argued in 2009 that mutations which raise the mutation rate can speed tumor growth across many possible fitness landscapes. A tumor needs several genetic changes to become dangerous. Mutator mutations boost genomic instability, supposedly fast-tracking those changes.

The rival view holds that simple repeated selection of faster lineages explains the pattern without mutators. Beckman's analysis tests the mutator idea mathematically across landscapes. If mutators truly help, tumors carrying them may behave and respond differently. The paper is theory, but theory that shapes how oncologists interpret the mutation loads seen in real cancers.
plos-pone-0005960:
The valve that lets blood leave the heart stiffens as years pass. Eli Weinberg, Frederick Schoen and Mohammad Mofrad built a computer model of that slow change in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers both normal aging of the aortic valve and the disease called calcific aortic stenosis, where hard nodules stiffen the valve flaps.

A model lets the team test how local strain in the tissue may drive the buildup of calcium over time. That link between force and disease is hard to watch in a living heart. The work gives valve science a tool for asking what starts the stiffening, and where a future treatment might step in early.
plos-pone-0006060:
Rotavirus sends crowds of young children to clinics and hospitals each year. Joke Bilcke, Pierre Van Damme, Marc Van Ranst and colleagues gathered the world's counts in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper is a systematic review and meta-analysis of how often symptomatic rotavirus infection occurs, drawing on community studies that followed children where they live.

No pooled estimate of this kind existed before, though the number drives the math on whether vaccines pay for themselves. A firm incidence rate steadies cost-effectiveness studies and health budgets alike. The review gives vaccine planners, above all in poorer countries, a shared figure to plan against instead of scattered local guesses.
plos-pone-0006160:
Prey grow slower when predators are near, and the textbook blames skipped meals. Ulrich Steiner and Josh Van Buskirk tested a rival account in 2009: that predators change prey metabolism itself. Their PLOS ONE paper examines the growth and predation risk tradeoff, which usually assumes reduced activity explains why defense costs growth.

Predator-induced changes in metabolism cannot explain the tradeoff, the title concludes. Ruling out a plausible mechanism is progress, since it sends the field back to behavior and other costs with better focus. The result keeps a classic ecology question open, and open in a more precise place than before.
plos-pone-0006260:
Half of the human protein set still lacks a known job, years after the genome was read. Diana Hooi Ping Low and colleagues characterised one such unknown, a tectonin protein, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Its structure folds into repeated propeller shapes that can grip several partners at once.

The protein interacts with ficolin, an immune molecule, and binds LPS, a bacterial surface toxin. Those links place the unknown protein in the body's germ defence. Each solved unknown can reveal new pathways and cascades. The study is a reminder that the genome's parts list is still being annotated.
plos-pone-0006360:
Patients fighting tuberculosis and HIV together face stigma from both diseases at once. Sirinapha Jittimanee and colleagues surveyed such patients in Thailand in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Stigma and knowledge are believed to shape willingness to seek treatment and to stick with it.

The team measured what patients knew about their diseases and how stigma affected them. Both diseases are medically complex as well as socially stigmatising. Programmes that ignore shame may fail even with good drugs available. The survey gives Thai health services concrete points to address. Care that treats both the body and the mind stands a better chance to work.
plos-pone-0006460:
Tirta Susilo, Kate Crookes, Elinor McKone, and colleagues compared face reading in children and adults for PLOS ONE in 2009. People tend to recognize faces of their own age better than faces of other ages. Why that happens was unclear. One candidate cause is holistic processing, seeing a face as a whole rather than part by part.

Using the composite task, a test that reveals whole-face processing, the team studied child faces. Their title reports stronger holistic processing in children than in adults for those faces. The result supports the idea that experience tunes face reading. It helps explain why own-age faces feel easier to remember.
plos-pone-0006560:
Gerardo Zardi and co-authors studied a shell-boring parasite and mussel invasions in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stress from other living things may work with harsh settings to slow or aid an invasion. It can also change how invaders and native species compete. The team studied endolithic parasitism, where small organisms bore into shells. They worked on both invasive and native mussels in a place where conditions swing a lot.

A parasite that weakens invaders more than natives could slow an invasion down. One that harms natives more could speed it up. The mussels show why invasion results are hard to guess from species lists alone. Both the place and its parasites shape the outcome.
plos-pone-0006660:
Victoria Morgan and co-authors merged two kinds of brain scans in PLOS ONE in 2009. MRI can map the brain in two ways: how areas wire together and how they fire together. That power sparked wide interest in studying both maps as one. Functional MRI shows which areas turn on at the same time. Diffusion MRI traces the white matter cables that link areas.

By joining the two, the team could study how structure and function relate in brain networks. Strong cables should back strong joint firing, but the two do not always match. Those gaps are of real interest for science and care. Their joint approach helps work on epilepsy and other network ills of the brain.
plos-pone-0006760:
Nowel Azzouz and co-authors mapped partnerships of a major RNA control complex in yeast in PLOS ONE in 2009. The complex is called CCR4-NOT. It has nine subunits in yeast, including the deadenylase Ccr4. In the nucleus it connects to transcription. In the cytoplasm it helps break down messenger RNA.

The team showed the complex physically interacts with TRAMP. It also interacts with the nuclear exosome, an RNA shredding machine. Physical contact plus functional effects tie the systems together. RNA quality control thus works as a connected network. Understanding the network explains how bad transcripts are caught and destroyed.
plos-pone-0006860:
Rebecca M. Green and colleagues exposed a tiny worm to cigarette smoke in PLOS ONE in 2009. Smoking is the major cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and lung cancer. Bacterial infections help drive COPD as airway immunity weakens. The worm Caenorhabditis elegans served as a living model. It has a simple innate immune system that researchers know well.

Smoke exposure changed the worms' innate immunity in vivo. The model lets scientists screen immune effects quickly and cheaply. Findings in worms can nominate pathways to test in mammals. That speeds the search for how smoke weakens lung defense. It may eventually support treatments for infection-prone COPD patients.
plos-pone-0006960:
K. G. Guruharsha, Mar Ruiz-Gomez, H. A. Ranganath, and colleagues mapped a muscle gene's control in fruit flies in PLOS ONE in 2009. Muscle fibers form when myoblast cells fuse together. A gene called dumbfounded, also known as kirre, is an early player in that fusion. It must be switched on in founder cells, which attract other myoblasts to fuse with them.

The team charted where and when this attractant gene turns on. Its regulation proved complex in both space and time. A fixed number of founder cells is chosen from a pool of equals. Precise gene timing is what marks those founders out.
plos-pone-0007060:
Daisuke Nishizawa, Makoto Nagashima, Ryoji Katoh, and colleagues linked pain relief genes to surgery in PLOS ONE in 2009. Opioids are standard drugs for strong pain. Yet people differ widely in how much opioid they need. The team focused on a potassium channel subunit, GIRK2, encoded by the gene KCNJ6.

They compared KCNJ6 variants with painkiller needs after major abdominal surgery. Patients' genes tracked with how much analgesic they required. Such links point toward personal pain prescribing. A gene test before surgery might one day set the first dose more accurately.
plos-pone-0007160:
Juliane Bremer, Mathias Heikenwalder, Johannes Haybaeck, and colleagues tested prion risk factors in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Susceptibility to prion infection depends on the agent's strength and on gene modifiers. Host and environmental risk factors were largely unknown. The activation state of the immune system was one suspect, since prions travel through immune tissues.

The team immunized mice repeatedly before exposing them to prions from the body periphery. Immunization increased their susceptibility to the infection. That result is counterintuitive and important. It suggests immune stimulation can help prions take hold, with lessons for vaccine timing near exposure risks.
plos-pone-0007260:
Eleni A. Markakis, Masanori Sasaki, Karen L. Lankford, and colleagues tested brain progenitor cells for spinal cord repair in 2009. Progenitor cells from adult brain tissue are tools for studying remyelination. Remyelination restores the fatty sheath that lets nerves conduct signals quickly after demyelinating damage occurs.

Cells from neurogenic brain regions had already shown remyelination potential. The authors take cells from the progenitor fraction of adult olfactory bulb tissue. They test whether those cells become remyelinating glia in demyelinating spinal cord lesions. Their PLOS ONE paper reports convergence toward that repair role.
plos-pone-0007360:
Aurélie Fort, Magali Cordaillat, Catherine Thollon, and colleagues studied sodium channels in artery contraction in PLOS ONE in 2009. Voltage-gated sodium channels had been found in arterial muscle cells. Patch-clamp measurements confirmed their electrical currents, but no information showed whether these channels play a functional role in contraction of arteries.

The authors test that role in the rat aorta. They present new insights into how sodium channels contribute to contraction. Their work gives sodium channels a place in blood vessel tone. That place could matter for understanding blood pressure control and vascular disease.
plos-pone-0007460:
C. Patrick Doncaster published a theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how ecologists explain patterns of species abundance. A famous framework, Hubbell's neutral theory, assumes all species have identical vital rates. That simple premise predicts real patterns surprisingly well. Yet many ecologists doubt species are truly interchangeable. Doncaster examined a softer assumption called ecological equivalence.

Under equivalence, species are alike in the ways that matter for the model, not identical in every detail. He argues this is a realistic and testable alternative to neutral theory. Framing it rigorously lets scientists compare the two ideas against field data. The paper is a contribution to theory rather than experiment. It gives a long-running debate a cleaner set of options.
plos-pone-0007560:
Ronald Hancock and Yasmina Hadj-Sahraoui published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on preparing cell nuclei for study. Nuclei are usually isolated in salty solutions that keep them compact. The real cell interior, though, is not a salt bath. It is crowded with large molecules. The authors questioned whether standard ionic conditions distort what nuclei look like and how they behave.

They isolated nuclei using inert macromolecules that imitate the cytoplasm's crowding. The approach preserves nuclear structure under conditions closer to life. A more faithful preparation gives a truer view of the genome's home. Details like chromatin packing depend on the surroundings, so the surroundings should be right. The study offers cell biologists a gentler, more realistic way to handle the nucleus.
plos-pone-0007660:
Heidi Vebø and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on Enterococcus faecalis, a bacterium with a double life. It normally lives harmlessly in the human gut. In hospitals, it turns opportunist, causing bloodstream and other infections. The team read the bacterium's full transcriptome, all the genes it switches on, while it grew in blood. That environment is where the commensal becomes an invader.

The blood-grown bacteria ran an adaptive program distinct from gut life. Genes for surviving the bloodstream's defenses and scarcity switched on. Reading that program shows how the turn to pathogen happens. It also lists candidate factors that hospital strains need and gut strains may not use. Such lists guide the hunt for drug and vaccine targets. The study catches a familiar microbe in the act of changing sides.
plos-pone-0007760:
Andrew Ramsay and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It models TB testing services in Malawi under new policies and tools. A recent WHO policy changed how smear microscopy, the basic TB test, should be done. Low-cost fluorescence microscopes were also becoming available.

The team used a hospital laboratory register in Lilongwe as their base. They estimated effects on case detection and laboratory workload. Better microscopes could find more cases without crushing lab staff. Modeling first lets a poor country weigh gains against costs. The study supports smarter roll-out of new TB diagnostics.
plos-pone-0007860:
Vishal Prashar and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It captures a single water molecule at work inside HIV's key enzyme. HIV-1 protease cuts viral proteins into working parts. It is a premier target for AIDS drugs.

Designing blockers requires knowing exactly how the enzyme performs its cut. X-ray analysis revealed a catalytic water molecule sitting in the active site. It was found there alongside a product peptide, the piece just cut. That snapshot sharpens the picture of the transition state. Drug designers can use it to build tighter-fitting inhibitors.
plos-pone-0007960:
Michael Holmes and colleagues took stock of gene-guided prescribing in PLOS ONE in 2009. The field, pharmacogenetics, promises drug choice and dose matched to a person's genes. Their review gathered studies from across the field and judged the strength of the proof behind each claim.

Much of the promise still rested on thin or mixed proof. A few gene-drug pairs stood on firm ground, but many awaited solid trials. The sober survey helps doctors and funders tell ready tools from early hopes, so patients get tests that truly help rather than costly guesses.
plos-pone-0008060:
Federica Crostarosa and colleagues built a monkey model of two infections meeting in one body for PLOS ONE in 2009. Herpes simplex virus type 2 raises the odds of catching and passing HIV, even when no sores show. Testing prevention gels needs a model where both viruses meet as they do in people.

Macaques given vaginal herpes and an HIV-like virus let the team watch the pair interact and test microbicide gels against them. A faithful model can weed out weak gels before human trials. That saves time, money, and risk for the women such gels are meant to protect.
plos-pone-0008160:
Cheryl Olman and colleagues mapped a flaw in brain scans of the memory center in PLOS ONE in 2009. The medial temporal lobe holds key memory structures, but it sits near air and bone. In functional MRI, those borders warp the magnetic field and bend or erase the signal.

The team charted where the bending and loss are worst, and how they shift with scan settings. Honest maps of a flaw are the first step to fixing it. Memory research leans hard on this brain zone, so cleaner scans there mean firmer claims about how memory works.
plos-pone-0008260:
Eva-Liis Loogväli and colleagues examined the mitochondrial molecular clock in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Scientists use mitochondrial DNA changes to date genetic events. Among living humans, the clock seems to tick faster than species comparisons suggest. The rate from human-chimpanzee comparisons looks slower. That mismatch limits how clocks can be calibrated across species.

The authors set out to explain the imperfection of the hominid clock. If the rate changes over time, dates for migrations and splits shift. Fixing the clock affects much of human evolutionary history. Their analysis helps readers judge how firm those dates are.
plos-pone-0008360:
Kerstin Svensson and colleagues presented a PCR array for Francisella in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Francisella bacteria include dangerous pathogens that need precise identification. Clinical and environmental isolates must be typed quickly and reliably. The team built a real-time PCR array for hierarchical identification. Typing markers came from comparisons of many genomes and genes.

Twenty-three canonical single nucleotide differences anchor the typing scheme. Hierarchical typing first places an isolate broadly, then refines it. A robust, rapid, flexible assay serves outbreak response and research. It helps labs tell harmless relatives from true threats.
plos-pone-0008460:
Jessica Saykally and co-authors report a gene effect in female mice in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Four large human studies had mapped an obesity gene to a part of chromosome 10. That region holds the gene for ZEB1, a factor that controls other genes. ZEB1 also shapes how some cell types mature. The team test its role in body fat.

When ZEB1 is changed in female mice, fat gain is held back. The effect marks ZEB1 as a repressor of adiposity, or fat buildup. The sex-specific result is itself a clue. It opens a new path for study of weight control.
plos-pone-0008560:
Venkaiah Betapudi and co-authors study motor proteins in spreading cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Non-muscle cells express multiple myosin II motor proteins. Forms include myosin IIA, IIB, and IIC, transcribed from different genome loci. Their sequences are significantly homologous, so they were believed to overlap in function. The team test that assumption during cell spreading. As cells spread, they extend flat sheets called lamellipodia at their edges.

They find myosin forms with different functions determine lamellipodia fate. One form may extend a sheet while another retracts it. Distinct motors thus steer a single structure in opposing ways. The result revises the view that these ubiquitous motors are interchangeable.
plos-pone-0008660:
Donal O'Shea and co-authors study natural killer cells in obesity in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Obese individuals who smoke have a fourteen year reduction in life expectancy. Both obesity and smoking are independently associated with increased malignancy risk. Natural killer cells are critical mediators of anti-tumor immunity. They are compromised in obese patients. The team measure NK cell function in obese subjects. They also test susceptibility to the effects of cigarette smoke.

They find NK function is impaired in obesity. Smoke exposure further weakens those already compromised cells. That double hit may explain part of the cancer risk. Supporting NK cells could be a target for obese smokers.
plos-pone-0008760:
Siva Panguluri, Shephali Bhatnagar, Akhilesh Kumar, and colleagues listed the genes behind muscle loss driven by inflammation. Their mouse study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A signal called TWEAK can waste skeletal muscle when it stays high. Chronic diseases often raise such signals and shrink muscle. The gene program that carries out the wasting was only partly known.

The team profiled both regular genes and microRNAs in wasting muscle. Patterns emerged for growth, breakdown, and energy pathways. Several microRNAs shifted alongside the classic wasting genes. The combined list gives drug hunters more targets for protecting muscle in chronic illness.
plos-pone-0008860:
Zijun Xiao, Chuanjuan Lv, Chao Gao, and colleagues turned whole cells into factories that recycle their own helpers. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Many useful enzymes need a costly helper molecule called NAD in its plus form. Buying the helper at factory scale is prohibitively expensive. Regenerating it inside the cell would cut costs sharply. The oxidized form, needed here, had been harder to recycle than its partner.

Their biocatalyst cells regenerated the helper while making chiral chemicals. Chiral products, with left- and right-handed forms, are prized in pharmacy. Self-recycling cells make green chemistry more practical. Industry gains a cheaper route to fine chemicals.
plos-pone-0008960:
Thomas Hussenet and co-authors named a gene that drives a common lung cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is frequent and aggressive. Cancers often grow by making extra copies of genes that push cell growth. One stretch of chromosome 3 is copied again and again in these tumours.

Scanning that stretch pointed to SOX2, a gene known for keeping stem cells young. Tumours had multiplied SOX2 and switched it on at high levels. Extra copies turned a normal developmental gene into a cancer driver. The finding marks SOX2 as a target worth testing for future lung cancer drugs.
plos-pone-0009060:
Udi Gluschnaider and co-authors found a way to slow prostate cancer cells by blocking their rubbish disposal, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Prostate cancer is common, and its growth depends heavily on the androgen receptor's signals. Advanced cases are first treated by cutting those signals off. Nearly all patients eventually relapse despite that early success with treatment.

Beta-TrCP is part of the cell's protein-tagging machinery for disposal. Inhibiting it raised levels of the aryl hydrocarbon receptor inside the cells. That rise, in turn, cut the cancer cells' growth in the team's experiments. The result suggests a fresh angle of attack on a very common cancer.
plos-pone-0009160:
Hongxia Ma and co-authors infected rabbits with three hepatitis E viruses to compare them, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Farmed rabbits in China had been found carrying a new hepatitis E genotype. Its genome is organised like the mammal-infecting genotypes 1 to 4. Yet its sequence matches them only loosely.

Rabbits are common lab animals, so cross-infection matters practically. The team dosed rabbits with the rabbit virus and with genotypes 1 and 4. Comparing infections showed which strains rabbits can host. The answer guides both animal research and hepatitis E ecology. Each virus was tracked through the infection it caused.
plos-pone-0009260:
Katsuaki Suzuki and co-authors published this rat brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Parkinson's disease is known for movement problems, but depression and thinking troubles often come first. Those early symptoms do not respond to dopamine replacement drugs. Their causes inside the brain are poorly understood.

The team destroyed dopamine neurons in the rat midbrain using a toxin called 6-hydroxydopamine. New cell birth in the hippocampus, a memory center, then decreased. The antidepressant fluoxetine reversed that drop. The result links dopamine loss to a change in the hippocampus, a possible root of Parkinson's mood symptoms.
plos-pone-0009360:
Shweta Bansal and co-authors published this pandemic flu study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The 2009 H1N1 flu hit school-age children much harder than adults. Older adults seemed to carry some leftover immunity. But that alone might not explain the wide age gap in infections.

The authors modeled how the age pattern of cases shifts during a pandemic. Contact patterns, like children mixing densely at school, play a role alongside immunity. Getting the age pattern right changes practical choices, from school closures to vaccine order. The study shows demography itself as a force shaping an epidemic's course.
plos-pone-0009460:
Keizo Takao and a large team tested mice that lack a brain protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein is CaMKIV. It helps pass signals from the cell surface to the genes in the nucleus. That relay is thought to lock in long term memory. Mice without the protein went through a wide set of behavior tests.

The tests covered learning, movement, social acts, and responses to fear and stress. Comparing these mice with normal ones shows which acts need CaMKIV and which do not. The full picture helps separate firm memory storage from other brain jobs. It gives later work a clear map of this one relay.
plos-pone-0009560:
Iain MacLeod and Tony Minson studied herpes simplex virus at the cell surface in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus wears several proteins on its coat. Four of them are needed for it to enter a cell. Virus particles missing one of those four cannot enter. They can still stick to the cell's surface, though. The team asked what that sticking alone does.

Binding by itself set off signals inside the cell. The cell responded before any entry took place. So the virus starts talking to its host at first touch. Those early signals may shape how the infection unfolds, and they could be targets for blocking it.
plos-pone-0009660:
Qing Zhou and co-authors compared proteins in a dividing parasite in PLOS ONE in 2010. Trypanosoma brucei causes sleeping sickness. Inside the parasite sits a structure called the bi-lobe, which must copy itself before the cell can divide. The team compared the parasite's proteins to find new parts of that structure. Their proteomic screen turned up a previously unknown bi-lobe protein.

The new protein proved necessary for the bi-lobe to duplicate and for division to proceed. A part found only in the parasite's machinery is a possible drug target. Blocking division would stop the parasite from multiplying in the blood. The study adds a piece to a machine unlike any in human cells.
plos-pone-0009860:
Two lemur species can share one forest yet live on very different energy budgets. Bruno Simmen and colleagues measured energy use and body makeup in both. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Lemurs are primates found in the wild only in Madagascar.

Total energy expenditure is all the energy an animal burns in a day. The lemurs were free-living and sympatric, meaning they live side by side in the wild. Comparing neighbors shows how body composition matches lifestyle and diet. Such budgets help explain how similar species divide one habitat.
plos-pone-0009960:
Two large receptor proteins shed their outer parts, and those parts have jobs of their own. Martin Dietrich and colleagues tested what the shed pieces do in living animals. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The proteins are LRP1b and LRP4, relatives of the LDL receptor. Their ectodomains are the parts that stick out of the cell. Anchorage independent means working without staying attached to the cell. The team found those domains have anchorage independent functions in vivo. A shed piece, it turns out, is not just waste.
plos-pone-0010060:
The authors were Sanjay Kansra, Shenglin Chen, Madhavi Bangaru, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study covered hormone drugs and pituitary cells called lactotrophs. These cells make prolactin, and their growth is tied to estrogen receptor alpha. The team had found that receptor matters even when no estrogen is present.

They compared drugs that either break down the receptor or merely modulate it. One drug, ICI 182780, rapidly promoted receptor loss and slowed cell growth. Tamoxifen and raloxifene did not act the same way. The contrast helps explain how anti-estrogen drugs differ, cell by cell.
plos-pone-0010160:
The authors were Justin Valley, Paul Swinton, W. John Boscardin, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study aimed to improve embryo choice for IVF. Picking the best embryo is critical to a successful live birth. Clinics still choose largely by eye, judging shape and development, which is subjective and gives limited information.

The team used light-induced dielectrophoresis, an electric method guided by light, on mouse embryos. The goal was a non-invasive, measured way to grade embryo quality. A reliable physical marker could raise IVF success rates and reduce repeat treatment cycles.
plos-pone-0010260:
The authors were Koji Tsutsumi, Tetsuya Takano, Ryo Endo, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study examined a brain enzyme called AATYK1. The enzyme is abundant in the brain and helps nerve fibers grow. It is also involved when cerebellar granule neurons die, though its precise function remained unknown to researchers before this study.

The team investigated how another enzyme, Cdk5, modifies AATYK1 by adding phosphate. They found that this modification suppresses a second kind of phosphate tag on the same protein. Layered controls like this fine-tune how nerve cells grow and respond to damage.
plos-pone-0010360:
Naia Morueta-Holme, Camilla Fløjgaard and Jens-Christian Svenning assessed climate risk for a rare mammal in PLOS ONE in 2010. Warming is already shifting where species can live. Animals stuck in a small range have nowhere easy to go. Yet how sensitive such species truly are was not well measured. The team used range models to test that sensitivity.

Their models projected where the animal's climate space would move. They then weighed what that means for protecting it. Small-range species may need help earlier than common ones. Reserves drawn for today's climate may miss tomorrow's refuges. This study gives planners a way to spot that mismatch in advance. It treats one rare mammal as a test case for many.
plos-pone-0010460:
Nathan Ford and colleagues asked whether early pill-taking habits predict long-term HIV control, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Skipping antiretroviral doses lets the virus rebound and gain resistance. Earlier studies linked adherence and virus suppression at single time points. This team followed a patient group for five years. They tested whether adherence measured at the start foretold later failure.

Early habits did carry lasting information about risk. That makes early support for new patients especially valuable. Clinics could flag strugglers sooner and help before failure sets in. Five-year follow-up is rare and gives the claim weight. The study turns a simple measure, early adherence, into a planning tool for lifelong treatment.
plos-pone-0010560:
Dustin Baldridge and colleagues described body-wide connective tissue disease in mice lacking a collagen helper protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. Faults in three genes cause brittle bone disease by reducing a key collagen modification. One of those genes makes cartilage-associated protein, Crtap. The team studied mice with Crtap removed entirely. They examined the animals comprehensively, beyond bones alone.

The disease proved generalized, affecting connective tissue across the body. That breadth matches the human condition better than a bone-only view. Mouse models that capture the full picture help test treatments fairly. Collagen is everywhere, so its faults should be too. This study documents that spread in detail for one brittle-bone gene.
plos-pone-0010660:
Mark Vermeij and colleagues showed that baby corals swim toward sound, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Coral larvae drift in open water for days before settling. Choosing the right spot to settle decides whether a larva lives or dies.

In choice chambers, larvae moved toward recorded reef sounds. Healthy reefs are noisy places, full of snapping shrimp and fish calls. Quiet, damaged reefs lack that chorus. Sound may thus guide larvae to living reefs and away from dead ones. The result suggests that protecting reef soundscapes, and even playing sounds back, could help reefs recover.
plos-pone-0010760:
Michael Nickerson and colleagues explained how a gene fault clouds the cornea, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Schnyder corneal dystrophy runs in families and slowly clouds the eye's front window. Fatty deposits of cholesterol build up in the cornea, blurring vision. Faults in the gene UBIAD1 were known to cause it, but not how.

The team showed the gene makes an enzyme that works in mitochondria, adding a tail to a vitamin K related compound. Disease faults changed how that enzyme behaves. Linking a rare eye disease to basic cell chemistry opens paths to a precise diagnosis and, in time, a targeted treatment.
plos-pone-0010860:
Neetu Kumra Taneja, Sakshi Dhingra, Aditya Mittal and co-authors published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The TB bacterium can lie dormant inside the body for years, and low oxygen is one signal thought to push it into that resting state. A two-part sensor system then switches on a dormancy program.

The team found that vitamin C, at levels found in the body, can trigger the same program. The vitamin mops up oxygen, and as oxygen fell the bacteria switched on their dormancy genes and slowed growth. Early and sustained phases of the response ran through different parts of the sensor system. Taneja and colleagues add a common nutrient to the list of dormancy cues. That matters because dormant TB is the hardest form to kill with drugs.
plos-pone-0010960:
Ben Raymond, Scott Shaffer, Serguei Sokolov and co-authors published this seabird study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sooty and short-tailed shearwaters are among the most numerous seabirds on Earth, roaming the Southern Ocean in huge flocks. Knowing where they feed, and why, matters for managing that ocean's ecosystems, so the team combined bird tracking with ocean data.

They merged tracks from birds breeding in three regions of New Zealand and Australia with at-sea sightings, water measurements, plankton and trawl data, and wind records. Birds from all regions converged on the Polar Front zone, especially one longitude band, and their feeding matched prey and wind patterns there. Raymond and colleagues show how two wide-ranging species share a vast ocean, information conservation planners need as Southern Ocean fisheries and climate shift.
plos-pone-0011060:
Michael Apicella, Deborah Post, Andrew Fowler and co-authors published this tularemia study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Capsule sugars coat many dangerous bacteria and have yielded successful vaccines, but the capsule of Francisella tularensis, the tularemia germ, had been suspected for years without ever being isolated. The authors developed an antibody that recognizes it and used that handle to characterize the material.

The antibody bound a diffuse, very large sugar molecule that stains poorly with standard methods but shows with a glycoprotein stain. The same capsule appeared in all fourteen type A and B strains tested, and it could be purified largely free of other bacterial components. Apicella and colleagues finally pin down a conserved surface feature of a high-concern pathogen. A shared capsule is exactly what a vaccine designer hopes for.
plos-pone-0011160:
Mehla, Bivalkar-Mehla, Zhang and colleagues tested a sea derived compound on HIV in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV can hide in resting cells, beyond the reach of standard drugs. The compound, bryostatin, was tested both for waking hidden virus and for blocking fresh infection.

Bryostatin woke latent virus through two signaling paths inside cells. At the same time, it hindered new infection in a way not tied to cell entry receptors. Pairing a wake up step with a killing step is a leading cure strategy. This dual action makes the compound a useful tool for that research, even before any clinic use.
plos-pone-0011260:
Gertsenstein, Nutter, Reid and colleagues sped up mouse engineering in PLOS ONE in 2010. Making gene altered mice from stem cells of a standard strain was slow and unreliable. The team combined those stem cells with embryos from outbred mice, a mixing method called aggregation, to create chimeras more efficiently.

The chimeras passed the altered genes to their offspring at good rates. That shortcut shortens the path from a lab made gene change to a living mouse line. Faster mouse making accelerates hunts for disease genes across medicine. Labs gain a practical method they can adopt without exotic equipment.
plos-pone-0011360:
Sarah Gold and co-workers traced in 2010 how bluetongue virus gets inside animal cells. Bluetongue is a disease of sheep and cattle spread by biting midges, and its virus must enter host cells to copy itself. Many viruses enter through a standard gateway that uses a cage-like protein coat, but this virus seemed to take another route.

Working with hamster kidney cells, the team showed the virus enters by a gulping process in which the cell swallows fluid and virus together, without the standard coat. That side door explains how the virus can infect cells even when the main gateway is blocked. Knowing the entry route matters for animal health. A drug or vaccine that jams this particular doorway could slow outbreaks that cost farmers heavily in lost livestock.
plos-pone-0011460:
Cristian Salgado-Luarte and Ernesto Gianoli compared in 2010 how rainforest seedlings cope with being eaten, in sun and in shade. Young plants in a temperate rainforest face hungry herbivores while also competing for light. A seedling can resist attack with defenses, or tolerate it by regrowing, and the better strategy may depend on how much light it gets.

Seedlings in sunny gaps and shaded understory indeed leaned on different strategies, and each strategy succeeded best in its own setting. Light thus reshapes the whole terms of the battle between plant and herbivore. The finding helps explain which species claim which corners of the forest floor. For forest managers and restoration work, it warns that planting a species in the wrong light may strip it of the defense strategy it evolved to use.
plos-pone-0011560:
Iris Müller and co-authors filmed chromosomes in living human cells in 2010 and found a contrast between outer calm and inner motion. During interphase, the long working stage between divisions, chromosomes occupy set territories in the nucleus. Whether those territories are frozen solid or quietly restless inside bears on how genes find partners and regulators.

The chromosomes kept a stable overall morphology while their internal structure reorganized dynamically over time. The genome is thus a restless tenant in a fixed house, its rooms stable but its furniture always moving. That internal motion may be how genes reach the machinery they need without wrecking the nucleus's order. Imaging living cells, rather than fixed dead ones, was essential to see it: fixation would have presented the motion as stillness and the conclusion would have been wrong.
plos-pone-0011660:
Zachary Demorest and co-authors tested a partnership inside the antibody-making machinery, in PLOS ONE in 2010. An enzyme called AID starts three processes that diversify antibodies by altering DNA. AID mostly sits outside the cell nucleus and must enter it to work, and a protein called CIB1 that binds AID looked like a possible helper.

The team disrupted the interaction between AID and CIB1 and checked the antibody processes. Gene conversion and class switch recombination carried on without the partnership. The clear negative result prunes a plausible helper from the model and redirects attention to other partners.
plos-pone-0011760:
Tin Tin Su examined how early embryos respond to DNA damage in a marine cnidarian, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Around the mid-blastula transition, embryos reorganise their rapid cell cycles, adding gap phases and switching from maternal to their own genetic control. Studies in frogs and flies had shown damage responses also change at this stage.

Su exposed embryos of Hydractinia echinata to a DNA-damaging agent and watched their cell cycles respond. The ancient animal's reaction illuminates the deep roots of damage control, showing how very early embryos balance fast division against protecting their DNA.
plos-pone-0011860:
Prakash Vempati, Feilim Mac Gabhann, and Aleksander Popel built a computer model in 2010 of how a growth factor escapes from tissue. VEGF, a signal that promotes blood vessel growth, is often stored bound inside the extracellular matrix, the mesh around cells. Enzymes such as plasmin and matrix metalloproteinases can cut it loose.

The model puts numbers on that release: how fast the cutting happens and how much free VEGF results under different conditions. Vessel growth depends on the timing and amount of this signal, so guessing is not enough. A tested model lets researchers predict how blocking an enzyme would change vessel patterning before trying it in animals.
plos-pone-0011960:
Sarath Kalapala and co-workers tested in 2010 a suspected link between a ribosome change and antibiotic response in a mycobacterium. The bacterium was Mycobacterium smegmatis, a fast-growing stand-in for its tuberculosis-causing relatives. A mutation called K42R in ribosomal protein S12 had been proposed to alter how 16S rRNA mutants respond to a class of antibiotics, the 2-deoxystreptamines.

The team found that the K42R change does not affect that susceptibility. A clean negative result of this kind is valuable: it retires a plausible but wrong idea before more work is built on it. Antibiotic resistance research advances as much by closing false leads as by opening new ones.
plos-pone-0012060:
Jacob van Etten and Robert Hijmans set out in 2010 a way to settle where our crops were first tamed, by making three kinds of proof agree. Work on plant roots in the past has leaned on just one: the seeds and husks dug from old sites, or the genes of crops and their wild kin. Each kind alone leaves gaps, but more and more of both are now on hand.

Their plan folds the dug-up plant past and the gene past into one map-based model that draws the start points and spread routes of tamed plants. A model that must please spade, seed, and gene at once is hard to fool. Knowing where farms were born, and which roads crops took, also shows where their wild kin still live and most need guarding.
plos-pone-0012160:
Stephanie Ortigue, Corrado Sinigaglia, Giacomo Rizzolatti, and co-authors recorded brain activity while people watched others act, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Watching someone grasp a cup gives two kinds of information at once: what the hand is doing, and what the person means by it, such as drinking. The team used dense scalp recordings to follow how the brain's left and right halves handle each kind.

Their high-speed brain maps separate the instant reading of an act from the reading of its intent. Understanding others' actions is the base of learning by imitation, empathy, and social life itself. Work like this also informs care for people whose social reading is impaired, as in some brain injuries.
plos-pone-0012260:
Steven Offer, Qiang Pan-Hammarström, and Lennart Hammarström searched DNA repair genes for the roots of antibody deficiency, in PLOS ONE in 2010. In these syndromes, patients cannot make a full range of antibodies and suffer repeated infections, yet more than nine cases in ten have no known genetic cause. Building diverse antibodies requires B cells to cut and rejoin their own DNA, a process that starts with a deliberate break.

Because that cutting leans on DNA repair machinery, the team examined repair gene variations in these patients and found unique ones worth attention. A repair flaw would explain infections and might also warn of cancer risk. Each candidate gene found gives affected families a possible answer and doctors a new test to offer.
plos-pone-0012360:
Magdalena Gulliksson, Ricardo Carvalho, Erik Ullerås and co-authors asked how low oxygen affects mast cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Mast cells guard tissues and drive allergy and swelling, and inflamed tissue often runs short of oxygen. Yet how oxygen shortage alone changes mast cell survival and the chemicals they release was not well known.

The team grew human mast cells with little oxygen and tracked survival and mediator release. The cells stayed alive and adjusted what they secreted, showing they can keep working in starved tissue. That matters for asthma, wounds, and tumors, where mast cells act in low-oxygen zones and shape how disease unfolds.
plos-pone-0012460:
Juliette Martin, Krishanpal Anamika and Narayanaswamy Srinivasan reclassified the huge kinase family of proteins, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Kinases add phosphate tags to other proteins and run most cell signaling; there are hundreds of them in humans alone. Past family trees used only the kinase region itself, ignoring the rest of each protein.

By classifying kinases on both their kinase and non-kinase regions, the team got a tree that better matches how the proteins actually work. The extra regions often decide what a kinase binds and where it acts. A truer family tree helps predict the job of unstudied kinases, many of which are drug targets in cancer.
plos-pone-0012560:
Morgan Davidson, Jill Larsen, Ian Yang and colleagues documented the loss of a small RNA in a lung cancer type, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. MicroRNAs are tiny RNAs that dial down target genes, acting as brakes on growth programs. Losing a brake can free cancer. The team focused on lung squamous cell carcinoma, a smoking-linked cancer with few targeted drugs.

MicroRNA-218 was deleted and downregulated in these tumors, removing its brake on target genes. A lost brake is both a clue to how the cancer forms and a possible marker in tissue or blood. Restoring such microRNAs is an experimental therapy idea this kind of survey feeds.
plos-pone-0012660:
Ahmed and Zerihun surveyed who actually owns and uses treated bed nets in Uganda. Nets treated with insecticide are a proven guard against malaria, above all for young children and pregnant women. Their 2010 study examined the health programme of BRAC, a large local aid group, and asked whether it reaches the poor.

They checked net ownership and use across income groups in the programme's area. A malaria tool only works if the families at most risk really sleep under it. Their equity check shows whether a pro-poor promise holds in practice.
plos-pone-0012760:
Gowen, Wong, Larson and co-authors built a safer arena-virus infection model and used it to test a new drug idea. Several arenaviruses cause severe bleeding fevers and count as emerging public threats. Work on them is slow because the most dangerous ones need top-level containment labs.

Their 2010 Tacaribe virus model offers a workable stand-in for testing treatments. With it they explored an aristeromycin-like compound's power against the virus. A good model that more labs can use speeds the search for drugs against a feared virus family.
plos-pone-0012860:
Liang, Gao, Lin and co-authors silenced an overactive cell-cycle protein to stop breast cancer in mice. Cyclin E is made in excess in many cancers, including breast cancer, and high levels of both its full and shortened forms track with poor outcomes. Their 2010 study used small interfering RNA to target cyclin E in breast cancer cells.

Silencing slowed cancer cell growth in dishes and suppressed tumour development in a breast cancer mouse model. A target that is high in tumours and low elsewhere is exactly what RNA drugs need. The work supports cyclin E as such a target.
plos-pone-0325860:
Kazuya Umeno and Yoshihiro Itaguchi explored whether imagining movement with both hands before one hand helps people actually move better, a question with stakes for stroke rehabilitation. Mental practice is known to engage motor brain areas, and two-handed imagery may engage them more strongly. Their 2026 experiment assigned seventy-six healthy young adults to imagery orders or a no-imagery control group, using a palm ball-rolling task.

Only the group that imagined two-handed movement first, then one-handed, improved real performance more than controls. Brain wave measures of motor activation were stronger early on for that group but faded with practice, and they tracked performance only loosely. The authors suggest order matters: two-handed imagery seems to prime the system, while reversing the order adds little.
plos-pone-0332560:
James John and co-authors examined unmet social needs among families in multicultural and rural parts of Australia. Families facing disadvantage often cannot reach the social and health services meant for them. Their 2026 study re-analysed trial data from culturally diverse communities in South Western Sydney and the rural Murrumbidgee region.

A standard survey counted each family's unmet social care needs. Because need counts varied more widely than simple models allow, the team used a regression form built for overdispersed counts. Parental mental health sat at the centre of the analysis, alongside social and demographic drivers. John and colleagues aim to show services which family traits predict unmet need, so outreach can start where the gaps are deepest.
plos-pone-0334060:
Anna Fekete and colleagues ran a registered experiment on whether art can dull pain. Forty-two women brought artworks and music they found deeply beautiful to the laboratory, then kept a hand in ice water while experiencing music alone, visual art alone, both together, or neither. The team measured how long participants tolerated the cold, plus stress hormones, heart signals, and self-reports.

Music and the combined experience let women endure the ice water far longer than visual art alone. Yet no art form changed measured stress in the body, and people who easily lose themselves in experiences benefited most. The authors conclude art's pain relief works mainly through absorption and attention, not body chemistry.
plos-pone-0336560:
Rachel Mariani and colleagues tested whether shining light through grape leaves and reading the reflection can measure leaf traits that normally require slow laboratory work. They covered twelve wine grape cultivars and twelve traits, including the gas-exchange and water traits that decide how a vine handles heat and drought. The samples varied widely between and within cultivars.

Spectral readings captured that variation, showing the method can detect differences not just between species but between cultivated varieties of one crop. Breeders and growers need trait data at scales no laboratory pipeline can supply, for example when screening hundreds of vines for drought behavior. A leaf scan that substitutes for days of measurement turns that screening from a bottleneck into a routine.
plos-pone-0336760:
Lokeswara Rao Sajja and colleagues are working on a mechanical heart valve that resists clotting without a lifetime of blood-thinning drugs. Their 2026 laboratory study copies a trick from real blood vessels, whose inner coating carries a slight negative charge that pushes platelets away. A small pacemaker-like device applies a gentle voltage across the valve's surface to imitate that coating.

Nine valves sat in human blood or platelet-rich plasma for half an hour, some switched on and some off. At the strongest setting tested, about ninety-six percent of the surface stayed free of deposits, and the electricity did not damage blood cells or trigger clotting. The team calls this a safe starting point before animal trials.
plos-pone-0338360:
Calvin Epidu and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of advanced HIV disease in Ugandan children and teens. They used clinic records from forty-eight busy facilities in the west of the country. They followed more than five thousand young people who started treatment between 2016 and 2023. They noted who arrived with advanced disease, and what happened to them.

Nearly one in five had advanced disease. Among children under five, the share was over two-thirds. Just over half of those with advanced disease were still in care at the study's end. About one in twelve had died. Deaths clustered in the first three months of treatment. Malnourished children survived at lower rates. The authors argue for earlier diagnosis and food support, to cut the early death toll.
plos-pone-0340560:
Richmond Balinia Adda and Conrad Pwayirane build a data driven guide to health system resilience for one hundred ninety-five countries, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Readiness scores exist, but governments struggle to turn them into spending priorities. Working from the full 2021 edition of a worldwide health security scoring system covering six domains, the authors distilled a single resilience measure. It captures most of what those domains share. They then asked which domains drive it independently.

Detection, in country health capacity, and prevention carried the strongest independent weight, with detection first. Countries then fell into two broad types: a balanced high performing third, and a larger two thirds group with lower, uneven abilities, weakest exactly in prevention and basic capacity. The typology suggests different strategies: protect strengths in the first group, and fund detection plus core services first in the second. The framework makes resilience investment comparable and concrete.
plos-pone-0341960:
Dinh Duc Truong asked firms in Vietnam a plain question. When green rules press, who spends on clean kit? He used a World Bank survey of firms in the land. He weighed the press of rules, firm traits, and how hard each firm found it to raise cash. The sums let the press and the cash squeeze meet and clash.

Rules did push firms to spend green, but not by much. Tight cash cut green spends on its own. It also dulled the push of rules to near nil for the most squeezed firms. Truong says rules need cheap loans at their side to work at scale.
plos-pone-0344360:
Megumi Shiomi and her team searched the genes of Japanese patients for the roots of a faulty heart rhythm. The fault comes and goes, so it is hard to catch in time. It can lead to stroke if missed. The team set about a thousand cases next to more than seven hundred controls. They also built a score that adds up many small gene effects.

All strong hits sat in one stretch of one chromosome, near a gene that helps build the heart. The score on its own sorted risk quite well. It did even better when mixed with health facts. The team says gene scores could flag who needs heart checks most.
plos-pone-0344860:
Emma Hudgins and co-authors weighed two ways of fighting the mountain pine beetle, a pest chewing through western North American forests and spreading farther as winters warm. The usual policy reacts to fresh sightings and short-term forecasts. Their alternative plans with long-range spread in mind, choosing survey and control spots for the future outbreak they prevent, not just the present one.

In their comparison, the forward-looking strategy shrank the future infested area substantially compared with the reactive approach, in some runs by more than half beyond it. A simpler version that used forecasts without full long-term feedback still beat the standard policy. The numbers make a management point that travels well beyond beetles: money spent reacting to today's map can look efficient while quietly losing the larger war.
plos-pone-0347160:
Irshad Sikandar Jamadar and colleagues built a computer model of breast cancer treatment that remembers. Ordinary tumour models treat each moment as fresh, but real tissues carry history in scarring, resistance, and immune memory. Their fractional-order model folds that memory into equations covering tumour growth, immune attack, drug resistance, and heat therapy, then runs five treatment schedules across four patient types.

Continuous treatment scored best overall, though the winning schedule shifted by patient: younger patients favoured continuous therapy at one memory strength. Frailer patients did best with adaptive dosing at another. Older patients peaked elsewhere. The immune killing rate proved the most powerful lever, with resistance close behind. Gains over memory-free models were small on average but meaningful in specific pairings. The authors stress that clinical testing must judge whether the theory holds.
plos-pone-0347860:
Yang Cao, Bingchuan Wu, and Miao Wen taught an optimiser to tune itself. Differential evolution is a workhorse method for hard engineering problems, but its behaviour hinges on strategy choices usually set by rules of thumb. Their version puts a reinforcement learning agent in charge of those choices, then polishes promising answers with a classic refinement method, forming a loop of setting, solving, and sharpening.

On a standard international benchmark suite, the self-tuning system proved robust on high-dimensional problems and outscored classic adaptive rivals. It also handled factory scheduling, a very different discrete puzzle, suggesting the framework travels well. The authors offer the design as a template for optimisers that learn online instead of relying on frozen heuristics, aimed at costly problems where every trial counts.
plos-pone-0348060:
Kerem Ersin and Berna Özge Mutlu test how mild electric stimulation of the inner ear affects balance and the feeling that a fake hand is one's own. The balance organs help the brain merge senses into a body sense. Their 2026 study runs forty-eight healthy adults through stimulation, a sham session, and checks at half an hour and an hour afterward.

Standing on one leg dipped at half an hour, then recovered by the hour mark. A stepping-in-place measure improved at both later checks. The fake-hand illusion grew stronger after real stimulation, peaking at an hour, though the sham also nudged it up, hinting at expectation effects. Timing matters if such stimulation is ever used to aid balance therapy.
plos-pone-0348260:
Kitiya Rujimongkon and colleagues tested ivermectin, the familiar anti-parasite drug, against breast cancer cells that respond to hormones and against cells that have learned to resist hormone therapy. Earlier work from the group showed the drug slows these cells and boosts tamoxifen. The 2026 study traced which growth pathways ivermectin switches off.

The drug curbed estrogen-driven growth and lowered the estrogen receptor itself plus HER2, two engines of resistant disease. It also damped signals running through the TGF-beta pathway while sparing a protective partner protein linked to better outcomes. The authors propose ivermectin as a repurposed candidate to prevent or break hormone resistance, pending animal and clinical tests.
plos-pone-0348360:
Hongjing Chang, Jing Zhao, Yuhao Sun, and Huan Ding asked ordinary readers to judge four English translations of a poem by Li Bai, the celebrated Tang dynasty poet. Classical Chinese verse is notoriously hard to carry across languages. The four versions of the poem used prose, free verse, rhyme, or word-for-word literal rendering, and four hundred three American readers rated them online.

The rhymed translation won the readers' favour, striking the best balance between meaning and musical beauty. Prose and literal versions conveyed content but pleased readers less. Because only Americans took part, the authors caution that other cultures may respond differently. Still, the study gives translators rare evidence from actual readers rather than theory alone.
plos-pone-0348760:
Ömer Karakoç, Samet Memiş, and Bahar Sennaroglu staged a tournament among thirty-five decision algorithms built on a fuzzy mathematics framework designed for reasoning under uncertainty. Each algorithm classified the same ten public datasets, and the team scored accuracy, precision, recall, and balance. Statistical tests that guard against lucky streaks confirmed the differences.

The fuzzy soft methods held their own against expectations for such abstract machinery. A clear leaderboard emerged, topped by one algorithm, with a small group tied just behind. The authors frame the exercise as a buyer's guide: people facing messy, uncertain classification problems in machine learning now have evidence. It shows which member of this large, confusing family deserves a first try. They also get a structured way to choose among the rest.
plos-pone-0348860:
Sasha R. Sioni and coauthors published a 2026 protocol in PLOS ONE for a scoping review of digital behavioral addictions among teenagers and young adults. Terms here are a tangle: gaming disorder is a recognized diagnosis, internet gaming disorder awaits study, and heavy social media or smartphone use are research labels, not diagnoses. The review will map how researchers define, measure, and count these problems, and what is known about causes, harms, treatments, and fairness.

The team will search nine databases plus grey sources without date or language limits, focusing on ages ten to twenty-four. Two reviewers will screen and chart everything by hand, with source-language checks for six other languages, so automation never decides eligibility. Instruments will be sorted into evidence tiers, and results kept separate by kind: causes, associations, harms, and treatment effects. The map should give a fast-moving field shared footing.
plos-pone-0349360:
Falk Wiegmann and Nancy Ford produce a practical reference for researchers who scan small animals with cone-beam micro-CT, in this 2026 technical note. Reconstructed image quality depends on a filter setting inside the standard reconstruction algorithm, yet papers routinely fail to report it. The authors rebuilt the same scanner data sixteen ways, combining four filter types with four sharpness cutoffs, and measured resolution, noise, and the smallest detectable feature under each.

The trade-off was steep: the sharpest settings roughly doubled measured resolution but multiplied image noise several-fold, while the smoothest settings made even moderate-contrast features several times larger before they became detectable. A mouse lung specimen illustrates the differences visually. The authors offer the side-by-side numbers so imaging scientists can choose settings deliberately and report them properly, instead of accepting defaults blindly.
plos-pone-0349560:
Xiumei Zheng and colleagues built concrete from desert sand and recycled rubble in 2026 work, aiming to cut both river sand mining and construction waste in dry regions of China. A treated mineral additive was added to tune the mix.

Samples varied the additive dose and the shares of desert sand and recycled aggregate. Strength, salt penetration, and pore structure were measured, and a grey theory model linked tiny pore patterns to big performance numbers. The mixes worked together better than expected, and the model predicted performance from microstructure. Such prediction could speed design of greener concrete for desert building.
plos-pone-0349860:
Roberta L Woodgate and colleagues worked with nineteen young people aged fourteen to twenty four across Canada on their mental health journeys through COVID. Youth directed art methods, maps of supports and life paths plus a chosen art piece, joined open interviews online. Themes were built from words and images together.

Three chapters emerged: chaos on entering the pandemic, inward reflection during it, and personal growth after it. Mental health dipped, steadied through self examination, and in many accounts strengthened by the end. Art based work let youth show turning points that interviews alone might miss. Services should honour that growth while staying ready for the next shock.
plos-pone-0350160:
Judit del Río, Norma Ratto, and co-authors used the magnetism locked into ancient kiln walls to re-date the last firing of metalworking furnaces at Quillay, an Inka-era settlement in northwest Argentina. Radiocarbon had placed the kilns in Inka times. Their 2026 archaeomagnetic study sampled five kilns and compared their recorded field direction and strength with models of Earth's past magnetic field.

All five kilns told the same magnetic story, meaning they were last heated together in one short episode. That episode dated not to the Inka occupation but to sometime between the late eighteen hundreds and the mid nineteen hundreds. The authors suggest a later wildfire or deliberate reuse of the chambers to recover copper from slag. The result rewrites part of the site's history.
plos-pone-0350460:
Juan Carlos Calderón-González and co-authors studied phase angle, a body scan measure proposed as a sign of muscle quality, in young adults in 2026. Whether it truly tracks strength, once lifestyle and body size are counted, was the open question.

More than eleven hundred adults had phase angle, muscle mass, and grip strength measured several ways, including strength scaled to height and low strength judged against world norms. Phase angle stayed linked with strength across methods and adjustments for health, diet, activity, and demographics. A quick, painless scan number that reflects real strength could help clinics screen for weak muscle early.
plos-pone-0350560:
