A digital program coached by staff helped bowel disease patients manage tiredness, pain, and urgent bathroom needs, yet a large trial found it no better than usual care. Vari Wileman and colleagues dug into what the coaches actually did, in this 2026 PLOS One process study.

Messages between coaches and patients were sampled and scored against a delivery checklist; fidelity stayed high throughout. Nineteen coaches were interviewed before and after about training, supervision, and the work itself. Their accounts explain how faithfully a program can be delivered and still miss its target, a distinction the authors say future digital health trials must plan for from the start.
plos-pone-0350660:
Wenfang Wang and co-authors built a single test in 2026 that detects four targets of the plague bacterium at once. Plague still occurs in pockets worldwide, and fast, certain detection guides both treatment and outbreak control.

The test reads four genes unique to the germ, each in its own channel, and was checked for stray reactions with other bacteria. It detected extremely small amounts and gave repeatable results across strengths. Serum samples from real cases were all caught. One combined run replacing four separate tests could speed plague confirmation in labs with limited staff and time.
plos-pone-0351060:
Mohammad Ali and colleagues set out a trial plan, with no results yet, to test heat therapy for long term low back pain in Bangladesh. Deep heat from shortwave machines stays popular in clinics there, even though world guidance counts it as low value. The trial will enrol just over two hundred adults at several Dhaka hospitals and clinics, split by chance into real or sham heat.

Both groups will get standard physiotherapy three times a week for four weeks. Pain, leg pain, activity limits, mood, sleep, and care use will be tracked to six months. A sham arm matters here: only a fair test can show whether a widely loved machine adds anything beyond good standard care.
plos-pone-0351160:
Marlon E Cobos leads a team mapping when and where four tick species actively hunt for hosts across the central Great Plains. Several disease-carrying ticks are spreading in the region, and risk follows the ticks' hunting behavior, not just their range on a map. The team fed two years of field surveillance, with both finds and confirmed absences, into new niche models tied to conditions at each sampling moment.

The models revealed seasonal rhythms that differed by species, showing when each tick's hunting range swells or shrinks across the plains. Cobos and colleagues argue that time-aware maps give health agencies a firmer base for timing warnings and control work than static range maps. Their framework also uses absence records that older models usually throw away.
plos-pone-0351560:
Dohyeon Lee and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study on shrinking huge data files from holotomography. This microscope method maps the inside of living samples without stains or labels. Modern systems produce terabytes of three-dimensional images. Storage and transfer then become real bottlenecks. The team stored data in a cloud-friendly format. They tested thirteen ways to compress the files, across many settings.

They used six datasets from five biological samples. For each method they compared file size, reopening speed, and network speed. One method, Pcodec, gave the most balanced results overall. Two others came close behind. The best choice depends on the bandwidth a lab has. The authors give guidance labs can use when setting up large imaging pipelines.
plos-pone-0351760:
Chih-Yu Chen, Kuang-Hui Chen, and Kang-Hao Lu checked a piece of gymnastics folklore with hard results. The claim is that performing later in a final helps a gymnast. They mined men's apparatus finals from three Olympic Games and nine world meets. Rankings, scores, and medals were tested against start position on each apparatus.

Almost nothing moved with start order. Rankings, difficulty, execution, and medals were flat nearly everywhere. One exception stood out: pommel horse. Gymnasts drawn in the second half there scored higher on execution and won more medals. Medal shares by continent were even across the board. The overall verdict flatters the judging system. Order effects look like the rare stain, not the fabric of results.
plos-pone-0351860:
Xi Chen, Jieqiong Wang, and Xinying Liu trace how one Japanese newspaper frames two related medical traditions. Their 2026 study mines four decades of the Asahi Shimbun, from 1984 to 2025. Kampo is Japan's own adaptation of classical Chinese medicine. Traditional Chinese Medicine is the mainland system it sprang from. Topic modelling and word-embedding analysis reveal the paper's habits of mind.

The newspaper keeps the two traditions clearly apart. Kampo appears inside everyday health concerns and questions of material supply. It sits close to concrete remedies and therapies. Chinese medicine, by contrast, is framed through culture, comparison, and outside reference. Its semantic neighbourhood is abstract: categories, institutions, systems. These frames stayed stable for forty years, flexing only with policy shifts. A shared origin, the authors show, does not guarantee a shared story.
plos-pone-0351960:
Saya Kaidarova and seven colleagues examine thyroid cancer patients in Kazakhstan for links between autoimmune thyroid disease and aggressive gene mutations, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. More than half of their two hundred and thirty-one patients also had Hashimoto's thyroiditis or Graves' disease. The team checked tumours for two mutations known to mark more dangerous papillary thyroid cancers.

The combined high-risk mutation pattern appeared more often in patients without autoimmune disease, alongside larger tumours and spread to lymph nodes. Hashimoto's patients carried fewer aggressive changes, while the small Graves' group showed livelier cell growth. The pattern hints that the type of thyroid autoimmunity may colour how a cancer behaves.
plos-pone-0352160:
Cillin Condon and four co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of a simple chair-rise test. It asks whether muscle power estimated from that test can flag frailty in older Irish adults. The data come from a national aging study. The team converted how fast people over fifty finished five sit-to-stand reps into a leg power estimate. They checked it against a standard frailty index.

Power fell with age. The fall was steeper in women and in people classed as frail. Cut-off values below which frailty risk rose matched findings from other countries. The power estimate predicted frailty about as well as standard clinic tests, like timed walking. The authors recommend it as a cheap, practical add-on for frailty screening in towns and villages. It complements fuller checks rather than replacing them.
plos-pone-0352260: Shoulder impingement syndrome — joint mobilization’s clinical efficacy systematically reviewed and meta-analyzed. This paper did so. The findings quantified hands-on therapy’s benefit. The research guided physiotherapy — the evidence for the mobilizing hand.
plos-pone-0352360:
Chen Wei and seven colleagues read a harvester drum's workload from its vibrations in this 2026 engineering study. Pepper harvesting machines must adjust on the move. Too much load wastes energy and damages fruit. Vibration signals reveal the drum's structural response. Torque signals reveal the crop pushing back. The authors model the two as one coupled chaotic system, borrowing classic chaos equations. A hybrid algorithm then fits the model's parameters to real behaviour.

Chaos theory supplies the measuring stick. The largest Lyapunov exponent gauges how fast the system's paths diverge, and it shifts with load state. Designed experiments pinned down the best operating settings. The result is a load estimate with a physical story behind it, not a black-box guess. Single signals and simple statistics proved less discriminating. For machine builders, interpretable load sensing promises steadier harvesting, fewer damaged peppers, and settings that adapt themselves in the field.
plos-pone-0352460:
Jonathan Chu, Shreyas Annaswamy, and Sanjay Desai hunted for chemicals that can switch off a calcium pump found in nearly every cell. The pump pushes calcium out of cells, and the version on human red blood cells is tied to sickle cell disease and to how severe malaria becomes. No clean blocker of the pump existed to guide drug work.

The team shrank a lab test using red blood cells and a dye that glows with calcium, then screened more than fifty-two thousand compounds. Almost none interfered with the pump, and none of the early hits held up on retesting. That near-empty result still matters: it suggests the pump offers very few places where a drug can grab hold.
plos-pone-0352660:
Hasan Ekinci and Ahmet Mallı model what makes sports professionals behave innovatively. Their 2026 study surveyed two hundred forty-three sports professionals in eastern Turkey. Feeling supported by others seemed a likely driver of fresh ideas at work. But earlier research had not mapped the mental steps in between. The authors tested motivation and mental flexibility as sequential links in the chain.

Perceived social support showed no direct link to innovative behaviour. Its effect travelled entirely through the two middle steps. Support first raised intrinsic motivation, the inner drive to do the work well. Motivation then fed cognitive flexibility, the ability to switch viewpoints. Flexibility, in turn, predicted innovative behaviour. For sports organisations, the lesson is layered. Backing staff is not enough by itself; work must also feed inner drive and flexible thinking.
plos-pone-0352760:
Sidharth Samantara and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One engineering paper on a new circuit design for connecting solar panels to the power grid without a transformer. Their switched-capacitor inverter uses three capacitors and twelve switches to produce a seven-level output while tripling the input voltage. The capacitors balance themselves automatically, and the design is built to avoid leakage currents that plague transformer-free systems.

Simulations and a working prototype confirmed the design behaves as intended. Compared with existing transformerless inverters, the authors report fewer parts under less voltage stress for the performance achieved. They frame the work as a contribution to affordable clean energy, since cheaper and more reliable grid-tied converters help solar power spread.
plos-pone-0352860:
Julia Perlinger and three colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study translating a burnout questionnaire into German and testing whether burnout comes in distinct flavors. The underlying theory separates workers who are frenetic and overinvolved, those who are underchallenged and bored, and those who are worn out and disengaged. More than six hundred German employees completed the translated questionnaire along with measures of depression, engagement, job demands, and support.

The translation held together statistically, and clustering the answers produced four groups: the three burnout types plus a non-burned-out group. Resources and demands deteriorated in a clear order from frenetic through underchallenged to worn out. The authors argue that naming a worker's subtype points to better-matched help than treating burnout as one uniform condition.
plos-pone-0352960:
Diallo, Ezzinbi, and Outada with Sallet proved results about epidemic math models in a 2026 paper. Their model extends the classic healthy, sick, recovered scheme with stages for exposure, mild and severe illness, hospital care, and intensive care. A version split by age groups was studied as well.

The authors show the model behaves sensibly, work out when an outbreak can take off, and find a unique final size for a single wave. Lasting immunity lets the disease die out under the right conditions, while fading immunity allows a steady state when spread is strong enough. Such proofs give health modelers firm ground for forecasts used in planning.
plos-pone-0353060:
Alsunbul and colleagues built a skin carrier for a common antifungal drug in a 2026 study. The drug treats yeast infections of the skin but sinks in poorly and washes away quickly. Tiny fat-based bubbles, tuned by a statistical design, were loaded with the drug and set into a gel.

Bubble size, charge, and drug capture were measured, and imaging confirmed smooth round bubbles with drug inside. In rats with skin yeast infection, the gel beat a leading store cream at a lower dose, with tissue healing to match. Better skin delivery could cut dose and treatment time for a very common infection.
plos-pone-0353160:
Nasir and colleagues asked whether fatty liver disease and metabolic risks track later thinking decline in a 2026 study. Records from dozens of American health organizations covered two decades. One matched comparison set pitted millions of adults with metabolic risks against healthy controls, and another compared liver patients with risk-only patients.

Outcomes included mild thinking impairment and two kinds of dementia, tracked after matching for age, sex, and background. People with prior brain disease or advanced liver disease were excluded to keep the question clean. If liver disease adds risk beyond shared metabolic factors, brain screening may belong in liver clinics.
plos-pone-0353260:
Fangfang Chen, Cindy Sing Bik Ngai, and Ming Liu wrote this 2026 PLOS One study comparing how Chinese and American government space agencies present themselves on social media. The team gathered posts from Chinese agencies on Weibo and United States agencies on X, then used text-mining tools alongside close reading to compare topics, forms of address, and word patterns.

Chinese agencies came across as state-linked yet friendly guides, mixing mission achievements with patriotism and collective pride. American agencies sounded more strictly professional, stressing research, exploration, and mission success with little mention of the state. The authors read these contrasting voices as products of each country's institutions and culture, and the comparison shows how even technical agencies shape a public identity through routine posts.
plos-pone-0353360:
Helena Grip and co-authors recorded brain activity and finger motion at the same time to study how fingers move one by one. Independent finger control underlies skilled hand use and depends on both body mechanics and brain control. Their 2026 study scanned twenty-five right-handed older adults while motion capture tracked each finger's bending.

An individuation index scored how cleanly each finger moved without dragging its neighbours along. Brain contrasts between fingers and thumb located control regions specific to each digit. Areas shared by poorly individuated fingers received closer analysis. Grip and colleagues link the paired recordings to rehabilitation, since stroke and injury often steal finger independence first.
plos-pone-0353460: Energy-dissipating pile-anchor structures — their energy dissipation characteristics simulated. This numerical study examined them. The findings guide engineers designing foundations that absorb seismic fury — buildings that sway without falling.
plos-pone-0353660:
Li, Mendias, and Cao reported a caution for tendon research using a popular mouse line in a 2026 study. The mice carry a switch meant to change genes only in tendon and ligament cells, letting researchers study those tissues cleanly. The team found the switch also fires in male reproductive cells.

Because of that hidden activity, sons inherited the switched gene in every tissue, even without inheriting the switch itself. The effect did not appear through females. A supposedly tendon-only change can thus become a whole-body change in the next generation. The authors urge labs to breed through females with this mouse line and to check offspring carefully.
plos-pone-0353860:
Nia and colleagues, in a 2026 design study, build a candidate vaccine against HPV16, a virus type that drives cervical cancer. Their vaccine strings together short pieces, called epitopes, from the viral E7 protein plus pieces from two heat shock proteins. Heat shock proteins can act as helpers that wake up killer T cells.

The twist is order: the team designed six versions with the pieces arranged in different sequences. They then used computer modeling to see which layout gripped immune receptors best and looked safe and stable. One layout, with the heat shock pieces placed ahead of the viral piece, scored best. The team then built that version in bacteria and cleaned it up for further study. Computer checks predicted it would be non-toxic and unlikely to trigger allergy. The work is an early step: real immune tests in animals and people still lie ahead.
plos-pone-0354160:
Nakachew Mekonnen Alamirew and co-authors asked how adults in northwest Ethiopia grasp ways to ward off long-term ills. Health literacy means the skill to find, grasp, and use health facts. It shapes whether advice turns into daily acts. Their 2026 study held group talks and deep chats with townsfolk and health staff in the Amhara region.

Four themes showed how literacy links with acts that prevent ills like diabetes and heart disease. Blocks sat in poor access to facts, in language, and in how clinics are run, not just in what folks know. Alamirew and colleagues say health plans must fit local reading skills and local life, or the advice will not land.
plos-pone-0354260: Menstruation in Bangladesh’s urban slums — unspoken cycles of shame and struggle. This qualitative study explored women’s lived experiences. The intimate accounts demand menstrual health responses that confront stigma — not just distribute pads.
plos-pone-0354360:
Nilmart and colleagues, in a 2026 study in Thailand, test how three ways of sitting change the body during twenty minutes of smartphone gaming. Young adults often play slumped on the floor or in chairs without back support, and neck pain is a common complaint. Forty-one healthy players each tried chair sitting with a backrest, chair sitting without one, and sitting cross-legged on the floor, in random order.

Neck and trunk angles, measured from photos over time, bent differently depending on position. Neck discomfort was the most common complaint, and it was most frequent in the cross-legged position, though its strength did not differ significantly between positions. A standard ergonomic risk score also rated cross-legged sitting worst. The authors' advice is simple and immediate: for gaming sessions, a chair with a back wins, and the floor position taxes the neck fastest.
plos-pone-0354460:
Margaret A Kypreos and four colleagues published this 2026 study of a gentler lung biopsy for people with interstitial lung disease, a group of scarring lung conditions. At a Texas medical center, patients underwent freezing-probe biopsies through a bronchoscope using a very thin probe hoped to bleed less than larger ones. Diagnoses before and after the procedure were compared.

The thin probe produced useful answers more often than ordinary forceps biopsies reported elsewhere, though less often than bigger freezing probes, and complications ran higher than expected. Kypreos advises sampling several lobes and taking more pieces to raise the yield.
plos-pone-0355160:
Simone Kager and a team of clinicians and engineers set out a trial plan, published in 2026. The plan covers a home exercise gym. It helps stroke survivors retrain a weak arm without a therapist in the room. Recovery needs many repetitions, yet outpatient therapy is scarce and travel is hard. Their plan lends each participant three complementary training devices for daily use at home over six weeks, while clinicians watch progress on an online dashboard.

Up to thirty survivors in the subacute and chronic phases will take part at one center. Checks at five points will weigh feasibility, safety, ease of use, arm benefit, and costs. Kager and colleagues argue that proving unsupervised home training safe and usable is the step that must come before any large effectiveness trial.
plos-pone-0355460:
Sujeong Kang and Eunkyung Kim review in 2026 how researchers measure daily stress in the body of typically developing children. Their scoping review covered two decades and searched medical, psychology, and education sources. They separated short sharp stress from longer lasting stress and noted child age, setting, and body markers used.

Fifty seven studies qualified. Short term stress work was more common, and hormone measures, above all cortisol, dominated over nerve, brain, or immune markers. Repeated daily saliva sampling rose for a time then eased. The map shows where evidence is thin and where stronger, broader methods are still needed.
plos-pone-0355560:
Tinh Tran Phu Do and colleagues examined what lifts farm productivity across twenty-nine Asian countries over two decades. Their 2026 study links harvest output with renewable energy use, digital technology, finance, natural resources, and the quality of institutions. They used long-run statistical methods suited to country panel data, with extra checks for robustness.

Renewable energy, digital access, finance, and stronger institutions each came with higher farm productivity. Natural resource wealth pointed the other way, which the authors read as a resource curse effect. Finance and institutions also fed back into productivity in both directions. The team advises policies that spread clean energy and digital tools in farming, plus credit aimed at green projects.
plos-pone-0355860:
Elisabetta Versace led a team of eight authors studying how dance is best taught, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Teachers demo moves either facing the class or facing away, and each view poses problems for learners copying the steps. The team tested which viewing angle works better, and how skill level and mental load change the answer.

Versace's study was preregistered, meaning its design and tests were locked in advance. That choice makes the findings more trustworthy as guidance for teachers and choreographers. Dance training is a large field with strong habits but thin evidence. Clear results on something as basic as which way to face can improve lessons for beginners and experts alike.
plos-pone-0355960:
Zonghe Ding and colleagues tackle a guidance problem for automated guided vehicles. These are the driverless carts that ferry goods around warehouses and factories. The problem is that sensors lie. Standard navigation math assumes the lies follow tidy patterns. Their 2026 paper pairs a predictive controller with a set-membership filter. Instead of guessing a probability spread, the filter fences the vehicle's true state inside a shrinking geometric boundary.

That boundary feeds directly into the controller. It acts as a safety margin that breathes with conditions. So the vehicle slows or swerves when uncertainty balloons. In simulations under three kinds of noise, the approach reached its targets more often. It also held up better than two established controllers. For warehouses that cannot afford collisions, guarantees beat averages.
plos-pone-0356060:
Benjamin Mbonshi and colleagues measured worm infections in Zambian children who receive HIV treatment. Soil-transmitted worms and HIV overlap in the region, and weakened immunity may invite both. Their 2026 study sampled children aged five to fifteen at clinics in two western districts, testing stool, blood, and treatment records.

About one child in nine carried at least one worm infection, most often roundworm. Infection odds rose as immune cell counts fell and as virus levels climbed. Missed HIV doses carried the strongest risk of all. Clean water access did not explain the pattern once other factors were counted. Mbonshi and colleagues recommend folding routine worm screening and deworming into children's HIV care.
plos-pone-0356260:
Xiuyang Yuan and colleagues upgraded a lightweight image recognition model so drones can spot cracked and shattered insulators on power lines. The model had to cope with rain, snow, fog, and glare. Their 2026 study assembled nearly four thousand inspection images across weather conditions. Real and synthesized examples were mixed. The detector was rebuilt with a phone-grade backbone, an attention module, and improved feature fusion and box fitting.

The rebuilt model beat its baseline on every accuracy measure across repeated tests. It stayed tiny enough for drone-mounted hardware. It also outscored two rival lightweight detectors. The authors acknowledge the synthetic weather images as a weakness. They plan more real-world collection. Reliable automated inspection would cut the cost and danger of hunting failing insulators by eye.
plos-pone-0356360:
Rocky E Stroud and colleagues describe the first forty-three thousand participants of NeuroGAP-Psychosis, a case-control study hunting genetic and environmental roots of psychotic disorders in Africa. Their 2026 descriptive paper profiles recruits from Ethiopia, Kenya, South Africa, and Uganda between 2018 and 2023, comparing patients with psychosis against controls across countries.

The mix differed sharply by country. Schizophrenia dominated diagnoses in Ethiopia, while bipolar disorder led in Uganda, and men ranged from under half of recruits in Uganda to two thirds in Ethiopia. The authors attribute much of the variation to recruitment areas, consent languages, and local diagnostic habits rather than biology. The portrait sets up the genetic analyses to come and cautions against treating the four countries as one population.
plos-pone-0356460:
Ali Reza Yusefi and fellow researchers interview nurses and supervisors in Iranian hospitals about what makes written nursing records good in suicide care. Notes in such cases carry weight for safety, handovers, and legal protection. Across several hospitals, the team spoke in depth with a varied group of front-line nurses, head nurses, and clinical supervisors, then sorted their accounts into themes.

Eight linked themes emerged, spanning work setting and support, staff knowledge and skill, ongoing training, teamwork and communication, staffing balance, and motivation. Yusefi and colleagues argue that record quality is a system property, not just a personal habit. Hospital leaders who want safer suicide care, they say, must fix staffing and training alongside any form redesign.
plos-pone-0356560:
Anup Bhat and fellow clinicians study daily activity and walking capacity in South Asian adults living with bronchiectasis, a lung condition that scars airways and causes breathlessness and tiredness. Most past evidence comes from Western patients, and sex differences in the region are little explored. About fifty stable patients completed activity surveys, breathlessness ratings, a six-minute walk test, and health status forms, alongside records of disease severity and past flare-ups.

Less active patients reported worse breathlessness, while longer time since diagnosis linked to slightly higher activity. Women walked shorter raw distances than men, though not once body-based expectations were applied. Bhat and colleagues say activity support should be part of routine care, with attention to breathlessness as the main brake.
plos-pone-0356760:
Saad Zahid, Muhammad Nawaz, and Kanwal Zahra analyzed how Pakistani newspapers portray drug addiction, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Media framing shapes public stigma and the policies voters will accept. The team applied a topic modeling method called Latent Dirichlet Allocation to print media coverage of addiction.

Zahid's discovered topic patterns reveal whether coverage informs the public or mainly moralizes about users. Moralizing coverage deepens stigma, which keeps people from seeking treatment. Informative coverage can do the opposite. Media researchers and health advocates in Pakistan gain a map of the current framing, and editors gain a mirror. Automated topic analysis lets the team judge years of coverage at a scale no hand reading could match.
plos-pone-0357260:
Lu Yuwen and Shuyu Chen tackle a common headache in medical machine learning: rare disease groups have too few patient records to train a good model. Their 2026 framework invents extra records for the small group using a generative model, then improves those records in rounds. Borrowed real-style samples act as anchors so the invented data do not drift away from true patient patterns during the rounds.

Across seven clinical datasets, models trained with the boosted data sorted patients better than models using rival boosting methods. Checks also showed the invented records kept tricky traits of the rare group, such as skewed and multi-peaked value patterns. Yuwen and Chen offer the method for settings where collecting more real rare-case records is slow or impossible.
plos-pone-0357360:
Abdulaziz Mohammed Alismail and Abdulaziz Rashed Alghamdi asked school supervisors in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province what keeps them loyal to their work. These supervisors coach teachers and help schools improve. Yet what drives them is rarely studied outside the West. A few hundred rated their inner strength, their sense of real say, their trust in their own skills, and their loyalty to the job. The team then mapped how the parts link.

Inner strength fed both real say and skill trust in a strong way. All three traits fed job loyalty in a direct way as well. Real say did not feed skill trust, so the two paths to loyalty stayed apart. Still, each path carried part of the link from inner strength to loyalty. The pair suggest that districts build inner strength and real say side by side, if they want staff who stay.
plos-pone-0357460:
Danwen Zheng and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on the tangled body-and-mind symptoms of lung cancer patients receiving immunotherapy. Checkpoint inhibitors improve survival, but symptom mixes vary hugely between patients, and treating them one by one misses the pattern. Nearly a thousand patients were profiled into symptom types, factors modeled, and each type's network mapped for core symptoms and bridges.

Three types appeared: a high-burden group with combined physical and emotional distress, an emotionally dominant group, and a mild, adaptive group covering nearly half the patients. Smoking history, advanced stage, and poor physical function strongly marked the high-burden group, while living with family and combination therapy protected against it. Each type had its own core symptom: fatigue, sleep disturbance, and diminished enjoyment of life. Simulated interventions on the networks suggested different first targets per type, a step toward care matched to the patient.
plos-pone-0357560:
Mohammad Senisel Bachari, Asgar Khademvatani, and Mahdi Iranfar tackle risk planning for large construction projects in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. Big builds face risks that interact, and older planning methods tend to treat each phase separately. Their framework joins the whole chain, from spotting risks and judging them to picking responses, into one system that can weigh fuzzy, judgment based inputs.

A case study on a real liquefied petroleum gas pipeline project puts the framework to work. It sorted twenty distinct risks and twelve possible responses, then used an optimization model to choose the best six responses within the project's limits. That chosen set cut the project's total risk value by more than a third, showing how the method turns expert judgment into a concrete plan.
plos-pone-0357660:
Belay Merkeb Zewude and co-authors check stool samples from HIV patients on treatment at public hospitals in Ethiopia's North Shoa Zone, counting gut parasites and hunting their risk factors. Parasites hit HIV patients hard, and local rates in this zone were unmeasured. Several hundred patients gave samples and answered structured questions in the first half of a recent year, with lab checks done by three complementary methods.

About three in five patients carried at least one gut parasite, a high share for people already in regular care. Statistical models linked infection to daily life factors gathered in the survey. Zewude and colleagues argue that parasite screening and water and hygiene support belong inside routine HIV care in the zone, not as an afterthought.
plos-pone-0357960:
Albert E. Zhou and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on how physician-scientists fare in the residency match for competitive specialties. MD-PhD graduates are prized for research, but nobody had checked whether sought-after specialties prefer them. The team combined national data spanning 2007 to 2024 for six competitive fields, comparing match rates and representation between MD-PhD and regular MD applicants.

Representation of MD-PhD trainees stayed broadly stable. Dermatology and diagnostic radiology gave them strong match outcomes, while orthopedic surgery's success rate for them declined over the period, and the surgical specialties in between swung inconsistently. Specialty pay and research funding levels explained little. What tracked best with MD-PhD success was the presence of dedicated training programs in the specialty, though even that link was not statistically firm. Aspiring physician-scientists should weigh a specialty's training infrastructure, they suggest, not its prestige or pay.
plos-pone-0358360:
Shuming Cui led a team of five authors who studied how pro basketball has changed, in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They used team records and shot location data from twenty-one NBA seasons, spanning 2004 to 2025. Two trends drew their focus: shots clustering at the rim and beyond the arc, and the game's pace settling after 2018.

Cui's group tracked how the mid-range shot faded as teams chased more valued shots. They also charted how pace rose, then steadied. For coaches, analysts, and fans, the study puts hard numbers on a change many viewers sensed. It shows how data-driven choices by teams reshaped the style of the whole league.
plos-pone-0358460:
Shelley A Adamo leads a team of seven finding a silver lining in starvation for a caterpillar, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Animals must defend against infection even when food runs out, an apparent contradiction the tobacco hornworm helps resolve. After two days without food, the caterpillars' blood chemistry shifted toward a pro inflammatory footing. The melanin based defense pathway ran hotter and darkened wounds faster. Meanwhile a key antioxidant, glutathione, quietly fell.

Boosting that antioxidant back up reversed the inflammation, identifying its decline as part of the trigger. One defense arm, the cell based nodulation response, did weaken. Yet when infected with live bacteria, starved caterpillars cleared more germs from their blood within hours than fed controls did. The twist: raising the antioxidant in starved animals increased their deaths. Chronic inflammation here is not damage but a rationing strategy, buying protection with a different currency.
plos-pone-0358560:
Mélanie Briard leads a team of eight profiling the airways of children with severe asthma at the level of microbes and compounds, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Twenty affected children and ten children without asthma gave lung washings, which underwent bacterial gene sequencing and fine detail chemical mapping. The aim was a local pattern of severe disease in the organ that matters, rather than another blood based guess. A second aim was testing whether subtypes separate chemically.

Severe asthma airways carried more diverse bacteria, not fewer. Several groups were enriched, including streptococci and Moraxella. Their chemistry shifted too: a pathway built on polyamines showed depleted arginine and raised spermine and spermidine, compounds tied to growth and inflammation. Integrated analysis linked the microbial and chemical patterns. The combined signature could eventually sort children whose severe asthma runs on different machinery, a first step toward treatments aimed at mechanisms instead of symptoms.
plos-pone-0359160: Kam and five co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on proving identity from the sound of the mouth. The method uses oral acoustic reflections, echoes that bounce inside a person's mouth and carry its unique shape. Such echoes could serve as a biometric, like a fingerprint. A mouth-based check could add a hard-to-copy layer to phone or door security.
plos-pone-0359660: Qu and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on whether gut microbes change how the body handles ticagrelor, a drug used to stop blood clots. Their work combined lab tests with tests in live animals. The title reports the core result plainly: no such interaction was found in either setting. For doctors who prescribe the drug, that finding eases one worry about how gut health might alter its effect.
plos-pone-0359860:
Marie Hendrickx, Laure-Anne Kerckhaert, Sara Willems, Rik Crutzen, Vera Verbestel, and Katrien Vanthomme wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article. It is a qualitative study set in Flanders, Belgium. Its subject is follow-up that comes too late after cervical screening, when women do not return on time after a result that needs checking.

The authors interview healthcare providers rather than patients, hearing how doctors and nurses see the delays and their causes. Provider views reveal system problems, like reminders or referrals failing, that patient interviews alone might miss. Screening program managers in Belgium and elsewhere can use these accounts to tighten follow-up so fewer women are lost.
plos-pone-0359960:
Nao Suzuki and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It compares the safety of two diabetes drugs, imeglimin and sitagliptin, for patients in Japan who live with type 2 diabetes. The work is a retrospective cohort study based on pharmacy records, looking back at real patients.

Comparing safety in everyday practice matters because trial patients are often healthier than clinic patients. Pharmacy records capture the people actually taking these medicines, including those with other conditions. Doctors choosing between newer and established diabetes drugs in Japan can use real-world safety comparisons like this one alongside trial evidence.
pmc-1043860:
Brennecke, Stark, Russell, and co-authors ask how tiny RNAs called microRNAs find the genes they control. MicroRNAs are short pieces of RNA that do not code for proteins, yet they tune gene activity in plants and animals. By 2005 their importance was clear, but the rules for picking targets were not.

The team tested, in a careful and stepwise way, the smallest set of features a target site needs. Their rules help explain how one small RNA can govern many genes at once. The work became a base for later tools that predict microRNA targets from sequence alone.
pmc-10477960:
Members of the GBD 2021 Osteoarthritis group measure the world burden of osteoarthritis from 1990 to 2020. No form of arthritis affects more adults than osteoarthritis does. It brings lasting joint pain and loss of movement, most often after age forty, and it grows more common as people age.

The team built counts for countries and regions and projected the burden forward to 2050. Their work sits inside a world push for healthy aging across the decade to 2030. Solid numbers help health systems plan joint care, pain services, and support for older adults. Counts are given for the world as a whole and for single regions.
pmc-13186560:
Reis and colleagues compared night and day shift healthcare workers in 2026 at a large hospital in southern Brazil. They asked how night work relates to metabolic syndrome, a cluster of blood pressure, waist, blood fat, and sugar risks. The cross-sectional study enrolled 156 staff and gathered work, sleep, diet, meal timing, body measures, blood pressure, and lab results.

Night workers had higher blood pressure, lower protective HDL cholesterol, and more than double the odds of metabolic syndrome. They ate more fat and less fiber, finished eating later, spread meals over a longer window, and fasted for less of the night, while ultra-processed food intake matched day workers. Curiously, among night workers a shorter eating window tied to slightly lower syndrome risk. The authors blame circadian disruption, the scrambling of the body clock, and misaligned eating, and urge workplace programs built for night staff.
pmc-13237060:
Elbermawi and colleagues feed gut bacteria on extracts of an iris flower to make health-promoting postbiotics. Postbiotics are the useful compounds bacteria leave behind. Diets that slow protein glycation, a sugar-driven damage process, may delay ageing diseases, and the iris extract is rich in compounds called isoflavonoids that could feed helpful bacteria.

Using the extract as the bacteria's food source, the team grew postbiotics and tested their antioxidant and antiglycation strength. They also checked whether the extract feeds good bacteria directly. A flower extract that boosts protective compounds could end up in functional foods aimed at healthier ageing.
pmc-13238260:
Azamtta and colleagues report a heart valve defect found, remarkably, in a woman of seventy. In a parachute mitral valve, all the cords that should fan out to two muscles instead anchor to one, shaping the valve like a parachute. The defect is congenital and rare, and it can narrow or leak the valve, disturbing blood flow through the heart.

Her single papillary muscle was also calcified, hardened with calcium over a lifetime. Heart ultrasound revealed the valve's unusual shape, as it usually does. Most such valves declare themselves far earlier in life. A case surfacing at seventy widens doctors' sense of how quietly this defect can ride along for decades.
pmc-13241360:
Rindell and colleagues at the University of Turku counted mitochondrial diabetes cases across Southwest Finland. Records from 2000 to 2022 were screened at the university hospital. One thousand four charts yielded nine confirmed cases, topped up by a research cohort. Seventeen patients with genetic confirmation formed the final group.

Diabetes arrived at a mean age of thirty-five, unusually young for type 2. Fourteen of seventeen patients also had hearing impairment, a telling companion sign. Insulin typically began about three and a half years after diagnosis. Prevalence worked out under three cases per hundred thousand residents.
pmc-13241460:
Weidmann's team at Munich's chronic fatigue center built two short questionnaires for exhausted young patients. Post-infection illness and ME/CFS slash school attendance and social life in the young. Ninety-one patients aged ten to 25 validated the new activity and participation scales. Scores run from zero to one hundred.

The activity scale fit a single factor excellently with strong internal consistency. Both scores tracked established fatigue and quality-of-life yardsticks closely. They also separated ME/CFS cases from other post-infection patients reasonably well. Weidmann offers the pair as pragmatic screening tools for clinics.
pmc-13242360:
Saragih's team in Semarang pooled randomized trials of online psychosocial education for adult cancer patients. All were run outside clinics, at home. Six sources yielded fourteen studies and 1,509 patients. Outcomes spanned fear of return, distress, and quality of life. Risk of bias was graded with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool.

Fear of return fell sharply after the programs, though the pooled effect was small. Distress scores and life scores pointed the right way without quite reaching the mark. Spread was high for distress, low for the rest. The authors endorse nurse-led digital support that can scale up.
pmc-13242460:
Luis Castillo-Olamendi and colleagues studied how calcium signals switch on recycling inside plant cells under salt-like water stress. Their paper appeared in Planta in 2026, using the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. When water grows scarce, plant cells break down and reuse damaged parts through autophagy. The team tracked a tagged protein called ATG8i and watched calcium levels with a glowing sensor line.

Osmotic stress triggered a calcium surge, strongest where the stem meets the root. That zone also filled with ATG8i-marked autophagosomes, the small sacs that carry cargo to be recycled. Blocking calcium entry from outside the cells weakened the response. The sacs overlapped with the endoplasmic reticulum, hinting at a targeted form of recycling for that structure. The authors conclude that calcium acts as the messenger linking water stress to this cleanup system.
pmc-13244260:
Two related enzyme products came before the EFSA Panel on Food Enzymes drawn from a non-modified Aspergillus mold strain made by Shin Nihon Chemical. The opinion appeared in the EFSA Journal in 2026. One product keeps both its protein-cutting activities, oryzin and leucyl aminopeptidase; the other is heat-treated to leave only the aminopeptidase. Together they are meant for fourteen food manufacturing processes across the industry.

One process removes the enzyme entirely, so exposure was modeled for the other thirteen and stayed low even for high consumers. Genetic damage tests came back clean. A ninety-day rat study set a no-harm level far above human exposure. The safety margin topped a thousand-fold for the native enzyme and ran larger for the heat-treated one. Both products were free of living production cells. The panel concluded neither enzyme raises a safety concern under its intended uses.
pmc-13245060:
Silvia Angelillo and colleagues surveyed what Italian female university students know and do about cervical cancer screening. Their cross-sectional study appeared in Human Vaccines and Immunotherapeutics in 2026. One thousand students in Caserta and Naples answered questions on HPV, cancer risk, and the Pap test.

Knowledge was middling: the average score was 12.6 out of 20, and only a sliver of students scored perfectly. Scores ran higher among older students, medical students, the HPV-vaccinated, and those who had learned from healthcare workers. Barely one in eight felt personally at high risk. Among students old enough to be screening-eligible, about two-thirds had actually been screened. The authors read the gaps as a communication failure more than apathy. Their remedy: put health workers in front of students, tie vaccination to screening, and fix the low risk perception.
pmc-13246560:
Çift, Kutlu, and Çoban built a prediction tool for a surgical emergency in this 2026 World Journal of Urology paper. In testicular torsion, a twisted cord cuts blood flow, and surgeons must judge quickly whether the testicle can be untwisted and saved or must be removed. The team analyzed one hundred seventeen past surgical cases, hunting for features that separated the two outcomes.

A hybrid search algorithm picked seven useful features, led by how long symptoms had lasted and a platelet measure rarely studied before. Their best model, an ensemble method called CatBoost, predicted the outcome with about ninety percent accuracy, and explanation tools showed why each prediction leaned as it did. A web app and paper scoring chart put the model at clinicians' fingertips, pending outside validation.
pmc-13246760:
Luo, Ma, Yang, and co-authors engineered a multi-tool nanoparticle against glioblastoma, in this 2026 Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy paper. Glioblastoma resists immunotherapy partly because its surroundings suppress immune attack, and the blood-brain barrier blocks most drugs. The team built particles wrapped in membranes from bone-derived neutrophils, white blood cells that naturally cross into brain tumors.

Inside sat two weapons: a light-activated dye that heats and poisons tumor cells under near-infrared light while glowing for imaging. CRISPR gene editing that silences CD73, a gene helping tumors suppress immunity. In their experiments the particles reached the tumor, reprogrammed its environment toward immune attack, and triggered systemic antitumor immunity. The authors present it as a combined gene-and-light therapy platform.
pmc-13247660:
Galindo-Vázquez and co-authors validated two short mental-health questionnaires for Mexican cancer patients, in this 2026 Palliative and Supportive Care study. The PHQ-9 screens for depression and the GAD-7 for anxiety, and both are used worldwide, but their performance in Spanish-speaking oncology patients needed checking. Three hundred fifty-seven adults in treatment at a Mexican cancer hospital completed the culturally adapted Spanish versions.

Factor analysis showed the depression scale splitting into two related dimensions and the anxiety scale holding together as one, with both showing acceptable to good internal consistency. Model fits were adequate, and scores related sensibly to other measures. The authors conclude both brief tools are valid and reliable for spotting depression and anxiety symptoms early in Mexican oncology care, supporting routine screening.
pmc-13248960:
Batubara and co-authors report a benign tumor in an unexpected place, in a 2026 case report from Indonesia. A thirty-four-year-old woman had severe monthly pain in her lower left abdomen and a growing pelvic mass. Scans suggested a dermoid cyst on an ovary alongside endometriosis cysts on both ovaries, a common enough picture that the true source stayed hidden.

During surgery the large cyst proved to grow from her left fallopian tube, not the ovary. Tissue testing confirmed a mature cystic teratoma there, an exceedingly rare site for this tumor. The authors remind clinicians to include tubal teratoma when weighing complex pelvic masses, since only the operation and pathology settle the question.
pmc-13249060:
Kumar, Bender, and Durnwald tested text message support after pregnancy, in a 2026 implementation study. Some patients show impaired glucose tolerance during pregnancy without developing gestational diabetes, and their long-term diabetes risk then goes largely unmanaged. The team's BRIDGE program sent twelve weeks of postpartum texts urging blood sugar testing and a primary care visit.

Compared with a historical group, participants completed the key blood test at more than three times the rate within a year. Scheduling of primary care visits also rose sharply, and adding a focused postpartum visit sped testing further. One gap persisted: fewer than sixty percent of those visits included counseling about the glucose finding, a target for improvement.
pmc-13249160:
Jiang and Li built a scoring model for how cities withstand sudden disasters, in a 2026 PLOS One paper. They assembled housing, infrastructure, economic, and population data for twenty-five districts in two Chinese cities, Changchun and Hohhot. Three yardsticks anchored the system: how fast a city responds, how efficiently it allocates resources, and how many facilities serve each resident.

Expert weighting and a ranking method then compared districts at different service levels, producing short-term and long-term investment advice for each city. The authors checked their weighting scheme for consistency and sensitivity. They conclude current models capture city stability reasonably well, while noting room to sharpen the indicators.
pmc-13250260:
Majeed and a large team review yarrow, a traditional medicinal plant, as a modern health ingredient. Their 2026 Food Science and Nutrition paper surveys Achillea millefolium, a plant used for centuries in many healing traditions. Flowers, leaves, and stems each carry different active compounds, which helps explain the plant's many folk uses.

The review covers the plant's chemistry, its antioxidant and antimicrobial actions, and reported effects on diabetes, inflammation, and cancer pathways. It also examines yarrow combined with other plants, drugs, and nanoparticle carriers, plus uses in cosmetics and foods. The authors judge the ingredient broadly promising, with wound healing among its best-known uses. They call for better-designed formulations and stronger clinical testing of its products.
pmc-13250860:
Yin and co-authors present the first systematic look at drug resistance across all sixty-nine HIV-1 recombinant forms found in China. Their 2026 Emerging Microbes and Infections study catalogs strains that mix genetic pieces of other HIV types. Data run through 2025 and span four generations of these circulating recombinant forms.

Several forms carried moderate levels of resistance passed to newly infected people, and far higher levels in patients about to start treatment. One mutation type, V179D/E, appeared across many forms and may weaken a key drug class when combined with other changes. The authors say the survey gives China baseline data for choosing first-line drugs wisely. They also call for laboratory testing of how these natural mutations affect the newest strains.
pmc-13251760:
Tang and Li review home-based cardiac rehabilitation delivered by phone and internet for coronary artery disease patients. Their 2026 Journal of Multidisciplinary Healthcare paper searches studies from 2015 to late 2025 across four databases. Heart rehabilitation at home has grown fast, yet its true effectiveness stayed debated.

The review finds home telerehabilitation improves heart outcomes, lung fitness, treatment adherence, and quality of life. Programs using app follow-ups and wearable monitors cut deaths and readmissions and raised exercise tolerance in the studies surveyed. Mood and metabolic measures also improved, with adherence beating center-based programs. Technology hurdles, data security, and weak policy support still block wider rollout, so the authors want large multicenter trials.
pmc-13255760:
Su and colleagues traced why Hulunbuir sheep are born with short tails, using single-cell sequencing of embryos from the short-tailed breed and from long-tailed Hu sheep. The short tail traces to a loss-of-function change in the T gene, a master regulator of body axis development. Embryos were profiled at two early stages, and a mouse model carrying the same mutation provided cross-species checks.

Mutant embryos showed signs that the apical ectodermal ridge, a signaling strip guiding tail outgrowth, regresses too early. Bone morphogenetic signaling rose while a key growth factor fell, undermining ridge survival. The same mutation killed mouse embryos outright, underlining species differences. The work nominates markers for tail-length breeding.
pmc-13256260:
Zhao, Strober, Hou, and co-authors present a method that measures how much of a disease's heritability is shared with other diseases through pleiotropy. Earlier work estimated genetic links one helper disease at a time. Their PHBC method instead uses a whole matrix of links, with a Monte Carlo fix for sampling noise, across United Kingdom Biobank diseases.

Across fifteen diseases, about twenty-seven percent of heritability was shared with a modest helper set. Expanding to sixty-two diseases and traits pushed the share to roughly half. Dropping even the most useful disease groups lowered the figure only slightly, and genetic pleiotropy topped what shared symptoms alone would predict. The authors conclude pleiotropy runs through common disease genetics.
pmc-13257160:
Wang compared five ways of drying Polygonatum cyrtonema, a medicinal rhizome, weighing speed against quality. Hot air, infrared, microwave, freeze, and vacuum drying were tested for drying kinetics, color, rehydration, microstructure, and antioxidant retention. A mathematical model was fitted to each method's moisture curve.

Microwave drying was fastest by far, taking a tiny fraction of freeze-drying's eighteen hours, but retained fewer polysaccharides. Infrared dried quickly and kept color well, yet damaged microstructure and active compounds. Freeze and vacuum drying best preserved antioxidants and flavor, though freeze-drying's energy cost limits industrial use. The author judges vacuum drying the best overall balance for production.
pmc-13257660:
Zhenyu Bao and co-authors model how ultra-high-performance concrete cracks under pulling forces. Ordinary models fit stress-strain curves but ignore the fibers that give this concrete its toughness. Their 2026 approach listens to the material instead, using acoustic emission signals as a running measure of damage.

Tensile tests varied steel fiber length and dose while sensors counted tiny cracking sounds. A fiber factor fed those signals into a damage equation checked against fourteen published datasets. After correction, predictions landed within a few percent of measured values. Built into beam simulations, the model matched real load-bending behavior well.
pmc-13262560:
Boon Tat Yeap and colleagues survey how lockdown life treated university staff on Borneo. Malaysia's Movement Control Order forced academics and support staff into remote work almost overnight. Their cross-sectional study collected four hundred twenty-seven responses during the order's first phase.

A standard questionnaire scored physical, psychological, social, and environmental quality of life. Scores spread widest on the environmental side, covering money, safety, and home conditions. Gender made no difference, but education, years employed, marriage, and family income all shifted results. Better-educated and longer-serving staff coped measurably better, pointing to where support should aim in future disruptions.
pmc-13263760:
Tan Van Nguyen and colleagues explore whether frailty hits older Vietnamese women and men with diabetes differently. Six hundred forty-four clinic patients aged sixty and up were graded by Fried's frailty criteria across two hospitals. Their 2026 observational study then tracks six months of hospitalizations.

Three in ten participants qualified as frail, with women modestly ahead of men. Frailty raised hospitalization risk in both sexes, but the link ran stronger in women. The authors read this as grounds for sex-aware diabetes care in aging patients. Screening grandmothers and grandfathers by the same cutoffs may miss unequal danger, they suggest.
pmc-13323160:
Berg and co-authors test a virtual reality animation for teaching drug absorption in this 2026 study. Absorption and bioavailability, the share of a dose reaching the blood, are hard for pharmacology students to picture. Weak pharmacology knowledge is one cause of medication errors. Students who had finished a basic pharmacology course watched the animation at five international sites.

In total 133 students completed a questionnaire, and about half said the animation changed their understanding of absorption. Thirteen medical students in Bergen also joined focus group interviews. Their comments formed three themes about linking pharmacology to other subjects, balancing engagement against overload, and learning deeply while facing exams. Berg concludes the tool works well and engages students, but it must allow self pacing so learners are not overwhelmed.
pmc-13367960:
Mennillo and colleagues apply single-cell spatial transcriptomics, a method mapping which genes are active in individual cells at their exact tissue locations, to archived colon biopsies in 2026 gastroenterology research. The biopsies, preserved in paraffin blocks from healthy controls, ulcerative colitis patients, and patients with checkpoint-inhibitor colitis, were arrayed together for comparison. Three datasets tested different commercial imaging panels, asking which combination best resolves the cell networks that organize inflamed gut tissue.

One platform, MERSCOPE, failed on these samples: only 0.17 percent of its cells passed quality control, so it was dropped from the analysis. Custom Xenium panels of 290 and 480 targeted genes, plus an expanded panel of roughly 5,000 genes, performed the core comparisons. The custom panels gave better sensitivity and cell-type resolution on the old paraffin tissue. Mennillo presents the collection as a practical resource for studying colitis cell networks in routine clinical biopsies.
pmc-13369960:
Ordunez and a large regional panel set priorities for joining up heart, kidney, and metabolic care. Their 2026 paper reports Phase 3 of HEARTS 2.0, the Americas adaptation of the World Health Organization's HEARTS initiative. These conditions overlap heavily yet are usually managed separately, and the panel aimed to pick interventions primary care services can actually deliver together.

A multidisciplinary panel appraised 45 candidate interventions using structured evidence reviews, evidence-to-decision frameworks, and anonymous rating rounds. It prioritised 38 for implementation. Hypertension care remains the entry point. The package adds early diabetes and kidney disease detection, lifestyle support, and risk-based combination drug therapy. It also adds task-sharing with non-physician staff and structured long-term follow-up. The authors present the list as the evidence base for updating the HEARTS clinical pathway at scale.
pmc-13374360:
Assaeed and colleagues survey the plant life of Rawdhat Khuraym, a depression near Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, now part of a protected reserve system, in 2026 desert ecology research. Rawdah meadows collect rainwater and support rich vegetation for the Arabian desert. The team documented the site's floristic composition across seasons and classified plants by life form and family. They related vegetation patterns to soil properties to inform sustainable management of the protected area and its grazing and recreation pressures.

The survey recorded 89 species from 30 families in the protected depression. Annuals made up 57.3 percent of species, finishing their life cycles in wet spells, while perennials formed 42.4 percent of the flora. Four families, Asteraceae, Poaceae, Fabaceae, and Brassicaceae, supplied 50.6 percent of species found. No species appeared on the international threatened list. Assaeed frames the inventory as the reference against which change in the reserve can be judged.
pmc-13385460:
Pownall and colleagues review how training for mental health staff takes in the United Nations global goals. Those goals span health, schools, fair work, and the climate. The team screened the field and read forty-seven papers in full. Three broad ways of teaching came out. One used active, sharp thought on hard issues. One used group work across fields. One used hands-on service in real settings.

Use of the goals is growing, but it stays patchy. Few courses line up with each other. Staff who teach get little training for this work. No firm guide links the goals to mental health training. The review sets out steps to close those gaps.
pmc-13396460:
Sun and co-authors use, in 2026, deep learning to improve the chiroptical properties of perovskite-coated titanium dioxide nanohelices, spiral structures that twist light. Chirality measures how strongly a material responds to left- versus right-circularly polarized light, summed up by the dissymmetry factor glum. The team coated helical titanium dioxide cores, grown by glancing-angle deposition, with achiral perovskite shells and trained models to inverse-design structures hitting target optical responses.

The tuning lifted the dissymmetry factor of the perovskite system from 0.20 to 0.35 in the reported experiments. The learned design rules then transferred across material classes: applied to polymer-based chiral organics using F8BT, the approach produced a 74 percent enhancement of glum, from 0.50 to 0.87 in the new designs. The authors argue that inverse design trained on one luminophore family can accelerate discovery in others, a shortcut for engineering light sources that emit or detect polarized light.
pmc-13400860:
Baysal and Eşkazan revisit, in a 2026 letter, the PLASMIC score used to predict severe ADAMTS13 deficiency in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, a rare blood emergency where fast prediction guides plasma exchange. They discuss a recent multicenter reevaluation by Singh and colleagues, which exposed a diagnostic gap in older patients. Sensitivity fell to 62 percent among patients aged 60 and over, a vulnerable group in whom comorbidities can confound the score's traditional parameters.

Working through the score item by item, the letter endorses simplification, singling out mean corpuscular volume as the weakest link.
