pmc-4001360:
Ru, Li, Wang, and their team built TCMSP in 2014, a database for the study of herbal drugs. Modern drug research and traditional Chinese herbal practice often clash, in part because how herbs act in the body is poorly understood. TCMSP was made to close that gap and speed drug discovery from herbs.

The database links herbs to their chemical parts, the body targets those parts hit, and the diseases tied to those targets. Users can trace a whole chain from plant to molecule to effect. That systems view helps researchers pick the most promising herbs and compounds for lab tests, instead of testing blind.
pmc-4833860:
Menzel, Ng, and Krogh presented Kaiju in 2016 for metagenomic classification. Metagenomics studies microbes from environmental and clinical samples without culturing them. It matters for ecology and for human health, and studies were growing to larger scales.

Recent fast programs compared DNA against genomic references, but Kaiju takes a protein-level approach for sensitivity. It classifies reads by matching translated sequences against a protein database. That catches distant relatives that DNA matching misses. Fast and sensitive classification is the gateway to knowing which microbes are in a sample and what they might be doing.
pmc-5082560:
Burgess, Davies, and Thompson wrote in 2016 about a bias in two-sample Mendelian randomization. Such analyses are often performed using summarized data from two separate samples. In a one-sample analysis, weak instruments bias the causal estimate toward the simple observational association.

The paper examines what happens when the two samples overlap in participants. Overlap can push a two-sample estimate toward the same bias that affects one-sample work. The size of the problem depends on how much overlap exists and how weak the instruments are. Knowing this helps researchers design studies and judge published causal claims with care.
pmc-5756260:
Nina Hessvik and Alicia Llorente reviewed exosome formation and release in 2017. Exosomes are tiny membrane bubbles that cells shed into their surroundings. They form inside a cell compartment and escape when that compartment fuses with the cell surface.

Once dismissed as cell waste, exosomes are now known to carry proteins and RNA between cells. The review gathers what is known about the machinery that builds them and controls their release. It also notes the many open questions about how cargo is chosen. For readers new to the field, it gives a clear map of a fast-moving area.
pmc-7737760:
Rose Oughtred and colleagues described in 2020 the BioGRID, a free public database that collects known interactions between proteins, genes, and chemicals. Every entry is curated by hand from published experiments, rather than scraped automatically. The database covers many species, from yeast, worm, and fly to mouse and human.

By the time of this report it held close to two million carefully checked interactions, and it keeps growing as curators read new papers. Researchers query it to see what a protein partners with, which often hints at what the protein does. In an era of huge automated datasets, BioGRID's value lies in the slow human checking behind each record.
podcast-dannyjones-XmVQFX2Pp60:
Chris and Emily Bledsoe join Danny Jones to talk about a NASA-linked study of UFO contact and what they call spiritual beings. The episode title calls the study forbidden. The Bledsoes are known for close contact claims that drew interest from officials.

The guests tell their story of bright orbs, close sightings, and the officials who came to ask questions. They argue the events point to beings with a spiritual side, not just craft in the sky. Jones lets them lay out the full tale in order. The library files the episode as an archive record, so readers can judge the claims for themselves.
podcast-tuckercarlson-xHjM_aNYI60:
Tucker Carlson warns that the United States is drifting toward civil war. He calls such wars the worst kind any nation can face. The cause, he says, is a gap between groups that no longer share a life.

The title ties his warning to ICE protests and street riots. Carlson argues that clashes over enforcement show how deep the split runs. He urges fast action before violence hardens into habit. The episode is grave from start to finish. It speaks to viewers who already fear the country is breaking apart.
prestwich-flint-implements-amiens-abbevi:
Joseph Prestwich, a respected British geologist, reported on flint tools to the Royal Society in 1860. He had visited gravel pits at Amiens and Abbeville in France, and at Hoxne in England. Worked flints lay there beside bones of extinct animals.

Prestwich confirms the claims of Boucher de Perthes, long dismissed in Britain. His standing made the verdict hard for the Royal Society to ignore. The paper effectively ended the debate over the antiquity of man. From 1860 onward, deep human history was established science in Britain. French workers had been reporting such finds from the Somme gravels for years.
ruskin-unto-this-last-1860:
John Ruskin published Unto This Last in 1860, four essays on the morals of economics. Ruskin attacks the idea that wealth is mere buying power and cheap labor a gain. True wealth, he argues, is life itself: health, justice, and noble work. There is no wealth but life is his famous summary.

He defends fair wages, honest goods, and work that honors the worker. The essays first appeared in a magazine and shocked its readers. Gandhi read the book, translated it, and called it a guide for his own life. It became a founding text of ethical economics. Its claims still challenge market orthodoxy.
sully-memoirs-vol-1-1760:
Maximilien de Béthune, Duke of Sully, was Henri IV's great minister, the man who rebuilt France's finances after civil war. His Mémoires of 1638 record that partnership of king and servant. Volume one here opens the English translation printed in 1760, after Charlotte Lennox's version of 1756, in a set of five volumes.

Sully writes of war, taxes, roads, and farms with a steward's pride in order restored. The memoir presents Henri and himself as a team that dragged France from ruin to strength. Historians check his boasts, yet no source shows the reign's inner work like this one. Volume one begins the classic ministerial memoir of the age.
sully-memoirs-vol-2-1760:
Volume two continues the English Sully, the Memoirs of Maximilian de Bethune, Duke of Sully, in the printing of 1760. Sully's French Mémoires date to 1638, a generation after Henri IV's murder ended their work together. The English set, after Charlotte Lennox's translation of 1756, runs to five volumes.

In these pages Sully goes on counting what good government costs and what it saves. Campaigns and councils mix with budgets, grain stores, and plans for France's wealth. The minister's voice is brisk, certain, and never shy about his own merit. Readers meet statecraft here as daily labor, not glory. Volume two keeps that practical epic moving.
sully-memoirs-vol-3-1760:
Sully's Memoirs reach volume three in the English translation printed in 1760, after Charlotte Lennox's version of 1756. Maximilien de Béthune, duc de Sully, had been Henri IV's right hand in war and finance. His Mémoires of 1638 set down how the two men governed France between them.

Volume three holds more of that double portrait: a king of charm and drive, a minister of ledgers and iron will. Sully recounts reforms in tax and farming, and the plots that ringed the throne. The work became the classic memoir of a great minister, trusted and argued with ever since. Its middle volume keeps the reign's machinery in plain view.
sully-memoirs-vol-4-1760:
Volume four of the English Sully, printed in 1760 after Charlotte Lennox's translation, continues the Memoirs of the Duke of Sully. The French original of 1638 tells how Henri IV and his minister pulled France out of civil war. The English set runs to five volumes, this one standing near its close.

War finance, diplomacy, and court intrigue fill Sully's later pages, all told from the minister's chair. He writes to defend his record, and the defense is detailed enough to test. Few memoirs show so clearly how a state is fed, armed, and kept solvent. Volume four carries that lesson through the reign's high years. The voice stays crisp, proud, and practical.
sully-memoirs-vol-5-1760:
Volume five completes the English Memoirs of Maximilian de Bethune, Duke of Sully, in the printing of 1760. Sully's Mémoires of 1638, Englished after Charlotte Lennox's version of 1756, fill five volumes in all. The duke had served Henri IV as soldier, treasurer, and chief adviser through France's recovery.

The closing volume ends the reign and its minister's long service together. Sully's theme never changes: a kingdom thrives when its money is honestly kept and wisely spent. His pride in that record runs through every page, and readers can weigh it against the facts he supplies. The set stands as the classic ministerial memoir of early modern Europe.
sybil-or-the-two-nations-pg3760: Disraeli's Sybil, or The Two Nations, exposes the deep divide of Victorian England. Rich and poor live side by side as strangers in a single land. This passionate political novel helped spark the movement for social reform. A landmark of the social conscience in English fiction.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing: Volume ten of Casanova's memoirs: adventures multiply. The Venetian's story grows richer. A life lived to the full. Tenth volume: the adventures multiply, a life lived at full stretch, the tale grows richer, adventures come thick and fast.
the-origin-of-species-from-the-westminst: Thomas Henry Huxley's Westminster Review essay on the Origin: April 1860. The most famous review ever written, for Darwin. The bulldog's manifesto. Huxley's famous review defends Darwin, the bulldog's opening bark, the most famous review ever written.
titus-andronicus-pg2260: The banquet of revenge ends this edition: Titus serves Tamora her sons baked in a pie, and the stage fills with corpses. Shakespeare's bloodiest tragedy, Grand Guignol before its time. Horror and poetry in shocking embrace.
tob-0160:
Rudolf Steiner's manual for higher knowledge appears in Max Gysi's translation as The Way of Initiation, the same work titled How to Attain Knowledge of the Higher Worlds. Steiner lays out meditative exercises and the moral preparation he considered necessary before perceiving spiritual worlds. Reverence, patience, and control of thought precede any exercises in concentration.

Shorter and more practical than his lecture volumes, the manual functions as the student's handbook and Anthroposophy's front door. Steiner warns against seeking experiences for sensation's sake and stresses healthy judgment throughout. Readers get the disciplined, stepwise program behind his movement's spiritual training, presented by its founder as a path anyone earnest may attempt.
tob-10260:
A short grimoire on calling spirits circulated for centuries under the name of Henry Cornelius Agrippa as a fourth book to his Three Books of Occult Philosophy. Scholars agree Agrippa did not write it. It appeared after his death and fed on his fame.

Unlike Agrippa's learned theory, the fourth book gives practice: names of spirits, seals, hours, and steps for calling them up and questioning them. Magicians copied its rites into later grimoires, and it helped fix the image of the learned magician at work. Readers can compare its plain ritual craft with the deep system of the real Agrippa.
tob-10960:
Porphyry was Plotinus's student, editor, and biographer, and Thomas Taylor's Select Works present him in several of his strongest modes. Selections include his case for abstinence from meat, his allegorical reading of the cave of the nymphs in Homer, and material connected with his famous attack on Christianity, a work mostly lost.

Taylor preserves the sharp mind of antiquity's most formidable pagan philosopher. Porphyry argues vegetarianism on spiritual and ethical grounds, reads epic poetry as philosophy in disguise, and cross-examines Christian claims with a scholar's tools. Philosophy here has its gloves off. Readers meet the opponent early Christians themselves considered their most dangerous critic.
tob-4160:
Rudolf Otto, a German theologian, published The Idea of the Holy in 1917, and John W. Harvey's English translation spread it worldwide. Otto argues that religion rests on something reason cannot capture: the numinous, felt as mysterium tremendum, a mystery that makes a person tremble and draws them at once.

Awe before the wholly other, he says, comes before doctrine, morals, and creed. Every faith, from tribal rites to high liturgy, carries that shudder at its core. The book changed how scholars describe religious feeling. Few works of theology from the last century are still assigned, quoted, and argued with as this one is.
tob-9160:
Thomas Heath edited and translated the Works of Archimedes, the greatest mathematician of the ancient world, in the volume verified from the 1919 scan. On the Sphere and Cylinder, the Measurement of the Circle, and the Sand-Reckoner stand among its treatises. Archimedes of Syracuse proved results that calculus would not match for nearly two thousand years.

He bounds pi, weighs the crown, and counts the grains of sand that would fill the universe, all with strict proof. Heath's edition adds a famous account of a lost method of discovery. Eureka's author stands here in full: playful, rigorous, and centuries ahead of his readers.
treaty-of-berwick-1560:
England and Scotland conclude the Treaty of Berwick in 1560. Elizabeth's England allies with Scotland's Protestant lords by its terms. French power in the north is the foe both sides fear.

English arms and gold back the Scots against their French-backed regent. The pact helps secure the Scottish Reformation in its cradle year. Old enmity between the two kingdoms starts its turn toward union. A Protestant Britain takes shape along the line this treaty draws. Few short pacts mark so clear a hinge in British history and faith. Within months, Scotland's parliament had cast off Rome and the old mass.
turgenev-first-love-1860:
Isabel Hapgood translated First Love and its companion stories into English in 1904. Turgenev's title novella, written in 1860, is told by Vladimir, now middle-aged, recalling his sixteenth summer. At a neighboring villa he falls for Zinaida, a young princess who keeps a court of older admirers.

Vladimir spies, dreams, and suffers until he learns that his own father is Zinaida's secret lover. The shock ends his boyhood in a single night of watching. Turgenev called the tale his most personal work, drawn from his own youth. Hapgood's version stands beside Garnett's Turgenev as a distinct translation. The novella remains a classic study of first desire and disillusion.
turgenev-on-the-eve-1860:
On the Eve, Turgenev's novel of 1860, is given here in Constance Garnett's translation. Elena Stahova, a thoughtful young Russian girl, finds the suitors her parents favor too small for her dreams. She meets Insarov, a poor Bulgarian student burning to free his homeland from Turkish rule.

Elena chooses Insarov against her family's wishes, ready to share his cause and his exile. Their marriage takes them toward Italy, where illness waits on the road to war. Turgenev wrote on the eve of the freeing of the serfs in Russia. His new man and new woman point past the gentry world of his earlier books. The novel asks what a life should be spent on.
u-s-copyright-renewals-1960: The Copyright Office's annual catalog for 1960 records which older works had their copyrights renewed that year. Such volumes helped the publishing and entertainment industries keep track of who owned what as decades of books, songs, and films aged. Researchers today mine them for the history of American copyright and the afterlives of forgotten works.
un-ga-res-1760:
Pressure on Britain over Southern Rhodesia mounts in Resolution 1760, adopted by the UN General Assembly on 31 October 1962. The Assembly recalls its 1960 call to end colonial rule, which it says applies in full to the colony. Four months before, it had ruled that Southern Rhodesia is a land not yet self-governing under the Charter. It also backs the people's fixed right to rule themselves and to form a free African state.

The Assembly had heard people who came to plead the case in person. It notes with deep regret that Britain had still not moved to call a meeting on a new constitution, with full African voice in the room. Votes like this one built the long UN campaign against the white minority regime in Rhodesia.
un-ga-res-3160:
Eight years of drift over the Falkland Islands, called the Malvinas by Argentina, draw a rebuke in Resolution 3160, adopted on 14 December 1973. In 1965, the Assembly had urged Argentina and the United Kingdom to open talks at once on the islands' fate. The call rested on the Charter and on the 1960 vote to end colonial rule, with the good of the island people in mind.

Grave concern fills the text: in eight years, no real step toward a fix had been made. The call for talks is pressed again, with fresh weight. The sovereignty fight that froze here in 1973 would thaw, nine years later, into the Falklands War of 1982.
un-ga-res-a-69-60:
Peace can be built by gathering guns, argues Resolution A/69/60, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its theme is the firming of peace through workable disarmament steps. A whole and joined approach to such steps, the text holds, is often a must before peace can hold and grow in lands torn by war.

The steps are named in plain terms. Arms gained by illicit trade or illicit making must be gathered and dealt with by safe hands, best by destruction. The same goes for arms and rounds that state chiefs declare spare. Such work, done well, lays the base for peace work that lasts past the last cease-fire.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1760 (XVII), adopted on 31 October 1962, kept up pressure on the question of Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly restated the people's right to self-rule and to form an independent African state. It voiced deep regret that Britain had still not called the all-party conference demanded in resolution 1747 (XVI). The conference was to replace the rejected 1961 constitution.

The text warned that forcing that constitution through, and holding votes under it, would worsen an already tense situation. Britain was asked to suspend the constitution and cancel the coming elections. It was asked to grant full voting rights to all without discrimination. It was also asked to let the Acting Secretary-General help bring the sides together.

General Assembly Resolution 3160 (XXVIII), adopted on 14 December 1973, returned to the Falkland Islands, also named Malvinas. The Assembly voiced grave concern that eight years had passed since its 1965 call for talks. The talks were between Argentina and the United Kingdom on who held the islands. No real headway had been made.

The text approved the decolonization committee's chapters on the islands and declared that the talks had to speed up. Both governments were urged to proceed without delay toward a peaceful settlement of the sovereignty dispute. The settlement would end the colonial state of affairs. They were to report the outcome by the next session at the latest.

Resolution 69/60 of the General Assembly backs practical disarmament measures as a way to strengthen peace after conflicts. These include taking in and destroying illicit or surplus small arms and ammunition. They include disarmament, demobilization and reintegration of former fighters. They include mine clearing and keeping stockpiles secure. The Assembly stresses including such steps in peacekeeping missions with the host state's consent. It backs the Programme of Action Implementation Support System for matching needs with resources. It urges giving to the United Nations trust facility for work on arms control.
un-sc-res-1160: United Nations record keeping gives this text the number 1160, and the catalog dates it 1993. Resolutions are the way the Council states its decisions, and member states are expected to take them seriously. Preserving the text in this form keeps a small piece of diplomatic history open to any reader. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1260: Numbered 1260 in the Council's sequence, this resolution is catalogued as a 1999 entry in the United Nations official record. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1360: Number 1360 marks this Security Council text in the official record, catalogued here at 1999. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1460:
Children caught in war gained a stronger pledge from the Council in January 2003. On 30 January 2003 it backed the Secretary-General's call for an era of application. Old promises to protect children now had to be put into practice. The Council recalled its line of resolutions on children and armed conflict. Reports on women, peace, and security also fed into the text.

Parties that recruit or use child soldiers must stop at once. The Council voiced plans to talk with groups that break the rules. It asked United Nations agencies to coordinate their child protection work. It also pushed for action plans to end the use of children in fighting. Monitoring of abuses formed part of the scheme.
un-sc-res-1560: Number 1560 in the sequence, this 2004 resolution records a formal decision of the fifteen-member Security Council. Its text comes from the official record through English Wikisource. The paragraphs follow the body's long-standing pattern, moving from noted facts and recalled actions to the specific steps the Council voted to require or request.
un-sc-res-1660:
The Yugoslav tribunal gained a new kind of judge in 2006. Trials were long, and a judge's illness could stall them for months. On 28 February 2006 the Security Council amended the tribunal's statute. Reserve judges could now be named from the pool of ad litem judges. The tribunal's president made the proposal. A reserve judge would sit through a trial from the start.

If a trial judge could not continue, the reserve could step in. No testimony would need to be heard twice. The annex rewrites two articles of the statute. It sets the chambers at sixteen permanent judges plus temporary ones. The reform served the court's drive to finish its work. It was a practical fix to a real weakness in long trials.
un-sc-res-1760:
Liberia's sanctions were kept under expert review on 20 June 2007. The government had rebuilt steadily since January 2006, and its timber rules had ended the log measures. Liberia had just joined the Kimberley Process as a participant. The expert panel's report of 24 May 2007 was before the Council. The arms embargo and asset freeze of resolutions 1521 (2003) and 1532 (2004) had been reviewed against their lifting terms.

The Council found that progress toward those terms was still not enough. The remaining measures therefore stayed in force. It asked the Secretary-General to set up a new Panel of Experts within one month. The panel would follow up the sanctions, check for breaches, and judge the freeze's working. All states and Liberia's government had to cooperate with the panel in full and give it free access. The Council stayed actively seized.
un-sc-res-1860:
Resolution 1860 addressed the war in Gaza that began in late December 2008, when Israel launched a major offensive after rocket fire from the strip. Civilians on both sides were suffering, and aid could barely reach Gaza's people. The Council called for an immediate ceasefire.

The text demands a durable truce, open crossings for food and medicine, and an end to weapons smuggling into Gaza. It also restates support for a Palestinian state beside Israel. Its careful wording, and the United States choosing not to block it, make the resolution a much-studied record of wartime diplomacy.
un-sc-res-2260: Côte d'Ivoire is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 2260, adopted on 20 January 2016. The country had held a calm presidential election in October 2015. Peace, justice work, and the economy were all moving forward, though some weakness remained. A report from the Secretary-General had advised drawing the peacekeeping operation down.
un-sc-res-260:
Security Council Resolution 260, adopted on November 6, 1968, recommended Equatorial Guinea for membership in the United Nations. Spain had granted the small west African land independence on October 12 of that year, closing a colonial chapter that ran back to the 1700s. The new state applied for its UN seat within weeks of raising its flag.

The General Assembly admitted Equatorial Guinea on November 12. The council's text is the standard brief form used for new members. But the moment was part of a vast change. Africa's map was being redrawn as colony after colony became a sovereign state. Each such vote added a voice to the Assembly's growing majority of new nations.
un-sc-res-360:
Cyprus slid deeper into crisis when the Security Council acted on 16 August 1974. Further military operations on the island had gravely worsened the situation after the first Turkish intervention in July. All states had declared respect for Cyprus's sovereignty and independence. The Council called the fighting a most serious threat to peace in the eastern Mediterranean.

The Council recorded its formal disapproval of the one-sided military actions taken against the Republic of Cyprus. It urged the parties to obey all its earlier resolutions, including the withdrawal without delay of foreign military personnel not present under international agreements. Talks called for in resolution 353 (1974) had to resume at once, in a spirit of cooperation. Their outcome was not to be shaped by gains won through military action. The Secretary-General was asked to report as needed, and the Council stayed seized of the question permanently.
un-sc-res-460: The decision entered as Resolution 460 forms part of the Council record catalogued for 1968. These short legal texts often sit at turning points, since the Council acts when peace or security is at stake. The text here follows the English Wikisource transcription of the official record, so readers get the Council's own wording. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-60: Words on a page were the work of Security Council Resolution 60, passed on 29 October 1948. A small team is formed: the United Kingdom, China, France, Belgium, and the Ukrainian Soviet Republic. Its task is to weigh all changes put to a draft text on Palestine, and, with the Acting Mediator's help, to draw up a fresh draft for the Council. The step was house work inside the long talks on a lasting fix for the land.
un-sc-res-660:
Iraqi tanks rolled into Kuwait on 2 August 1990, and the Council met the same day. It judged the invasion a breach of international peace and security. It acted under Articles 39 and 40 of the Charter, the parts that cover such breaches. Resolution 660 was adopted that day, by fourteen votes to none.

The Council condemned the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait. It demanded that Iraq withdraw all its forces at once, without conditions. The forces had to return to the positions they held on 1 August 1990. Iraq and Kuwait were called on to begin intensive negotiations at once, to settle their differences. The Council backed efforts toward that end, above all those of the League of Arab States. It also decided to meet again as needed, to take further steps to secure compliance with the resolution.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: UN Security Council Resolution 1160 — the landmark 1998 resolution imposing an arms embargo on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia over Kosovo. It targeted Belgrade’s war machine. The 1998 Kosovo embargo is the landmark: Belgrade’s Kosovo war machine formally targeted.

Security Council resolution 1260, adopted on 20 August 1999, backs the Peace Agreement signed in Lomé on 7 July 1999. The agreement was between the Government of Sierra Leone and the Revolutionary United Front (RUF). The Council commends both sides and the West African force ECOMOG, and calls on the parties to carry out the agreement in full.

To support the settlement, the Council provisionally expands the United Nations Observer Mission in Sierra Leone, UNOMSIL. It expands it to up to 210 military observers, working under ECOMOG's protection. It strengthens its political, human rights and child protection work. It calls on the RUF and all other armed groups to disarm and join the demobilization programme at once. It notes the agreement's plans for a Truth and Reconciliation Commission and a Human Rights Commission.

A shorter renewal than usual is granted to Iraq's oil-for-food programme in this text from July 2001. Earlier renewals had run 180 days. This time the Council chose 150 days, starting 4 July 2001, while it weighed changes meant to improve how aid reached Iraqis.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council kept the core rules first set in 1995 in force for the new period. Priority spending on food, nutrition, and health continued, along with United Nations checks that goods were shared fairly across the country. A full review of the programme was also ordered, a sign that the next renewal could bring wider changes.

Children in war zones gained a push from paper rules to real practice in 2003. On 30 January, the Council adopted Resolution 1460 without dissent. It builds on the child-protection texts of 1999 to 2001. The Secretary-General's fresh report lay before it. One legal note stands out in the text. Signing up children under fifteen is now a war crime in the new world court's statute.

The text backs the call for an era of application. Fine words must now be enforced on the ground. States must end impunity and try those who commit crimes against children. UN agencies and warring parties must turn the standards into daily practice. The push fed the watch lists that later named offending forces year by year.

Ethiopia and Eritrea's border still had not been marked out, years after the Algiers peace agreements, when their mission UNMEE was extended on 14 September 2004, until 15 March 2005. The Boundary Commission's 2002 ruling was meant to be final and binding, yet demarcation had stalled.

Both parties are called on to cooperate fully with UNMEE and remove all limits on its movement and work at once. They are pressed to work promptly with the Boundary Commission, including paying dues and naming field liaison officers, so marking the border can proceed. Ethiopia is urged to show the political will to accept the boundary ruling without conditions.

Africa's most populous state joined the world body days after freedom. On 7 October 1960, the Council adopted Resolution 160 without dissent. The Federation of Nigeria had won freedom from Britain six days before. The date, 1 October, was the peak of the Year of Africa. No African state held more people.

Having weighed the bid, the Council urges the Assembly to admit Nigeria. Admission followed within days. Nigeria's voice soon carried far in the Assembly. The state grew into one of Africa's top diplomatic powers. It also became a major source of troops for UN peacekeeping. This single line opened that long career.

Long trials strain a court when a judge falls ill. The Hague court for the Balkan wars had no spare bench. If a judge had to quit mid-trial, the case could crack. Its head asked for a fix. Resolution 1660 passed on 28 February 2006. It changed the court's own rulebook.

Stand-in judges could now be named as reserves. A reserve would sit through each phase of a trial. If a judge could not go on, the reserve stepped in. The case would not have to start from scratch. Two parts of the statute were swapped out in full. The text spells out how trial rooms are built and what stand-ins may do. It is dry court craft, yet it saved real trials from collapse.

Liberia's slow recovery after civil war frames Resolution 1760, adopted on 20 June 2007. The Council praises the new government's progress since January 2006, notes the end of limits on Liberian timber exports, and welcomes Liberia joining the Kimberley Process, which tracks rough diamonds. Sanctions from Resolution 1521 were still under review, and the Council found too little progress to lift them.

The main step is a new Panel of Experts, with up to three members, to serve for six months and watch the sanctions. The Council says the UN Mission in Liberia still matters for safety and for helping the government control diamond, timber, and border areas. It also finds that Liberia still threatens peace in the region, even with the gains made.

A ceasefire in the Gaza war is called for on 8 January 2009. Fighting had escalated after a period of calm was not renewed, and heavy civilian casualties followed. Gaza, it is stressed, is part of the territory occupied in 1967 and of the future Palestinian state, and grave concern is voiced at the deepening humanitarian crisis there.

An immediate, durable ceasefire, fully respected by all sides, is called for, leading to the full withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza. Unimpeded aid delivery and distribution across Gaza and regular opening of the crossings for goods and people are demanded. All violence against civilians and terrorism is condemned, the relief role of the refugee agency UNRWA is welcomed, and new efforts toward a two-state peace are urged.

Sexual violence as a weapon of war is the focus of Resolution 1960, adopted on 16 December 2010. Despite repeated condemnation, such violence continued worldwide, in places becoming systematic and brutal, while few perpetrators faced justice. The Secretary-General's November 2010 report documented the slow progress. Command responsibility and the need to end impunity run through the text.

The Council demands that all parties to armed conflict stop all sexual violence at once. It orders a naming system: the Secretary-General's annual reports must list parties credibly suspected of rape and other sexual violence, and that list will guide UN engagement and possible sanctions designations. Parties must make time-bound commitments, with clear orders through their chains of command, and their follow-through will be tracked. It also orders monitoring, analysis, and reporting arrangements in the field, more women protection advisers in peacekeeping missions, and scenario-based training for peacekeepers.

Côte d'Ivoire's peacekeeping force is drawn down in Resolution 2260, adopted on 20 January 2016. The presidential election of 25 October 2015 had passed peacefully. It was a milestone for stability. The Secretary-General's December 2015 report recommended reducing the UN Operation in Côte d'Ivoire, UNOCI. Progress on reconciliation, justice, and economic recovery continued, though some fragility remained.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decides to decrease UNOCI's authorized military ceiling from 5,437 to 4,000 personnel by 31 March 2016. It recalls its request for a report by the same date with recommendations on the mission's future. The request was consistent with Resolution 2226 (2015). The Council says it intends to consider those recommendations promptly. It will do so in light of conditions on the ground.

Spain's last African colony won its freedom in October 1968. The small land on the Gulf of Guinea took the name Equatorial Guinea. Its bid for a UN seat moved fast. The bid papers were filed as S/8883. Resolution 260 passed with no dissent on 6 November 1968.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit the new republic. The Assembly did so days later. The state's first years were grim. A harsh ruler, Macias Nguema, seized power and drove out much of the skilled class. Oil wealth came far later. None of that was set in stone in 1968. The text records a hopeful first step: a small colony's end, and a new flag over the UN hall.

Cyprus in the summer of 1974 is the setting for Resolution 360, adopted on 16 August by eleven votes to none with three abstentions. A Greek-backed coup had triggered a Turkish military intervention, and a second wave of Turkish operations in mid-August sharply worsened the crisis. The Council had already passed five resolutions on the emergency that summer.

The Council put on record its formal disapproval of one-sided military action against the Republic of Cyprus. It pressed the parties to obey its earlier resolutions, including the call to withdraw foreign military personnel not present under international agreements, without delay. Talks under the earlier ceasefire resolution were to resume at once, and neither side was to let battlefield gains dictate their outcome.

Peace came to Rhodesia at the end of 1979, after talks at Lancaster House in London. The talks produced agreement on a constitution for a free and independent Zimbabwe. Genuine majority rule was part of the deal. Britain resumed its role as the ruling power for the transition. Resolution 460 was adopted on 21 December 1979.

The Council welcomed the end of fourteen years of rebellion. In light of the Lancaster House agreement, it acted on sanctions. Member states were called on to end the measures imposed on Southern Rhodesia since 1966. Those measures had been adopted under Chapter VII of the Charter. The sanctions committee created in 1968 was dissolved. The states that had enforced the sanctions were praised, above all the front-line states. The Council also called for urgent aid to rebuild the country, and for strict respect for the agreement.

Competing drafts for the Council's next step on Palestine were on the table in the autumn of 1948. The draft under discussion was the second revised draft in a Council document. Amendments and revisions had been suggested from several sides. Resolution 60 was adopted on 29 October 1948 to sort the drafts out.

The Council set up a sub-committee of five members. The United Kingdom, China, France, Belgium, and the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic sat on it. Its job was to consider every amendment and revision suggested to the draft. It also had to consult the Acting Mediator for Palestine. Together they would prepare a revised draft resolution for the Council to act on. The text is a working step inside the Council's own process, not a decision on Palestine itself.

Kuwait fell to Iraqi troops before dawn, and the Council answered the same day. On 2 August 1990, it adopted Resolution 660. Fourteen members voted yes and none voted no. Yemen took no part. The Council voiced alarm at the invasion. It found a breach of world peace and security.

Acting under the Charter, the text condemns the invasion in plain words. It demands that Iraq pull out at once, with no conditions. Iraqi forces must return to where they stood on 1 August. Both states are called to talks on their disputes. The Council backs Arab League efforts to that end. Iraq refused, and this text became the legal base for later steps.
virchow-cellular-pathology-chance-1860:
Rudolf Virchow gave twenty lectures in Berlin in 1858 that became Cellular Pathology. Frank Chance translated the German lectures into English in 1860. Virchow's famous rule, omnis cellula e cellula, holds that every cell comes from a cell. Disease, on his account, is disorder at the level of cells.

The lectures walk through sick tissues cell by cell, organ by organ. Fevers, tumors, and decay all get read as cellular events. His method tied the clinic to the microscope for good. The book founded cellular pathology as a discipline. Doctors learned to ask where, in which cells, illness sits. That question still guides medicine.
voltaire-candide-first-english-translati:
Voltaire's Candide reached English in this anonymous first translation of 1760, as Candidus; or, All for the Best. The London M. Cooper edition predates Smollett's famed version and includes a spurious contemporary Part II in print. Its haste shows the craze Candide caused the year after its French debut in 1759 across Europe.

Candide, taught that all is for the best, is kicked through war, earthquake, and the Inquisition. Pangloss's optimism survives hanging, dissection, and syphilis with its catchphrase absurdly intact at every disaster he meets. Eldorado, a Jesuit state, and a Venetian carnival crowd the picaresque tour of man's follies across continents. The close bids us cultivate our garden, a motto that outgrew the tale that bore it. This first English dress lets readers watch England meet Voltaire's wit at first hand.
